Payments Fundamentals (3)

Q1.What is a payment?Beginner

A payment is the transfer of value from one party to another in order to settle an obligation. When you buy a coffee, pay rent, send a salary, or settle a supplier invoice, you are making a payment. The obligation can come from a purchase, a loan, a tax, a salary agreement, or any commitment where one party owes value to another. The payment discharges that obligation, fully or partly, and creates a record that the debt has been reduced or cleared.

In a modern banking context, a payment almost always involves accounts held with regulated institutions and a set of instructions that tell those institutions what to move, from whom, to whom, and for what reason. The instructions travel as a payment message, while the actual value moves through accounts and settlement systems. A payment can be made in cash, by card, by cheque, by direct debit, or by an electronic transfer, but in every case the same core elements are present. There is a payer who owes, a payee who is owed, an amount, a currency, a value date, and a reason or reference that links the payment to the underlying business event.

Understanding payments this way helps you avoid a common mistake, which is to treat every money movement as the same thing. A salary payment, a supplier payment, a refund, and a loan repayment may look similar on a bank statement, but they carry different business meanings, different regulatory expectations, and different risks. Always ask what obligation is being settled, who bears the risk if the payment fails, and what evidence exists that the obligation was discharged. Those three questions shape how payment products are designed, how exceptions are handled, and how messages are structured.

Q2.What is a payment rail?Beginner

A payment rail is the infrastructure that carries a payment from one party to another. Think of it like a railway track. The train is the payment instruction, and the rail is the set of systems, rules, and connections that let the train reach its destination safely. A rail includes the network that moves the message, the clearing system that exchanges instructions between banks, the settlement system that moves value between banks, and the scheme rules that define cut off times, value dates, and liability when something goes wrong.

Common examples help make this concrete. In India, UPI, IMPS, NEFT, and RTGS are different rails with different speeds, limits, and settlement models. In the United States, Fedwire, ACH, and FedNow are separate rails. In Europe, SEPA Instant and TARGET2 serve different needs. Card rails are another family, where Visa and Mastercard networks carry authorisation and clearing messages between acquirers and issuers. SWIFT is not a rail in the settlement sense, because it carries messages, not value. It connects banks so they can instruct each other, but the value moves through correspondent accounts or settlement systems.

For a business analyst, the rail decides almost everything about the customer experience. It decides how fast the money arrives, how much the payment costs, what data can travel with it, what happens on a weekend or a holiday, and how failures and returns are handled. When you document a payment product, always name the rail, its settlement timing, its operating hours, its amount limits, and its message format. A payment that is technically correct but sent on the wrong rail can arrive late, cost too much, or fail reconciliation, and the customer will experience that as a failed payment.

Q3.What is the difference between a payment instruction and settlement? Why does the distinction matter in system design?Beginner

The payment instruction is the **pacs.008** or the **pain.001** that tells the bank to move money. Settlement is the actual movement of funds between banks that discharges the obligation. They are different events and they can happen at different times. When a customer submits a payment, the hub creates a pacs.008 and sends it through the clearing system. The clearing system processes it and returns a **pacs.002** with a status. When the status is ACSC, settlement has happened. Until then, the payment is only an instruction. The gap matters because a payment can be instructed but not settled, for example if the clearing house rejects it, or if the settlement account has insufficient funds. The bank must track both states separately. The **instruction status** tells the customer what happened to their request. The **settlement status** tells the bank whether the money actually moved. If you confuse the two, you tell a customer their payment is complete when the money has not moved yet. In the ledger, record the instruction time and the settlement time as separate timestamps. That is how you prove to an auditor exactly when each event happened.

Banking and Financial Infrastructure (3)

Q4.What is the difference between a branch, a subsidiary and an entity in payment routing?Advanced

These three words describe different legal structures, and they change how a payment moves. A branch is part of the same legal entity as the head office. A London bank with a branch in Singapore is one legal entity, so money moving between London and Singapore is an internal transfer, not a payment between two banks. A subsidiary is a separate legal entity owned by the parent bank. A UK bank with a subsidiary in India is two legal entities, so a payment between them is a real payment that must go through proper channels and be recorded as an intercompany transaction. An entity is the general word for a legal unit of the bank, and a large bank can have hundreds of entities across different countries. For payment routing, this matters because the hub must know whether the destination is internal, a subsidiary or an external bank. Internal moves are fast and cheap. Subsidiary moves need proper accounting and may need to go through a clearing system. External moves need a correspondent or a clearing system. A BA must understand this because the routing rules in the payment hub are built around the entity structure, and a wrong routing rule can send a payment down the wrong path.

Q5.What is a payment factory model and why do large banks use it?Intermediate

A payment factory is a model where a large bank centralises all payment processing into one shared service instead of letting each business unit run its own payments. In a bank like JP Morgan, the corporate banking team, the retail team and the private banking team all send their payment instructions to the same factory. The factory handles validation, routing, clearing and exceptions the same way for everyone. The benefit is scale and consistency. One team maintains the payment logic, one set of controls applies to all payments, and a change to a regulation is made once, not in five different systems. The factory also gives the bank a single view of all payment volumes, which helps treasury manage liquidity and helps risk manage exposure. The challenge is that different business units have different needs. A corporate client sending a large file of salary payments has different requirements from a retail customer making a single payment on a mobile app. The factory must handle both without slowing either down. The BA working in a payment factory has to balance these needs: standardise where possible, allow variation where the business genuinely needs it, and make sure the factory can cope with the combined volume.

Q6.How does a bank join a clearing system as a direct participant versus using an indirect clearer? What changes operationally?Intermediate

A **direct participant** connects to the clearing system itself, holds a **settlement account** at the central bank, and settles its own payments. The bank must meet the clearing system's technical, financial, and operational requirements, hold enough collateral, and staff an operations team that can manage the connection, the queue, and the settlement account through the day. The bank has full control over its payments, its cut-off management, and its liquidity.

An **indirect participant** uses a direct participant, called a clearer, to settle on its behalf. The bank sends its payments to the clearer, and the clearer settles them through its own central bank account. The bank does not need to meet the full clearing system requirements, and it does not need to manage a settlement account, but it depends on the clearer for timing and it pays the clearer a fee. Operationally, the indirect bank must still validate its payments and send them to the clearer before the clearer's cut-off, which is earlier than the clearing system's own cut-off. The bank also has less visibility, because it relies on the clearer to confirm settlement. Most smaller banks start as indirect participants and become direct when their payment volumes justify the cost and the control.

Payment Lifecycle (5)

Q7.What is straight-through processing and what breaks it?Beginner

Straight-through processing, or STP, means a payment goes from instruction to settlement without any human touching it. The instruction arrives, the system validates it, routes it, sends it to clearing and confirms settlement, all automatically. STP is the goal for large banks because it is fast, cheap and consistent. A bank like Standard Chartered aims for a high STP rate, often above 95 percent for standard payments. What breaks STP is anything that needs a human decision. A missing field, for example a beneficiary name that does not match the account, stops the payment. A sanctions hit stops it. A payment above a limit needs manual approval. A payment with an unusual pattern triggers a fraud review. A repair queue is where these payments sit until someone fixes them. The BA's job is to reduce the repair rate: improve validation at the front so bad instructions are caught early, improve data quality so fields are complete, and automate the common repairs so the operations team only handles the genuinely complex cases. Every percentage point of STP improvement saves the bank time and money, and gets payments to beneficiaries faster.

Q8.What is straight through processing, and how do you design a payment system to maximise it? What is a realistic STP rate?Advanced

Straight through processing means a payment goes from initiation to settlement without any manual touch. To design for it, you need four things. First, **complete data at initiation**. The channel must capture every mandatory field before the payment is accepted, so nothing is missing downstream. Second, **automated validation**. The hub checks the account, the balance, the sanctions lists and the message format without human help. Third, **clean routing rules**. The hub decides the clearing system, the settlement method and the charge option from static data, not from someone reading the payment. Fourth, **automated exception handling** for the common failures. If a payment is rejected for a missing field, the hub sends a clear message back to the channel instead of dropping it in a queue. The STP rate is measured as the percentage of payments that reach settlement without manual intervention. A good rate is above 95 percent. The remaining 5 percent are genuine exceptions: sanctions hits, insufficient funds, invalid beneficiary details. The goal is not 100 percent STP, because some payments genuinely need a human. The goal is to make sure the only payments that stop are the ones that should stop.

Q9.Walk me through a clean domestic credit transfer end to end, from the customer submitting the instruction to the beneficiary being credited. What does each stage look like when nothing goes wrong?Beginner

A clean domestic credit transfer has five stages, and in a good flow none of them needs a human hand. First the customer submits the instruction, usually from a mobile app or corporate channel, as a **pain.001** message. The bank validates it immediately, checking the account, the balance, the beneficiary details, and the sanctions lists, and answers with a **pain.002** acceptance. Second, the payment engine builds the interbank message, a **pacs.008** for a credit transfer, and routes it to the domestic clearing system. Third, the clearing system settles it, moving funds between the banks through their settlement accounts. Fourth, the beneficiary bank receives the **pacs.008**, credits the customer account, and sends back a **pacs.002** with ACSC status, which means settlement complete. Fifth, the customer sees the credit in their account and the sending bank receives a **camt.054** notification confirming the debit. The whole flow takes minutes, and every system agrees on the outcome. The signs of a healthy flow are a fast pain.002, no manual repair queue, an ACSC within the clearing window, and a camt.054 that matches the books exactly.

Q10.Explain straight through processing. How does a payment go from instruction to settlement with no manual touch, and what tells you the STP rate is healthy?Beginner

Straight through processing means a payment flows from initiation to settlement with no manual intervention. The customer submits the instruction through a channel, and the payment hub validates it automatically. The validation checks the account number format, the balance, the beneficiary details, and the sanctions lists, all in milliseconds. The hub enriches the payment, adding the routing details, the value date, and the settlement method from **static data**. It converts the instruction into the right interbank format, a **pacs.008** for a customer credit transfer, and sends it to the clearing system. The clearing system settles it and returns a **pacs.002** with ACSC status. The hub posts the accounting entries automatically, debits the customer, credits the settlement account, and sends the **camt.054** notification. The whole journey takes seconds to minutes. The signs of a healthy STP rate are a low repair queue, a high first-time-right percentage, and no manual touches on standard payments. When STP works well, operations staff only handle genuine exceptions, not routine payments that should have flowed through on their own.

Q11.A customer sends a payment and receives an ACSC confirmation within minutes. What does ACSC mean, and why does a fast confirmation matter?Beginner

A prompt ACSC confirmation means the payment settled, and it matters because it closes the loop for the customer. The sending bank sends the **pacs.008** to the clearing system. The clearing system settles it and the beneficiary bank credits the account. The beneficiary bank sends back a **pacs.002** with **ACSC status**, which means accepted, settled, and credited. The sending bank receives the ACSC, updates the payment status, and tells the customer the payment has arrived. The customer sees the confirmation in their app or receives a notification, and they can tell their supplier the money is there. The **camt.054** notification arrives with the debit, and the end-of-day **camt.053** confirms it. The whole chain from instruction to ACSC takes minutes for a domestic payment and hours for a cross-border one, depending on the corridor. What makes it clean is the **speed of the confirmation**. A customer who gets an ACSC within minutes knows the payment worked. A customer who waits a day for confirmation will call to ask. Fast confirmation is not a luxury, it is part of the product.

Domestic Payment Systems (15)

Q12.What is Fedwire?Beginner

Fedwire is the United States real time gross settlement system operated by the Federal Reserve. It is the system through which banks settle large value payments in central bank money, one transaction at a time, with immediate finality. When a bank sends a payment through Fedwire, the Federal Reserve debits the sending bank master account and credits the receiving bank master account, and the payment is final at that moment. There is no netting and no waiting for an end of day batch.

Fedwire is used for high value and time critical payments: interbank transfers, settlement of securities transactions, corporate treasury payments, and large customer payments where certainty matters. It operates during Federal Reserve business hours, which is a key difference from instant payment systems that run around the clock. Each payment is processed individually, and banks must have sufficient funds or intraday credit in their master account for the payment to settle. The system carries rich payment information, and it has been migrating to the ISO 20022 message format, aligning it with the global standard.

The name Fedwire is sometimes confused with FedNow, but the two are different tools. Fedwire is the wholesale, high value, gross settlement system that has underpinned the US financial system for decades. FedNow is the newer retail instant payment service for smaller, round the clock payments. A corporate treasurer sending a multi million dollar settlement would use Fedwire; a customer paying a supplier on a Sunday would use FedNow. Understanding which one applies is a basic test of US payments knowledge.

Q13.What is CHIPS?Beginner

CHIPS, the Clearing House Interbank Payments System, is a private sector US payment system operated by The Clearing House, and it is the main system for large value US dollar payments. It is used heavily for international payments: when a bank outside the US sends dollars to a bank inside the US, the payment very often clears through CHIPS. It also handles domestic large value transfers between US banks. CHIPS is a net settlement system, which is its defining difference from Fedwire.

In CHIPS, payments are not settled one by one in central bank money as they arrive. Instead, they are queued, offset against each other where possible, and settled on a net basis through a prefunded account at the Federal Reserve. This netting is efficient: it lets banks settle a large volume of payments with less liquidity than gross settlement would require. The system runs during US business hours, and at the end of the day the net positions are settled finally. Banks that use CHIPS must prefund their positions and manage their liquidity carefully, because a payment only releases when the netting and funding allow it.

CHIPS and Fedwire together form the backbone of US dollar clearing. Fedwire is the Federal Reserve operated gross settlement system; CHIPS is the private sector net settlement system. For cross border payments, the choice matters: a dollar payment routed through CHIPS will follow CHIPS rules, cut off times and liquidity arrangements, and the beneficiary bank will see it as a CHIPS payment. Anyone working in US dollar correspondent banking needs to know both systems, how they differ, and why a payment might be routed through one rather than the other.

Q14.What is Faster Payments (UK)?Beginner

Faster Payments is the United Kingdom real time payment system, launched in 2008 and operated by Pay.UK. It lets people and businesses send sterling payments between UK bank accounts in seconds, 24 hours a day, 365 days a year. It is the system behind most everyday instant payments in the UK: paying a friend, paying a bill, or a business paying a supplier. When you make an instant transfer from your UK banking app, it is almost certainly travelling over Faster Payments.

The system works through participating banks and payment service providers. The payer bank sends the payment instruction, the system validates and routes it, the beneficiary bank credits the account and confirms, and the payer sees the result within seconds. Settlement between banks happens on a net basis across the day through their accounts at the Bank of England, with several settlement cycles. The transaction limit is high enough to cover most retail and small business payments, and it has been raised over time; very large payments still go through CHAPS instead.

Faster Payments matters because it was one of the first national instant payment systems in the world, and it proved that real time retail payments could work at national scale. It changed customer expectations in the UK: standing orders, one off transfers and business payments that once took days now arrive in seconds. For learners, the key facts are its age, its operator Pay.UK, its 24 hour availability, and its role as the retail instant system sitting alongside CHAPS for high value and Bacs for bulk scheduled payments.

Q15.What is CHAPS?Beginner

CHAPS, the Clearing House Automated Payment System, is the United Kingdom high value payment system, operated by the Bank of England. It is the UK equivalent of Fedwire: a real time gross settlement system in which each payment is settled individually and immediately in central bank money, with finality at the moment of settlement. It is used for payments where value, certainty and timing matter most, such as house purchases, large corporate payments, and settlement between financial institutions.

A CHAPS payment is typically high value, and there is no upper limit in principle, although banks set their own limits and charges. The payer bank sends the instruction, the Bank of England debits the payer bank settlement account and credits the beneficiary bank settlement account, and the beneficiary bank credits its customer. The payment is irrevocable once settled. CHAPS operates during Bank of England business hours on working days, which is why a house completion payment is scheduled for a weekday and why same day CHAPS payments have a cut off time.

CHAPS is the system behind the moments that matter most in UK finance. When someone buys a house, the solicitor sends the purchase funds by CHAPS so the seller receives them with certainty on completion day. When a bank settles a large obligation with another bank, it uses CHAPS. The system migrated to ISO 20022 message formats, aligning it with the global standard. The contrast with Faster Payments is the point to remember: Faster Payments is the instant retail system for everyday payments, CHAPS is the gross settlement system for high value payments where finality in central bank money is non negotiable.

Q16.What is RTGS?Beginner

RTGS stands for Real Time Gross Settlement. It is a system in which each payment is settled individually, in real time, in central bank money, as soon as it is submitted and validated. There is no batching and no netting: every payment is processed on its own, and the funds move from the sending bank's account at the central bank to the receiving bank's account immediately.

The word gross is important. It means each payment is settled for its full value, not netted against other payments. If a bank sends ten payments of 10 lakh rupees each, RTGS settles ten separate transfers of 10 lakh rupees. That is different from a net settlement system, where those payments would be offset against incoming payments and only the net difference would move.

RTGS is used for high value payments because it eliminates settlement risk. Once a payment is settled in RTGS, it is final and irrevocable. The receiving bank can credit its customer with complete confidence that the money is there. In India, RTGS has a minimum of 2 lakh rupees per transaction and no maximum limit, and it is operated by the Reserve Bank of India.

The trade off is liquidity. Because each payment settles gross, banks need enough funds in their central bank account to cover each payment as it arrives. Central banks help by providing intraday liquidity, but banks must still manage their balances carefully throughout the day. RTGS is therefore the system of choice where finality and safety matter more than liquidity efficiency.

Q17.What is RTGS in India and what is the minimum amount?Beginner

RTGS, the Real Time Gross Settlement system, is India's high value payment system operated by the Reserve Bank of India. It settles each transaction individually and in real time, rather than netting transactions together in a batch. The word gross means each payment is settled for its full amount, one by one, in central bank money. RTGS is designed for large value, time critical payments such as interbank transfers, government securities settlements, and large corporate payments. The minimum amount for an RTGS transaction is 2 lakh rupees. There is no maximum amount, so transactions worth crores of rupees can be settled through RTGS. RTGS operates 24 hours a day, 7 days a week, including holidays, since December 2020. Before that, it operated only during banking hours. A customer initiates an RTGS payment through internet banking or a branch, providing the payee account number, IFSC, amount, and purpose. The payer bank debits the customer and sends the instruction to the Reserve Bank of India, which debits the payer bank settlement account and credits the payee bank settlement account immediately. The payee bank then credits the payee account. Because settlement is final and irrevocable once processed, RTGS is used where certainty and immediacy matter most. Fees are typically higher than NEFT or UPI, reflecting the high value and real time nature of the service.

Q18.A corporate client needs to send a £250,000 payment to a supplier in the UK today. How do you decide between CHAPS and Faster Payments, and what happens step by step once you choose?Intermediate

The first check is the amount and the value date. **Faster Payments** has a per-transaction limit that varies by bank, usually around £250,000 to £1 million, and it settles in seconds. **CHAPS** has no upper limit and settles in central bank money on the same day, but it costs more and runs to a cut-off, usually around 5 PM. For £250,000 the bank checks its own Faster Payments limit first. If the payment fits, Faster Payments is the default because it is cheaper and instant for the customer. If it exceeds the limit, or the client needs the certainty of central bank settlement, the bank uses CHAPS.

Once the route is chosen, the **payment hub** builds the instruction and sends it to the clearing system. For CHAPS, the hub sends the payment to the **Bank of England RTGS** system, where it settles gross in real time across the bank's central bank account. The hub waits for the settlement confirmation and updates the payment status to settled. For Faster Payments, the hub sends the instruction to the **Faster Payments central infrastructure**, the beneficiary bank credits the customer within seconds, and settlement between banks happens later through deferred net settlement. The bank then sends a confirmation to the client through the channel. The choice is driven by amount, cost, cut-off, and the settlement certainty the client needs.

Q19.A corporate client submits a payment at 4:45 PM for same-day settlement through CHAPS. The CHAPS cut-off is 5 PM. Walk me through what happens if the payment misses the cut-off.Intermediate

The cut-off is a hard deadline set by the clearing system, not by the bank. If the instruction reaches the **Bank of England RTGS** after the cut-off, it is rejected for same-day settlement. The bank cannot force it through. The first thing the **payment hub** does is check the status. If the payment was submitted before the cut-off but is still being processed, the hub tries to release it in time. If it misses, the payment is not lost, but the value date moves to the next working day.

The bank then has three jobs. First, update the payment status in the hub and the channel so the client can see the new value date. Second, tell the client proactively, because a missed value date can break a supplier contract or a property completion. Third, decide with the client whether to hold the payment for the next window or cancel it. If the payment is time-critical, the bank may offer an alternative route, such as **Faster Payments**, if the amount fits. The lesson for the business is that cut-off management is a control, not an inconvenience. The bank should warn the client when a payment is submitted close to the cut-off, and the hub should prioritise near-cut-off payments in its queue.

Q20.How does Faster Payments settle between banks if the customer sees the money instantly? Explain the deferred net settlement behind it.Beginner

The customer experience and the bank-to-bank settlement are two different things. When a customer sends a **Faster Payment**, the beneficiary bank credits the customer within seconds. That is the customer leg, and it is instant. But the banks do not settle with each other at that moment. Instead, Faster Payments uses **deferred net settlement**. Each bank's payments are recorded through the day, and at set times, usually three times a day, the central system nets all the payments between each pair of banks and settles only the net amount.

This means the beneficiary bank is taking a risk. It has credited its customer before it has received the funds from the sending bank. The risk is managed in two ways. First, each bank must hold collateral and prefund a settlement account, so there is money available to settle the net positions. Second, the netting cycles are frequent enough that the exposure never grows too large. If a bank fails to fund its net position at a settlement cycle, the central system can suspend it, and other banks stop accepting its payments. The key point for an interview is that instant for the customer does not mean instant between banks, and the deferred net settlement model is what makes Faster Payments possible without every bank holding huge central bank balances.

Q21.A Fedwire payment is sent in the US. How does Fedwire settle, and how is it different from CHIPS?Beginner

**Fedwire** is the **Federal Reserve's** real-time gross settlement system. Each payment settles individually, in central bank money, the moment it is sent. The sending bank's **Federal Reserve account** is debited and the receiving bank's account is credited immediately. There is no netting and no delay. Fedwire is used for high-value, time-critical payments, and it is final the moment it settles. If the sending bank does not have enough balance, the payment queues, and the bank can use the Federal Reserve's intraday credit facility.

**CHIPS** is different. It is a private-sector clearing house run by **The Clearing House**. CHIPS uses a hybrid model. Payments are queued and settled through a combination of real-time settlement and multilateral netting. Banks prefund a CHIPS account, and the system releases payments when the netting allows it. CHIPS is mainly used for US dollar payments, especially cross-border dollars, because it is efficient for high volumes. The key difference is that Fedwire settles in central bank money with immediate finality, while CHIPS settles through a prefunded account with netting, which is cheaper but carries a small delay. A bank chooses Fedwire when it needs certainty and finality, and CHIPS when it needs efficiency for large dollar volumes.

Q22.The bank sends a payment through CHIPS for a US dollar payment. How does CHIPS net settlement work, and what happens if a bank fails to fund its position?Intermediate

**CHIPS** settles US dollar payments through a combination of real-time settlement and multilateral netting. Each participating bank prefunds a **CHIPS account** at the start of the day. When a bank sends a payment, CHIPS checks whether the payment can settle immediately from the prefunded balance, or whether it should wait in the queue until incoming payments from other banks create enough offset. The system continuously looks for groups of queued payments that can be settled together by netting them, so each bank only funds the net amount, not the gross.

If a bank fails to fund its net position, the system cannot settle its outgoing payments. CHIPS will hold those payments in the queue and try again as more funds arrive. If the shortfall persists, the bank must add funds to its CHIPS account, either by moving dollars from its **Federal Reserve account** or by borrowing. In the extreme case, CHIPS can suspend the bank, and other banks stop sending it payments. The bank's treasury monitors its CHIPS position through the day, because a shortfall in CHIPS blocks dollar payments across all its clients at once.

Q23.Walk through a clean Faster Payments transfer in the UK. How does a payment move from one bank account to another in seconds?Beginner

Faster Payments works because it is built for speed. The customer sends a payment from their mobile app, and the sending bank validates it in real time, checking the sort code, the account number, and the balance. The bank sends the payment to the **Faster Payments** central infrastructure, which routes it to the beneficiary bank in seconds. The beneficiary bank credits the customer account almost immediately and sends back a confirmation. The whole flow takes seconds, not hours. The limits are clear, a maximum amount per payment and a maximum per day, and the bank tells the customer these limits upfront. The payment is **irrevocable** once sent, so the customer must check the details before confirming. The sending bank receives a confirmation that the payment was accepted, and the end-of-day statement shows the debit. What makes it clean is the real-time design. There is no batch, no overnight wait, and no clearing cycle. The payment moves directly from one bank to another through the central hub, and both banks update their customer accounts within seconds. For a customer paying a bill or sending money to a friend, this is the experience they expect, and the system delivers it reliably.

Q24.Walk through a clean CHAPS payment. How does a high-value same-day payment settle through the Bank of England?Intermediate

CHAPS is the UK high-value same-day system, and it works because settlement is real time and final. The corporate customer submits the instruction before the CHAPS **cut-off**, usually through a corporate channel. The bank validates it, runs sanctions screening, and applies the **four-eyes approval** for high-value amounts. The payment hub sends the **pacs.008** to the Bank of England, which operates CHAPS. The Bank of England moves the funds between the banks settlement accounts immediately, and the payment is **final and irrevocable** the moment it settles. The beneficiary bank receives the payment, credits the customer account the same day, and sends back a **pacs.002** with ACSC status. The customer gets confirmation the same day, and the end-of-day **camt.053** shows the debit. Treasury watches the settlement account balance throughout the day, because CHAPS payments are large and the bank must have enough liquidity. The cut-off matters. A payment submitted after the cut-off settles the next business day, and the customer must be told. CHAPS is clean because it is simple, one instruction, one settlement, one confirmation, all on the same day.

Q25.Walk through a clean Fedwire payment in the US. How does a high-value USD payment settle in real time through the Federal Reserve?Intermediate

Fedwire is the US high-value real-time system, and it works because the Federal Reserve settles each payment individually and immediately. The customer submits the instruction, and the bank validates it, checking the **ABA routing number**, the account, the balance, and the sanctions lists. The bank sends the payment to the **Federal Reserve**, which debits the sending bank's reserve account and credits the receiving bank's reserve account in real time. The payment is final the moment the Fed processes it. The beneficiary bank receives the payment, credits the customer account, and the customer sees the funds the same day. The sending bank gets a confirmation, and the end-of-day statement shows the debit. For a cross-border payment, the US leg works the same way. A payment from overseas arrives at a US correspondent bank through SWIFT, and the correspondent sends it onward through **Fedwire** for final USD settlement. The key point is that Fedwire settlement is **central bank money**, the safest form of settlement, because the Federal Reserve itself moves the funds. That is why high-value USD payments use Fedwire, and why it is trusted for the largest transactions in the world.

Q26.Walk through a clean direct debit collection, from the mandate to the debit to the biller being credited. How does the scheme protect the customer?Intermediate

A clean direct debit starts with a **mandate**. The customer authorises the biller to collect payments from their account, and the mandate is stored by the bank. On the collection date, the biller sends the collection instruction to their bank. The biller bank sends a **pain.008** to the debtor bank, carrying the mandate reference, the amount, and the collection date. The debtor bank checks the mandate, checks the balance, and debits the customer account. The funds move to the biller bank, which credits the biller account. The customer sees the debit in their statement, and the biller sees the credit. If the customer disputes the collection, they can request a **refund** within the scheme rules, and the bank processes it through a pacs.004 return. The scheme gives the customer strong protection, because a direct debit can be reversed if it was taken in error. What makes it clean is the **mandate**. The customer authorised the collection in advance, the amount and date are known, and both sides can reconcile against the mandate reference. A direct debit that works well is invisible to the customer, because the money simply moves on the agreed date.

Cross-Border Payments (6)

Q27.What is a nostro FX conversion?Intermediate

A nostro FX conversion is a currency conversion that a bank performs using the funds held in its own nostro account, rather than buying the currency in the market at the moment of the payment. For example, if BNP Paribas holds US dollars in its nostro account with Wells Fargo, and it needs to pay USD 367,574.90 to Banco Santander, it can use the dollars already in the account, with no FX trade needed. If instead it holds only euros in Paris and needs to pay dollars, it must sell euros and buy dollars, and that trade is settled by delivering dollars into the Wells Fargo nostro account. The conversion rate is the rate agreed for that trade, and the dollars are then available for the payment. Nostro FX conversions are managed by the treasury team, which watches the balance in each currency and decides when to buy or sell. If the dollar balance is too high, the team may sell dollars and buy euros to bring the balance back to target. If the balance is too low, the team buys dollars in advance. The conversion can be a spot trade for immediate needs, or a forward trade for a known future payment. The cost of the conversion is the FX spread plus any dealing charges, and it is separate from the payment charges deducted by the correspondents. Good nostro FX management means the bank always has the right currency in the right account at the right time, without holding large idle balances that earn little or no interest.

Read the full chapter →
Q28.A payment starts at a branch in London and ends at a beneficiary in Singapore. Walk me through the hops inside the bank.Expert

The customer gives the instruction at the branch, and the branch system sends it to the payment hub. The hub validates the instruction, checks the account balance and screens it for sanctions. Next the hub decides the route. For Singapore the payment will usually go through the bank's own network if it has a Singapore entity, or through a correspondent bank. The hub creates an ISO 20022 message, a pacs.008, and sends it to the Singapore entity or the correspondent. If the bank has its own Singapore branch, the payment moves internally. The London hub debits the customer's account, and the Singapore entity credits the beneficiary. The two entities settle between themselves through their internal accounts. If a correspondent is used, the payment goes over SWIFT to the correspondent bank, which then pays the beneficiary through the local clearing system in Singapore. At each hop the bank checks for a response. The pacs.002 status report confirms whether the payment was accepted or rejected. The hub tracks the payment by its UETR, so operations can see exactly where it is at any moment. The whole journey takes minutes to hours depending on the route and the cut off times.

Q29.A company in India pays a supplier in Germany 250,000 euro through a pain.001. The sending bank transmits the pacs.008, but the beneficiary bank flags a name mismatch and the funds sit uncredited for three days. How do you resolve it?Advanced

I read the **pacs.002** first. A status of Pending means the beneficiary bank is holding the payment, not rejecting it. That distinction matters, because a held payment can still be credited once the issue is resolved. I raise a **camt.029 investigation query** to get the exact mismatch detail from the beneficiary bank, because I need to know precisely which part of the name differs. Then I work the exception with the intermediary and the beneficiary bank, confirming the correct beneficiary name with the sender. If the name is **corrected and verified**, the bank applies the funds to the account and the payment completes. If it cannot be resolved, the payment comes back through a **pacs.004**. Throughout the three days I keep the corporate customer informed, because days of silence are what create escalations. A customer who knows what is happening will wait. A customer who hears nothing will escalate. Prevention matters too. I validate **beneficiary details at initiation**, including confirmation of payee where the corridor supports it, so a name mismatch is caught before the payment leaves, not three days later at the beneficiary bank.

Read the full chapter →
Q30.A cross border payment was processed with the wrong FX rate. The customer received less than they should have. How do you investigate and fix it?Advanced

The first step is to find the **source of truth** for the FX rate. In a bank, the treasury system publishes rates, and the payment hub must use the same rate the customer was quoted. If the hub used a different rate, the customer was overcharged or undercharged. Check the **rate timestamp** on the payment record and compare it against the treasury rate at that moment. Then check the **rate type**. A customer rate includes a margin, a wholesale rate does not, and mixing them up is a common error. Next, check the **currency pair direction**. EUR to USD is not the same as USD to EUR, and inverting the pair is a classic mapping bug. Also check whether the payment went through an **intermediary currency**. Some corridors convert EUR to USD to INR, and each leg applies its own rate. If the hub only applied one leg, the amount is wrong. Once you find the cause, correct the rate logic and then calculate the **financial impact** for every affected payment. The bank may need to compensate customers who were underpaid. Document the incident, fix the mapping, and add a **rate validation check** that compares the applied rate against the treasury rate within a tolerance before the payment is released.

Read the full chapter →
Q31.Walk me through a clean cross-border payment end to end, from the corporate customer instruction to the beneficiary credit. How do the instruction and the money move together?Beginner

A clean cross-border payment has two parallel tracks, the instruction track and the money track, and both must complete for the payment to land. The corporate customer sends a **pain.001** to their bank. The bank validates it, checks sanctions, checks the balance, and sends a **pain.002** acceptance. The bank then sends a **pacs.008** instruction to the beneficiary bank, carrying the full customer and remittance details. At the same time, the funds move through the correspondent chain. If the cover method is used, a **pacs.009** with settlement method COVE moves the money between correspondents through their **Nostro accounts**. Each hop sends back a **pacs.002** status, ACTC when accepted, ACSP when processing, and ACSC when settled. The beneficiary bank receives both the instruction and the cover, reconciles them using the shared **UETR**, and credits the beneficiary account. The beneficiary gets the funds on the promised value date, the sender gets an ACSC confirmation, and the **camt.053** statement at end of day shows the debit exactly as expected. When everything works, the customer never calls, because the payment simply arrives on time.

Read the full chapter →
Q32.Walk through a clean FX conversion on a cross-border payment. How does the rate get locked and the beneficiary receive exactly the quoted amount?Beginner

A clean FX conversion starts with the **rate being locked** at the moment the customer confirms the payment. The customer sees the rate, the amount in the source currency, and the amount in the target currency, and agrees. The bank executes the FX trade immediately, buying the target currency at the locked rate. The payment hub then sends the **pacs.008** in the target currency to the beneficiary bank. The beneficiary bank credits the account in the target currency, and the customer receives exactly the amount that was quoted. The bank sends a **pacs.002** with ACSC status, and the end-of-day **camt.053** shows the debit in the source currency and the FX trade. The keys to making it clean are a **transparent rate**, so the customer knows what they are getting, a **locked rate**, so the amount does not change between confirmation and settlement, and a **clear breakdown** of any charges, so the customer can see the rate and the fees separately. If the rate is not locked, the customer gets a surprise, and a surprise on an FX payment is a complaint waiting to happen. A clean FX payment is one where the amount credited matches the amount quoted, to the penny.

SWIFT and Correspondent Banking (17)

Q33.What is SWIFT?Beginner

SWIFT is the Society for Worldwide Interbank Financial Telecommunication. It is a global messaging network used by banks and financial institutions to send secure instructions and information to each other. When a bank in India needs to tell a bank in the United Kingdom to pay a beneficiary, it often sends that instruction over SWIFT. More than 11,000 institutions in over 200 countries are connected, and they exchange millions of messages every day, covering customer payments, bank to bank transfers, trade finance, securities, and treasury operations.

The most important fact about SWIFT, and the one beginners most often get wrong, is that SWIFT is a messaging system, not a payment system. It carries instructions, not money. It holds no accounts and it settles nothing. When a bank sends an MT103 payment instruction over SWIFT, the actual value moves separately, through correspondent accounts that banks hold with each other, or through a settlement system. SWIFT also provides a common language for those instructions, standard message types such as MT103, MT202, and MT940, so that a bank in any country can read a message sent by a bank in any other country.

SWIFT also provides services beyond messaging. It assigns BIC codes that identify institutions, it provides the gpi tracker that lets banks and customers follow a cross border payment, and it supports the migration to ISO 20022 messages. It sets security standards that members must follow, and it helps members screen messages and investigate failures. For a learner, the practical lesson is to treat SWIFT as the postal service of international banking: it delivers the letter reliably and securely, but it does not move the money inside the envelope. The money moves through banking accounts and settlement systems.

Read the full chapter →
Q34.What is SWIFT gpi?Beginner

SWIFT gpi is the Global Payments Innovation initiative, a service that makes cross border payments faster, more transparent, and more traceable. Before gpi, a cross border payment could take several days, the customer had no idea where the money was, and the final amount was uncertain because each intermediary could deduct charges without warning. Gpi was built to fix those three problems by setting service level rules for member banks, requiring same day processing, end to end tracking, and transparency on fees and foreign exchange.

The core of gpi is the tracker. Every gpi payment carries a Unique End to End Transaction Reference, known as the UETR, which stays with the payment from the debtor agent to the creditor agent. Each bank in the chain confirms when it received the payment, what charges it deducted, and when it forwarded the payment, and those confirmations feed the tracker. The debtor bank, and often the customer, can see the payment status in real time: whether it is with the debtor agent, an intermediary, or the creditor agent, whether it has been credited, and what fees were taken at each step. That visibility changes the customer experience from waiting in the dark to watching the payment move.

Member banks commit to processing gpi payments on the same day, to passing on remittance information unaltered, and to disclosing charges and exchange rates. For a business analyst, the practical question is always whether a given payment is gpi enabled, whether it carries a UETR, and whether each bank in the chain is a gpi member. If the answer is yes, tracking and investigation become much faster. If the answer is no, the investigation falls back to manual messages and phone calls.

Read the full chapter →
Q35.What is a nostro account?Beginner

A nostro account is an account that a bank holds with a foreign bank, in the foreign bank's currency. The word nostro is Latin for ours, and it is used from the perspective of the bank that owns the account. So if an Indian bank holds a US dollar account with a bank in New York, the Indian bank calls that account its nostro account.

The purpose of a nostro account is to make payments in that foreign currency. When the Indian bank's customer pays a supplier in the United States, the Indian bank instructs its New York correspondent to debit its nostro account and pay the beneficiary. The nostro account is prefunded, meaning the Indian bank keeps a balance there so payments can go out immediately without waiting for funds to arrive.

Managing nostro accounts is a real operational task. A bank must forecast how much it will need in each currency, keep enough balance to cover outgoing payments, and avoid leaving too much idle cash earning little or no interest. Too little and payments get delayed or rejected; too much and capital is tied up unnecessarily.

The same account is called a vostro account by the bank that holds it, which is simply the other side of the same relationship. Nostro and vostro are two names for one account, seen from opposite sides.

Q36.What is a payment versus a cover in correspondent banking?Intermediate

The serial and cover methods below are shown in their pre-migration MT form, because that form shows each method most clearly. Since coexistence ended on 22 November 2025, the same payment travels as a pacs.008 in serial, and as a pacs.008 plus a pacs.009 COV in cover. In correspondent banking, the payment and the cover are two different messages that together move money across borders, and the distinction matters most in the serial and cover methods. The payment message, usually an MT103, carries the full payment details to the beneficiary bank, including the debtor, the creditor, the amount, and the remittance information. The cover message, usually an MT202 COV, carries only the settlement instruction between banks, telling the correspondent how to move the funds to cover the payment. In the serial method, used mainly in the United States, a single MT103 travels from bank to bank in a chain, and each bank passes it on and settles with the next. In the cover method, used mainly in Europe, the MT103 goes directly to the beneficiary bank, while a separate MT202 COV moves the funds through the correspondent chain. The announcement, the MT103, usually arrives before the cover, so the beneficiary bank knows the payment is coming before the money arrives. Take the worked example. BNP Paribas Paris sends USD 367,574.90 to Banco Santander in Madrid. Under the cover method, Santander receives the MT103 directly, while the funds move from BNP Paribas through Wells Fargo, BIC PNBPUS3N, and then through Bank of New York Mellon, BIC IRVTUS3N, which holds the account for Santander, BIC BSCHESMM, before Santander credits its customer. The cover must carry enough information for sanctions screening, which is why the MT202 COV includes the underlying payment details.

Q37.What is a nostro fee?Intermediate

A nostro fee is any charge a correspondent bank levies for holding and operating a nostro account on behalf of another bank. The most common nostro fees are a monthly account maintenance fee, a per transaction fee for each payment or receipt processed through the account, a fee for statements and reporting, and a fee for investigations or repairs. The correspondent may also charge for liquidity services, such as an overdraft facility, and for FX conversion when it converts funds in the account. Nostro fees are set out in the account tariff agreed when the account is opened, and they are usually billed monthly. The account holder can pay the invoice by a separate payment, or authorise the correspondent to debit the nostro account directly. In practice, many nostro fees are small in isolation, for example USD 20 for processing a single payment, but they add up across thousands of payments a year, and they are one reason banks try to reduce the number of nostro accounts they hold. In the worked example, the USD 20 charged by Wells Fargo and the USD 22 charged by Bank of New York Mellon on the USD 367,574.90 payment are examples of nostro related transaction charges, deducted as the payment passed through each correspondent. Banks track these fees closely, because they feed directly into the total cost of a cross border payment and into the price charged to the end customer.

Read the full chapter →
Q38.What is SWIFT gpi in detail?Intermediate

SWIFT gpi, or Global Payments Innovation, is a service launched by SWIFT in 2017 to make cross border payments faster, more transparent, and easier to track. Before gpi, a sender had no way to know where a payment was, how much had been deducted, or when it would arrive. Gpi changes that by giving every payment a unique end to end transaction reference, the UETR, and by requiring every gpi bank in the chain to confirm receipt, to confirm credit, and to report any charges deducted. The payment is tracked from the sender bank to the beneficiary bank, and the sender can see each step, including the time each bank received the payment and the amount it passed on. Gpi also sets service level agreements, so banks must confirm credit within a set time, and it provides a case resolution service for problems. By 2024, most large banks had joined gpi, and more than half of all SWIFT cross border payments were gpi payments. Gpi does not move money itself. It runs on top of the existing correspondent banking network, using the same nostro accounts and the same settlement systems. What it adds is a tracking layer, a set of rules, and a shared data standard. A gpi payment therefore still passes through correspondents such as Wells Fargo and Bank of New York Mellon, but the sender can now see that it did, and how much each bank charged.

Read the full chapter →
Q39.What is gpi Case Resolution?Expert

Gpi Case Resolution is the SWIFT gpi service that helps banks solve problems with a gpi payment quickly, by giving them a shared case file linked to the payment UETR. When a payment is delayed, missing, or incorrect, the sender bank can open a case in the gpi Tracker, and it can send a message to the bank that currently holds the payment, asking for an update. The receiving bank must respond within the gpi SLA, and all messages in the case are stored in one place, so no one has to search through emails or phone notes. The case can cover many issues, including a payment that has not been credited, a wrong amount, a missing beneficiary, or a request for a refund. Case Resolution replaces the old MT195 and MT196 investigation messages for gpi payments, although banks can still use those messages for non gpi payments. The advantage is speed and clarity. Because the case is linked to the UETR, every bank in the chain can see the same information, and the sender bank can tell its customer what is happening without waiting for a reply to an email. Cases are closed when the problem is solved, for example when the payment is credited or returned, and the closure is recorded in the Tracker. Banks are expected to use Case Resolution for gpi payments, and SWIFT monitors how quickly they respond, as part of the gpi Observer. For customers, Case Resolution means a problem is less likely to sit unanswered for days.

Q40.What is a nostro account and how does a bank use it day to day?Beginner

A nostro account is an account a bank holds with another bank in a foreign currency. For example, a UK bank like Standard Chartered holds a US dollar nostro account with a bank in New York. When the UK bank needs to pay US dollars to a beneficiary, it instructs its nostro agent in New York to pay from that account. The nostro account is funded in advance, so the bank has to predict how much it will need each day. Treasury manages this. Every morning treasury looks at the expected payment volumes, the balance in each nostro account and the funding needed. During the day, payments draw the balance down. If the balance runs low, treasury tops it up by buying dollars or moving funds. At end of day the bank reconciles the nostro account against its own ledger. Any difference is an exception that must be investigated. The nostro account is critical because without it the bank cannot make payments in that currency. If the nostro is empty, payments queue or fail. That is why treasury and payments operations talk to each other constantly during the day, especially on high volume days.

Q41.How do correspondent banks work together on a cross-border payment?Intermediate

A cross-border payment usually passes through more than one bank because no single bank has a presence in every country. The sending bank, for example a UK bank, sends the payment to its correspondent bank in the destination country. The correspondent is a bank that has agreed to process payments on behalf of the sending bank. The sending bank holds a nostro account with the correspondent, and the correspondent debits that account when it pays the beneficiary. If the beneficiary's bank is different from the correspondent, the payment hops again to the beneficiary's bank through the local clearing system. Each bank in the chain checks the payment, screens it and takes its fee if the charge option allows it. The payment message, usually a pacs.008, travels with the payment and carries the instructions and references. The UETR lets every bank in the chain track the same payment. The challenge is that each bank has its own cut off times, its own fees and its own rules. A payment can be delayed at any hop, and the sending bank may not know where it is stuck without asking. That is why banks choose their correspondents carefully and monitor their performance.

Q42.A payment is sent through SWIFT to a correspondent bank. Explain the difference between the cover method and the serial method, and when you would use each.Advanced

In the **serial method**, the payment instruction travels from bank to bank along the whole chain. Each bank in the chain receives the **MT103** or **pacs.008**, checks it, and passes it to the next bank, until it reaches the beneficiary bank. The funds move with the instruction at each hop. This works well when the banks in the chain have direct relationships and the payment is straightforward.

In the **cover method**, the instruction and the funds travel separately. The ordering bank sends the payment instruction directly to the beneficiary bank, usually as an **MT103** or **pacs.008**, and separately sends a **cover payment**, an **MT202** or **pacs.009**, through the correspondent chain to fund it. The beneficiary bank credits the customer when it receives the instruction, and the cover settles the funds behind it. The cover method is used when the ordering bank has no direct relationship with the beneficiary bank, or when the payment needs to travel fast and the funding can follow. The risk is that the cover and the instruction can arrive at different times, so the bank must reconcile them carefully. If the cover is late, the beneficiary bank has credited a customer it has not yet been funded for.

Read the full chapter →
Q43.Your bank uses SWIFT gpi. How does the gpi tracker know where a payment is, and what does the bank do when the tracker shows the payment stuck at an intermediary?Intermediate

**SWIFT gpi** gives the bank a tracker that shows where a payment is at each step. Every bank in the chain updates the tracker when it receives and forwards the payment, and the tracker shows the status, the fees deducted, and the time at each hop. When the tracker shows the payment stuck at an intermediary, the first step is to check the **UETR** and confirm the payment is genuinely stuck, not just slow. Some intermediaries take longer, especially if they run batch processing.

If the payment is genuinely stuck, the bank contacts the intermediary directly, usually through a **SWIFT** message or a phone call to their operations team, and asks for the status. The bank also checks whether the payment failed a compliance screen at the intermediary, which is a common reason for a hold. The bank then tells the customer what is happening and gives a revised estimate. If the intermediary cannot release the payment, the bank may need to recall it with a **camt.056** and resend it through a different route. The key point is that gpi gives the bank visibility it never had before, but visibility alone does not move the payment. Someone still has to pick up the phone and chase the bank holding it.

Read the full chapter →
Q44.A payment used the cover method. The pacs.008 instruction and the pacs.009 cover have both settled, and now the customer payment needs to be returned. How do you unwind the cover leg?Expert

The cover is a separate settlement, so it gets a separate return. Returning the customer payment does not automatically unwind the cover. I recognise the two legs. The **pacs.008 instruction** travelled to the beneficiary bank, while the **pacs.009 with settlement method COVE** settled the funds between correspondents. To return the payment, I need a **pacs.004** for the customer leg and a separate pacs.004 for the cover leg. I match each return to its original using the **UETR and settlement references**, so nothing gets misapplied. I watch for partial amounts, because the cover returned may differ from the cover sent if charges were taken along the way. Both the original cover and its return hit the **Nostro ledger**, so both must be booked and reconciled. Reconciliation must pair all four messages, the instruction, the cover, the return of the instruction, and the return of the cover. If any one of the four is missing, the books will not balance. I test this as one scenario in UAT, because return flows that forget the cover leg are a classic defect. A payment hub that handles the customer return but leaves the cover sitting in the Nostro account has created a reconciliation break that will surface at month end.

Read the full chapter →
Q45.What is a nostro account, and how does the payment hub interact with it? What happens if the nostro balance is too low?Advanced

A **nostro account** is your bank's account with a correspondent bank in a foreign currency. When you send a USD payment from India, your bank debits the customer's INR account, converts to USD, and then instructs its correspondent bank in the US to pay from the nostro account. The nostro balance goes down. When you receive a USD payment, the correspondent credits your nostro account and the balance goes up. The hub must check the **nostro balance** before releasing a payment, because if the balance is too low, the correspondent will reject it. Treasury manages nostro funding by moving money between accounts, and they need a **real time view** of every nostro balance. The hub reports each payment to the treasury system as soon as it is released, so treasury always knows the expected balance. At end of day, the hub reconciles the nostro account against the **camt.053 statement** from the correspondent bank. Any difference is a break that must be investigated. The most common break is a payment the hub sent but the correspondent has not yet processed, which shows as a timing difference. A real break is a payment the correspondent processed but the hub never sent, which is a serious control failure.

Q46.Walk through a clean SWIFT gpi payment. How does the UETR and the tracker give the customer visibility at every hop?Intermediate

SWIFT gpi works because every payment carries a **UETR**, a unique end-to-end transaction reference, and every bank in the chain updates the status against that reference. The customer sends the payment, and the sending bank creates the UETR and includes it in the **pacs.008**. As the payment moves through each intermediary, each bank updates the **gpi Tracker** with its status, so the sending bank and the customer can see exactly where the payment is. The beneficiary bank credits the account and sends a **pacs.002** with ACSC status, which appears on the tracker. The customer can check the tracker and see the payment arrived, the amount credited, and any charges deducted along the way. The sender gets a confirmation, and the **camt.053** statement matches. What makes gpi clean is the **transparency**. Before gpi, a cross-border payment was a black box, and the customer had to call the bank to find out where it was. With gpi, the status is visible at every hop, the charges are visible, and the customer knows when the payment will arrive. A payment that is tracked end to end is a payment that rarely generates a complaint, because the customer can see it moving.

Read the full chapter →
Q47.Walk through a clean cover method payment. How do the pacs.008 instruction and the pacs.009 cover travel separately and come together at the beneficiary bank?Intermediate

The cover method works when the instruction and the money travel on separate tracks but arrive together. The sending bank creates two messages, both carrying the same **UETR**. The **pacs.008** instruction goes directly to the beneficiary bank, carrying the full customer and remittance details. The **pacs.009** with settlement method COVE goes through the correspondent chain, moving the funds between **Nostro accounts**. Each correspondent validates the cover, debits its Nostro account, and passes it on. The beneficiary bank receives the pacs.008 first, and waits for the cover to arrive. When both legs have arrived, the beneficiary bank **reconciles them** using the shared UETR, confirms the amounts match, and credits the beneficiary account. The beneficiary bank sends back a **pacs.002** with ACSC status on the instruction, and the cover chain is confirmed through the correspondent statements. The customer gets the funds on the promised value date. What makes it clean is the **UETR link**. Without it, the beneficiary bank cannot match the instruction to the cover, and the payment parks as an unmatched item. With it, the two legs come together cleanly and the payment completes without a phone call.

Read the full chapter →
Q48.Explain how the bank uses SWIFT gpi to track a payment when the pacs.002 has not arrived.Intermediate

**SWIFT gpi** gives the bank a tracker that is independent of the **pacs.002** flow. Every bank in the chain updates the tracker when it receives and forwards the payment, so the bank can see where the payment is even when the formal status message has not arrived. The operations team looks up the payment by its **UETR** in the gpi tracker and reads the latest status, the fees deducted at each hop, and the time the payment spent at each bank.

If the tracker shows the payment was credited to the beneficiary, the bank knows the payment completed and the pacs.002 was simply lost or delayed, and the status can be updated from the tracker. If the tracker shows the payment is stuck at an intermediary, the team contacts that bank directly. If the tracker shows nothing, the payment may not have entered the gpi network, and the team falls back to sending an investigation message, usually an **MT199**, to the next bank in the chain. The gpi tracker is a visibility tool, not a settlement system, so it tells the bank where the payment is but it does not move the payment. The bank still has to act on what the tracker shows.

Q49.The gpi tracker shows the payment as credited but the internal status is still pending. Which one is right and how do you fix it?Advanced

When the **gpi tracker** and the internal status disagree, the bank must find out which one is right. The gpi tracker is updated by every bank in the chain, so it reflects what the banks in the chain reported. The internal status reflects what the bank's own **payment hub** recorded from the **pacs.002** messages it received. A mismatch usually means a pacs.002 was lost, delayed, or not processed by the hub.

The operations team checks the settlement confirmation and the **camt.053** statement first. If the statement shows the funds left the bank and the gpi tracker shows the payment was credited, then the payment did complete and the internal status is wrong. The team updates the hub status manually and investigates why the pacs.002 was missed. If the statement shows no settlement, but the gpi tracker shows the payment as credited, the team contacts the beneficiary bank directly to confirm, because the tracker can be wrong if a bank updated it incorrectly. The team does not blindly trust either source. It uses the settlement evidence, the statement, and the tracker together to determine the truth. The customer is told the confirmed status, not the tracker status or the hub status alone.

Read the full chapter →

SWIFT MT Messages (17)

Q50.What is MT202 COV?Intermediate

An MT202 COV is the cover variant of the MT202 financial institution transfer, and it exists to solve a transparency problem. A plain MT202 moves money between banks for their own account, and it carries no customer details. If a plain MT202 were used to settle a customer payment, the intermediary banks and the creditor agent would see money moving with no idea who the underlying ordering customer or beneficiary was. That gap created a compliance and reconciliation risk, because banks could not screen the underlying parties or match the funds to the right customer instruction.

The MT202 COV fixes this by carrying the cover details. It is sent through the correspondent chain to move the funds that settle an MT103 customer payment, and it includes the key customer information from the MT103, such as the ordering customer and the beneficiary, in its fields. The MT103 itself is sent directly to the creditor agent with the full details, and the MT202 COV is linked to it by the same transaction reference and the same UETR, so the creditor agent can match the incoming funds to the customer instruction when both legs arrive.

For a business analyst, the MT202 COV is a good example of how message design responds to regulation. The plain MT202 was technically sufficient to move the money, but it was not sufficient for transparency. The COV variant adds the information that compliance, operations, and reconciliation teams need, without changing the underlying settlement mechanism. When you investigate a cover payment, always ask for both messages. The MT103 shows what the customer asked for, the MT202 COV shows how the funds travelled, and the shared reference and UETR prove that the two legs belong to the same payment.

Read the full chapter →
Q51.What is a payment investigation (MT192/195/196)?Intermediate

A payment investigation is the formal process a bank uses to find out what happened to a payment that is missing, delayed, or incorrect, and in the MT system it uses three messages. MT192 is a Request for Cancellation, sent when the sender wants a payment stopped before it settles. MT195 is a general Query, sent when the sender wants information, for example asking the beneficiary bank whether the payment was credited and on what date. MT196 is the answer to a query, sent by the bank that received the MT195, giving the status of the payment. Together, these messages form the investigation trail. In ISO 20022, the same work is done with camt.056 for a cancellation request, camt.028 for a status report, and camt.029 for the resolution of an investigation. An investigation is started when a customer reports a problem, for example saying the beneficiary has not received a USD 367,574.90 payment sent three days ago. The sender bank checks its own records, then sends an MT195 to the next bank in the chain, which forwards it until it reaches the beneficiary bank. Each bank replies, and the sender bank pieces together where the payment stopped. Investigations can take days, because each bank has its own cut off times and its own queue. Banks charge for investigations, often USD 25 to USD 50, and the charge may be passed to the customer if the investigation shows the bank did nothing wrong.

Read the full chapter →
Q52.A beneficiary calls to say they cannot match a payment to an invoice because the remittance information is cut off. The MT103 field 70 only shows part of the invoice number. What went wrong and how do you prevent it?Beginner

**Field 70** of the MT103, the remittance information field, holds a maximum of **four lines of 35 characters**, and anything longer is cut off. The sending bank put a long invoice reference into field 70, the message carried only the first 140 characters, and the beneficiary received a truncated reference they cannot match. The fix for this payment is to send the full reference to the beneficiary bank by a separate message, such as an **MT199** free format message, quoting the original MT103 reference so the beneficiary bank can link the two. The prevention is to use **structured remittance information** where the payment system supports it, or to keep the field 70 content short and put the full detail in the customer instruction channel, not in the SWIFT message. In the ISO 20022 world the **pacs.008** carries up to 140 characters of unstructured remittance information and structured references as well, which is one reason the migration matters. Tell the operations team to validate field 70 length before sending, and to reject instructions where the reference is too long, rather than letting the message truncate silently and creating a reconciliation problem at the other end.

Read the full chapter →
Q53.A corporate customer asks why their MT103 carries a field 72, sender to receiver information, and whether they can use it to add instructions for the beneficiary bank. Explain what field 72 is for and what it must never contain.Intermediate

**Field 72** is the sender to receiver information field in the MT103. It carries instructions from the sending bank to the receiving bank, such as asking the beneficiary bank to phone the beneficiary, to hold the payment for collection, or to apply a specific value date. It is bank to bank information, and it is not part of the payment instruction to the beneficiary. The corporate customer cannot use field 72 to send a message to the beneficiary, because the beneficiary bank may not pass it on, and the beneficiary will never see it. Field 72 must never contain **payment details** that belong in other fields, such as the amount, the account number, or the remittance information, because the receiving bank systems read specific fields and may ignore field 72 entirely. It must also never contain **sensitive information** that should not travel in a free text field, and it must never be used to work around a validation failure in another field. If the customer wants to send a message to the beneficiary, the right place is field 70, the remittance information, or a separate communication channel. Field 72 is a tool for banks to talk to each other about how to handle the payment, and using it for anything else creates confusion and failed payments.

Read the full chapter →
Q54.A payment travels through three correspondent banks. The operations team is unsure whether to send an MT202 or an MT202 COV to move the funds. Explain the difference and when each one is used.Intermediate

An **MT202** is a general financial institution transfer. It moves money between banks for their own account and carries no customer details. An **MT202 COV** is the cover variant, and it carries the underlying customer information from the related **MT103**, such as the ordering customer and the beneficiary. The rule is simple: if the funds being moved settle a customer payment, use the **MT202 COV**, because every bank in the chain needs to see who the underlying customer is for **sanctions screening** and reconciliation. If the funds are the bank own money, for example a treasury transfer or a liquidity movement, use the plain **MT202**, because there is no underlying customer. In the three bank chain, the MT103 travels directly to the beneficiary bank with the full customer details, while the MT202 COV travels through the correspondent chain to move the funds, and the two are linked by the same **transaction reference** and the same **UETR**. The beneficiary bank matches the cover to the instruction when both arrive. Using a plain MT202 for a customer payment is a compliance failure, because the intermediary banks cannot screen the real parties. Using a COV for a bank own transfer adds unnecessary data and can confuse reconciliation.

Read the full chapter →
Q55.A treasury analyst asks for an MT910 and an MT900 to check whether two nostro payments settled yesterday. Explain what these two messages are and how the analyst uses them.Beginner

An **MT900** is a confirmation of debit. It tells the account owner that their account has been debited, with the amount, the currency, the value date, and the reference of the original instruction. An **MT910** is a confirmation of credit, and it tells the account owner that their account has been credited, with the same details. The two messages are always sent by the **account servicing institution**, which is the bank that holds the account, to the account owner. The treasury analyst uses them to confirm that a payment actually left or arrived in the **nostro account**. If the bank sent a payment instruction and then receives an MT900, the debit is confirmed and the nostro balance can be updated. If the bank expected a receipt and receives an MT910, the credit is confirmed. If the expected MT900 or MT910 does not arrive, the analyst knows the payment has not settled and must chase it. These messages are the basic building blocks of **nostro reconciliation**, because they prove what actually happened to the account, as opposed to what the bank instructed to happen.

Read the full chapter →
Q56.A reconciliation analyst is unsure whether to use the MT940 or the MT942 for intraday nostro checking. Explain the difference between the two statements and when each one is used.Beginner

The **MT940** is the customer statement message.
