It is sent at **end of day** and gives the full statement for the account: the opening balance, every debit and credit during the day, and the closing balance. It is the official record used for end of day reconciliation. The **MT942** is the interim transaction report. It is sent **during the day**, often several times, and gives the transactions since the last report, with an interim balance. The analyst uses the MT942 for **intraday monitoring**, to check that expected payments have arrived, to spot unexpected debits early, and to manage liquidity during the day. The MT940 is used for the formal end of day reconciliation, because it is complete and final. The two messages have the same structure, but the MT942 is a snapshot and the MT940 is the full record. If the analyst tries to reconcile the books using only MT942 reports, they will miss transactions that arrive after the last interim report. If they wait for the MT940 to spot a problem, they will find it hours too late. Use the MT942 during the day to manage, and the MT940 at end of day to prove.

Read the full chapter →
Q57.A payment has not arrived after three days and the beneficiary bank is not responding to emails. The operations team wants to send an MT199 to chase it. Explain what an MT199 is, when it is the right message, and when a different message should be used instead.Intermediate

An **MT199** is a free format message. It is the general purpose message banks use to send information that does not fit into a structured message type. It is the right message when you need to ask a question, give information, or chase a payment, and there is no specific message type for what you want to say. For a missing payment, the MT199 should quote the original payment **reference**, the **UETR**, the amount, the currency, the value date, and the date it was sent, so the receiving bank can find it without asking for more information. But the MT199 is not always the right choice. If you want to request a **cancellation**, use the **MT192**. If you want to ask about a payment status formally, use the **MT195** enquiry. If you want to request a **recall** of funds, use the **camt.056** or the appropriate MT message for the scheme. The MT199 is also the wrong tool when the information is structured, because free text is hard for the receiving bank systems to process automatically and may sit in a manual queue. Use the MT199 for genuine free text communication, use the structured message when one exists, and always include the reference and the UETR so the receiving bank can act without coming back to you.

Read the full chapter →
Q58.A customer asks their bank to cancel a payment that was sent yesterday. The bank sends an MT192 request for cancellation, but the beneficiary bank replies that the funds have already been credited to the beneficiary. What happens now?Intermediate

An **MT192** is a request for cancellation. It asks the receiving bank to stop the payment and return the funds, but it is only a request, not an instruction the receiving bank must obey. If the funds have already been **credited to the beneficiary**, the beneficiary bank cannot simply take the money back, because the beneficiary now owns it. The beneficiary bank should reply explaining the position, and the sending bank must then ask the beneficiary to agree to return the funds voluntarily. This is done through a **recall**, usually a **camt.056** message, which asks the beneficiary bank to contact the beneficiary and request the return. The beneficiary can refuse, and if they do, the sending bank has no SWIFT mechanism to force the return. The sending bank must then tell the customer honestly that the money cannot be recovered through the payment system and that their options are to negotiate directly with the beneficiary or to take legal action. The lesson is that cancellation only works before the payment is credited. Once the beneficiary has the money, the payment system cannot undo it, which is why banks check payment details carefully before sending and why customers should check the beneficiary details before they confirm.

Read the full chapter →
Q59.A bank sends an MT195 to ask a correspondent bank about a missing payment. Three days later there is still no reply. Explain the MT195 and MT196 flow, what the deadlines are, and what the bank should do next.Intermediate

The **MT195** is an enquiry message. A bank sends it to ask another bank a question about a payment, such as whether it was received, whether it was credited, or why it has not arrived. The receiving bank is expected to reply with an **MT196**, which is the answer to the enquiry. The MT195 should include the original payment **reference**, the **UETR**, the amount, the currency, and the value date, so the receiving bank can identify the payment immediately. There is no universal deadline in the SWIFT rules, but market practice and **gpi service levels** expect a reply within one to two business days for a straightforward enquiry. If three days have passed with no reply, the bank should escalate: send a second MT195 marked urgent, copy the **relationship manager** at the correspondent bank, and raise the case in the **gpi Case Resolution** tool if the payment is gpi enabled. The bank should also tell the customer what is happening and give them a realistic timeline, rather than leaving them waiting in silence. If the correspondent bank still does not reply, the issue becomes a relationship matter, and the bank senior management should raise it through the correspondent banking team. The MT195 and MT196 exist precisely so banks can resolve these cases without phone calls and emails, but they only work if both sides respond.

Read the full chapter →
Q60.A corporate treasurer wants to send 500 salary payments to their bank in a single instruction instead of 500 separate payments. Explain how the MT101 helps and what the bank does with it.Beginner

The **MT101** is a request for transfer. It is the message a corporate customer sends to their bank to instruct multiple payments in a single message. Instead of sending 500 separate instructions, the treasurer sends one MT101 containing all 500 payment instructions, each with its own beneficiary, account, amount, and value date. The bank validates the MT101, checks that the customer account has enough funds, and then processes each instruction inside it, usually by generating individual **MT103** messages for the cross border payments or domestic clearing instructions for the local ones. The MT101 is designed for **bulk payments** such as salaries, supplier payments, and pension payments, where the same customer sends many payments on the same day. The customer must have an agreement with the bank to use MT101, and the bank must support it. The advantage is efficiency: one message, one authorisation, and one reconciliation point, instead of hundreds of separate instructions. The risk is that a single error in the MT101 can affect many payments, so the bank validates the whole file before processing, and the treasurer should check the bank acknowledgement to confirm how many instructions were accepted and how many were rejected.

Read the full chapter →
Q61.An operations analyst sees an MT205 and an MT202 for the same amount on the same day and thinks it is a duplicate. Explain the difference between the two messages and why both can be legitimate.Intermediate

An **MT202** is a general financial institution transfer, used to move money between banks. An **MT205** is a financial institution transfer **execution**, and it is used when the transfer is executed by a financial institution on behalf of another financial institution. The difference is in the role of the sender. The MT202 is sent by the bank that owns the funds. The MT205 is sent by a bank that has been instructed by another bank to execute the transfer, for example when a bank uses a **correspondent** to move funds on its behalf. Both messages can appear for the same underlying movement because they describe different legs of the same chain: one bank instructs, another executes. The analyst should not treat them as duplicates. Instead, they should check the **transaction reference**, the **related reference**, and the **UETR** to see whether the two messages belong to the same payment chain or to two separate payments. If the references match and the amounts are the same, the MT205 is the execution of the instruction that the MT202 represents, and the nostro entries should show one debit and one credit, not two. Treating an MT205 as a duplicate and reversing it would create a real break, so the rule is to always check the references before acting.

Read the full chapter →
Q62.The MT950 end of day statement shows three entries that do not appear in the bank nostro ledger. The amounts are small but the reconciliation cannot be signed off. Walk through how you investigate the break.Advanced

Start by confirming the **MT950** is the correct statement for the correct account and the correct value date, because a wrong account or a wrong date is the most common cause of a phantom break. Next, pull the **MT900 and MT910** confirmations for the day and check whether the three entries appear there. If they do, the entries are real and the nostro ledger is missing them. If they do not, the entries may be **charges, interest, or fees** applied by the account servicing bank, which appear on the statement but are not payment instructions and therefore never hit the payment ledger. Common examples are **correspondent charges**, **account maintenance fees**, and **interest adjustments**. Check the statement narrative for each entry: the MT950 field 86 carries the details, and a charge will usually be labelled as such. If the entries are genuine payments that the ledger missed, trace them back to the original instruction: was the payment sent, was it authorised, and did the ledger feed fail? If the entries are charges, the fix is to post them to the correct **general ledger** account and to update the reconciliation so the break clears. Never force the reconciliation to balance by posting an unexplained entry to a suspense account without understanding it. The sign off requires every entry to be explained, and a small unexplained entry is still a break.

Read the full chapter →
Q63.A bank agrees an FX rate with a customer for a cross border payment, but the MT300 confirmation from the counterparty shows a different rate and a different value date. What has gone wrong and how do you resolve it?Advanced

An **MT300** is a foreign exchange confirmation. It is the message one party sends to the other to confirm the details of an FX deal: the currencies, the amounts, the **exchange rate**, the **value date**, and the settlement instructions. If the MT300 shows a different rate and a different value date from what the bank agreed with the customer, there is a **confirmation mismatch**, and the deal cannot settle as it stands. The first step is to check the original deal record: the dealer ticket, the recorded conversation, or the electronic trading platform log. That record is the evidence of what was actually agreed. Next, contact the counterparty and ask them to check their record. Most mismatches are caused by a typing error, a wrong value date convention, or a misunderstanding about which rate applies. If the counterparty agrees their MT300 is wrong, they send a corrected MT300 and the deal proceeds. If they insist their version is right, the two banks must compare their deal records and agree which one is correct. The customer payment cannot be released until the FX deal is confirmed, because the amount the beneficiary receives depends on the rate. The lesson is to confirm every FX deal on the same day it is struck and to never let a mismatched MT300 sit unresolved overnight.

Read the full chapter →
Q64.A customer reports a cheque as lost in the post and asks the bank to stop it. The bank sends an MT111. Explain what this message does and what the customer should expect.Beginner

An **MT111** is a stop payment of a cheque. It is the message a bank sends to tell another bank, or to instruct its own systems, that a specific cheque must not be paid. The message carries the **cheque number**, the **amount**, the **currency**, the **account number**, and the **payee name**, so the paying bank can identify the exact cheque. Once the stop is in place, if the cheque is presented for payment, the paying bank will return it unpaid with a reason code indicating the stop. The customer should expect the stop to take effect quickly, usually the same day, but they should also know that a stop does not guarantee the cheque will never be paid: if the cheque was already presented and cleared before the stop arrived, the money has gone. The customer should also be told that a stop payment does not cancel the underlying obligation. If they owed the payee money, they still owe it, and they must arrange a replacement payment. The bank will usually charge a fee for the stop, and the stop remains in place for a set period, often six months, after which it may need to be renewed. The MT111 is a simple message, but it protects the customer from a lost cheque being used fraudulently.

Read the full chapter →
Q65.An MT103 arrives with field 50, the ordering customer field, containing only a name and no account number or address. The payment is held for compliance review. Explain why the field is incomplete, what the risks are, and how the payment gets released.Advanced

**Field 50** in the MT103 must identify the ordering customer fully. Under the **Funds Transfer Regulation** and the **travel rule**, the ordering customer information must include the name, the account number, and the address or another identifier, so that every bank in the chain can screen the real sender. A field 50 with only a name is incomplete, and the receiving bank cannot screen the payment properly, cannot identify the sender if there is a sanctions hit, and cannot return the funds to the right account if the payment is rejected. The payment is correctly held. The fix is to ask the **sending bank** for the missing information, either by an MT199 free format message or through the **gpi Case Resolution** tool, quoting the MT103 reference and the UETR. The sending bank should reply with the full ordering customer details, and the receiving bank then updates the payment record, completes the **sanctions screening**, and releases the payment. If the sending bank cannot provide the information, the payment must be rejected and returned, because processing a payment with incomplete originator information breaches the travel rule. The lesson for the sending bank is to validate field 50 before sending and to reject customer instructions that do not include a full name, account, and address.

Read the full chapter →
Q66.During the MT to MX migration, a bank converts an MT103 into a pacs.008. The conversion drops the remittance information because the MT103 field 70 is longer than the pacs.008 allows. Explain the data problem and how the bank handles it during coexistence.Expert

This is a **data truncation** problem, and it is one of the most common issues in the **MT to MX migration**. The MT103 field 70 allows four lines of 35 characters, and the pacs.008 unstructured remittance information allows 140 characters, so in theory they match. But the MT103 also carries information in other fields that have no direct equivalent in the pacs.008, and the **CBPR+ usage guidelines** define exactly how each MT field maps to the MX structure. When the mapping cannot carry all the data, the bank has three options. First, use the **structured remittance information** in the pacs.008, which can carry a structured reference and additional data in a way the MT103 could not. Second, send the extra information in a separate message, such as an MT199, linked by the UETR. Third, agree with the counterparty bank to accept the truncated data and to reconcile using the **UETR** and the transaction reference instead of the remittance text. During **coexistence**, when both MT and MX messages flow, the bank must test the translation in both directions and must validate that no critical data is lost. The long term fix is to move customers to **ISO 20022 native** instructions, where the data is captured in structured form from the start, rather than converting from MT and hoping nothing is lost.

Read the full chapter →

ISO 20022 and MX Messages (4)

Q67.What is ISO 20022?Beginner

ISO 20022 is the global standard for exchanging electronic messages between financial institutions. It defines a common language that banks, payment systems, market infrastructures and corporates use to describe payments, securities, trade and card transactions. Instead of each system inventing its own format, ISO 20022 provides a shared dictionary of business concepts, such as debtor, creditor, amount and value date, plus a set of message definitions built on top of that dictionary.

The standard is maintained by ISO Technical Committee 68 and is syntax independent in principle, but in practice almost all ISO 20022 messages today are expressed in XML. Each message type has a name, such as pacs.008 or pain.001, and a published schema that spells out exactly which elements are mandatory, which are optional and what values are allowed. Because the data is structured and labelled, a receiving system can parse a message without guessing what a free text field means.

ISO 20022 matters because it is replacing the older MT message formats on SWIFT and in many domestic systems. It carries richer data, for example full structured addresses, longer remittance information and explicit purpose codes, which helps with straight through processing, sanctions screening, reconciliation and regulatory reporting. Learning ISO 20022 is therefore essential for anyone working in payments operations, correspondent banking or payment product design.

Read the full chapter →
Q68.What is CBPR+?Intermediate

CBPR+ stands for Cross Border Payments and Reporting Plus. It is the working group that defines how ISO 20022 is used for cross border payments on the SWIFT network. ISO 20022 itself is a broad standard with many optional elements, and different banks could implement it in different ways. CBPR+ exists to prevent that fragmentation: it publishes usage guidelines that say exactly which elements are mandatory, which are optional, and which rules apply for cross border payments, so that a pacs.008 sent by a bank in Singapore is understood the same way by a bank in Germany.

The group is made up of banks, market infrastructures and SWIFT, and its guidelines are the practical rulebook for the migration. They cover message versions, character sets, address formats, charge bearer rules, and how the coexistence period was handled, when MT and ISO 20022 messages both flowed. CBPR+ also defined the translation rules used during coexistence, so that a payment starting as an MT103 could be converted to pacs.008 without losing information, and vice versa.

For anyone implementing ISO 20022, CBPR+ is the document that matters most after the standard itself. Reading the raw ISO 20022 schema tells you what is possible; reading the CBPR+ usage guidelines tells you what you must actually do. The guidelines are updated regularly, so implementation teams track new releases and plan their changes around them. If a payment fails between two banks, one of the first questions is usually whether both sides followed the same CBPR+ version.

Read the full chapter →
Q69.A payment engine produces ISO 20022 pacs.008 messages but the downstream clearing system still expects MT103. How do you handle the transformation, and what is the biggest risk?Advanced

Start from the message the engine produces and the message the clearing house expects. The engine works in **ISO 20022** and produces a **pacs.008**. The clearing house may still expect **MT103** on the SWIFT network, or it may accept pacs.008 natively. The transformation happens in a **mapping layer** between the engine and the clearing interface. Every field in pacs.008 must map to a field in MT103, and the mapping is not one to one. For example, pacs.008 carries structured debtor and creditor addresses with separate fields for street, town and country. MT103 field 59 has a limited character set and no structure, so the mapper must flatten the address and truncate it without losing the town and country. The **charge bearer** in pacs.008 maps to field 71A in MT103, OUR, SHA or BEN. The **end to end reference** maps to field 70. The dangerous part is data loss. If a field exists in pacs.008 but has no home in MT103, you must decide whether to drop it, park it in a free text field, or reject the payment. Document every decision in a **field mapping specification** and test each corridor with real examples. Always validate the mapped message against the clearing house schema before sending, because a single invalid field causes a rejection and a repair queue.

Read the full chapter →
Q70.How do you explain ISO 20022 migration to a business stakeholder?Intermediate

I explain ISO 20022 migration as a change of language, not a change of banking. Today the bank speaks one language for payments, the old MT messages, and it needs to learn a new language, the MX messages. The new language is richer: it carries more information, structured addresses, longer references and clearer data. The migration means the bank must be able to send and receive the new messages, translate between the old and the new during the transition, and handle the cases where the other bank has not migrated yet. I explain the business impact in plain terms: the new messages let the bank carry more information about a payment, which improves reconciliation and reduces exceptions. I explain the timeline: the migration happens in phases, and there are deadlines set by SWIFT and the clearing systems. I explain what the business needs to do: update customer communications, train operations on the new message formats, and test with the banks they send payments to. I avoid the technical detail unless asked. The stakeholder does not need to know the XML structure. They need to know what changes for the customer, what changes for operations and when it happens.

Read the full chapter →

SEPA and Instant Payments (16)

Q71.What is SEPA?Beginner

SEPA, the Single Euro Payments Area, is the framework that makes euro payments work the same way across Europe. Before SEPA, a payment from Germany to France was a cross border payment with different formats, timelines and charges from a domestic payment. SEPA harmonised that: within the SEPA area, which covers the eurozone plus several other European countries, a euro payment is treated the same whether it stays inside one country or crosses a border. The framework is governed by the European Payments Council and supported by EU regulation.

SEPA defines three main payment instruments. SEPA Credit Transfer, SCT, is the standard euro credit transfer, where the payer instructs their bank to send money to the beneficiary. SEPA Direct Debit, SDD, lets a creditor collect money from a debtor account with a mandate, which is how subscriptions and utility bills are collected across Europe. SEPA Instant Credit Transfer, SCT Inst, is the real time version, settling within seconds. All three use ISO 20022 message formats, which is one reason SEPA was an early large scale adopter of the standard.

For a learner, the important idea is that SEPA is not a single system but a set of rules, standards and schemes that banks and clearing systems implement. The actual clearing and settlement happens through systems such as STEP2 and the Eurosystem TARGET service, but the customer experience is defined by SEPA: one account, one format, the same timing and the same charging rules across the whole area. SEPA is the model many other regions study when they design their own harmonised payment areas.

Read the full chapter →
Q72.What is SEPA Instant?Intermediate

SEPA Instant, formally SEPA Instant Credit Transfer or SCT Inst, is the real time version of the SEPA Credit Transfer. It is a scheme from the European Payments Council that lets euro payments settle within seconds, 24 hours a day, 365 days a year, between accounts in the SEPA area. The target is a maximum of ten seconds from the payer bank sending the payment to the beneficiary bank confirming receipt, and most payments complete much faster. The scheme went live in 2017 and has grown steadily as more banks and payment service providers joined.

The mechanics are straightforward in concept and demanding in practice. The payer bank sends an SCT Inst instruction, the beneficiary bank must respond within the time limit, confirming that the account exists and the funds are credited or rejecting the payment with a reason. Settlement between banks happens through clearing systems such as the Eurosystem TIPS service, which settles in central bank money in real time, or through other clearing arrangements. Because the payment is instant and irrevocable, banks must run strong fraud and sanctions checks in milliseconds, and they must be available around the clock, which requires significant investment in systems and operations.

SEPA Instant matters because it changed expectations. Once instant euro payments exist, customers and corporates expect all payments to be instant, and the European Instant Payments Regulation now requires banks in the euro area to offer instant payments. The scheme has a transaction limit that has been raised over time, and it supports the same ISO 20022 message formats as the rest of SEPA. For anyone comparing instant payment systems globally, SCT Inst is the European reference point, and its design choices around speed, irrevocability and 24 hour operation are the ones other systems are measured against.

Read the full chapter →
Q73.Your bank is a direct participant in SEPA. A customer sends a SEPA Instant payment. Walk through what happens from instruction to settlement in under 10 seconds.Intermediate

The customer submits the payment through the channel, and the **payment hub** validates it, checks sanctions, and confirms the beneficiary bank is reachable for **SEPA Instant**. The hub formats the payment as a **pacs.008** and sends it to the beneficiary bank through the **SEPA Instant** clearing system, usually **TIPS** or a private clearing house. The whole journey must complete within 10 seconds, and the clearing system enforces a 20-second maximum.

The beneficiary bank receives the pacs.008, validates the account, and must respond within the time limit. If it accepts, it credits the customer immediately and sends back a **pacs.002** with **ACSC** status. Settlement between the banks happens in central bank money through TIPS at the same time, so there is no deferred settlement. If the beneficiary bank does not respond in time, the payment is rejected and the sending bank tells the customer it did not go through. The bank's hub monitors the response time on every SEPA Instant payment, because a slow beneficiary bank creates timeouts and customer complaints. The 10-second promise is a system-wide service level, not a marketing claim, and every bank in the chain is measured against it.

Read the full chapter →
Q74.Walk through a clean SEPA credit transfer, from the customer instruction to the beneficiary credit. What makes the SEPA scheme work so smoothly?Beginner

A SEPA credit transfer is clean because the scheme is standardised. The customer submits the instruction through their bank, and the bank validates it, checking the **IBAN** format, the balance, and the sanctions lists. The bank sends a **pacs.008** to the beneficiary bank, either directly or through a clearing system. The pacs.008 carries the IBAN, the amount, the end-to-end reference, and the remittance information. The beneficiary bank receives it, validates the IBAN, credits the customer account, and sends back a **pacs.002** with ACSC status. For a standard SEPA credit transfer, the funds arrive by the next business day. For a **SEPA Instant** payment, the funds arrive within ten seconds, and the beneficiary bank must confirm receipt with a pacs.002 carrying ACSC status within that window. The customer sees the credit in their account, and the sender gets confirmation. The end-of-day **camt.053** statement shows the debit. What makes it clean is the standardisation. Every bank in the scheme follows the same rules, the same message formats, and the same timelines, so a payment from one country to another works exactly like a domestic one.

Read the full chapter →
Q75.A customer sends a SEPA credit transfer and it comes back rejected with reason code AC01. The customer insists the IBAN is correct. Explain what AC01 means and how you help the customer fix it.Beginner

**AC01** means incorrect account number. The receiving bank checked the **IBAN** in the payment and found that it does not match a valid account. The customer may have typed the IBAN correctly as they see it, but the problem is usually a small error: a digit transposed, a character missing, or the IBAN copied from an old document after the account changed. The first step is to ask the customer to check the IBAN against the source, such as the beneficiary invoice or the beneficiary bank statement, character by character. The IBAN has a built in **check digit**, so a typing error can be detected, but it cannot tell you what the correct IBAN is. If the IBAN is genuinely correct and the payment still rejects with AC01, the account may be **closed**, or the beneficiary bank may not accept SEPA payments to that account type. Ask the beneficiary to confirm the IBAN with their own bank and to provide it in writing. Never guess the correction and never send the payment to a similar looking account. Tell the customer that the rejection is a good thing: it stopped the money going to the wrong place, and once the correct IBAN is confirmed, the payment can be sent again immediately.

Read the full chapter →
Q76.A customer sends a SEPA Instant payment. The money leaves their account, but the beneficiary bank does not confirm within 10 seconds and the payment times out. Explain what happens to the money and what the bank must do.Intermediate

A **SEPA Instant** payment must complete within **10 seconds**. If the beneficiary bank does not confirm receipt in that time, the payment **times out**. The money has already left the payer account, so the bank must now find out what happened to it. The payer bank sends an **investigation** message to the beneficiary bank, asking whether the payment was credited, rejected, or never received. There are three outcomes. If the beneficiary bank credited the payment but the confirmation was delayed, the payment is complete and the payer bank tells the customer it arrived. If the beneficiary bank rejected the payment, the funds must be **returned** to the payer, usually within one business day. If the beneficiary bank never received the payment, the payer bank must trace it through the clearing system, such as **TIPS** or the EBA Clearing RT1 system, to find where it stopped. The bank must keep the customer informed at every step, because the customer sees money gone and no confirmation, which is the most worrying experience in payments. The bank should also log the timeout as an operational incident, because repeated timeouts point to a problem with the beneficiary bank or the clearing connection, not with a single payment.

Read the full chapter →
Q77.A customer sees a direct debit on their account that they do not recognise. They say they never signed a mandate. Explain how a SEPA Direct Debit works, what the customer rights are, and how the bank handles the dispute.Beginner

A **SEPA Direct Debit**, or SDD, lets a creditor, such as a utility company, collect money from the debtor account, but only if the debtor has signed a **mandate** giving permission. The mandate states the creditor name, the amount or the collection pattern, and the debtor account. Without a valid mandate, the collection is not authorised. If the customer says they never signed a mandate, the bank must ask the creditor bank for a copy of the **mandate** and check it against the customer details. The customer has strong rights: under the SEPA rules, they can request a **refund** of an unauthorised direct debit within **13 months**, and the bank must return the money within **10 business days** of the claim while it investigates. If the mandate is valid and the customer simply forgot, the refund rules are different: for an authorised collection, the customer has **8 weeks** to request a refund, no questions asked. Tell the customer to check whether they signed a mandate when they took out a subscription or a contract, because many people forget. If there is genuinely no mandate, the bank refunds the money and tells the creditor to stop collecting.

Read the full chapter →
Q78.A SEPA Instant payment is credited to the beneficiary, but the payer then discovers the payment was sent to the wrong account because of a typing error. The payer asks for the money back. Explain the recall process and why the beneficiary can refuse.Advanced

A **SEPA Instant** payment is **irrevocable** once it is credited. The payer cannot cancel it through the payment system, because the money has already moved and the beneficiary bank has confirmed receipt. The only route is a **recall**, which is a request from the payer bank to the beneficiary bank, asking the beneficiary to return the funds voluntarily. The beneficiary bank contacts the beneficiary and explains the situation, but the beneficiary is **not obliged** to return the money. If the beneficiary agrees, the funds are sent back, usually as a new payment, and the case is closed. If the beneficiary refuses, or does not respond, the payer bank has no power to force the return through the SEPA scheme. The payer options are then to contact the beneficiary directly, or to take **legal action** if the amount justifies it. This is why **verification of payee** matters so much: it checks the payee name against the IBAN before the payment is sent, and it would have caught the typing error. Tell the payer honestly that the recall is a request, not a guarantee, and that the best protection is to check the details before confirming an instant payment, because once it is sent, it cannot be taken back.

Read the full chapter →
Q79.A customer is about to send a SEPA payment and sees a warning that the payee name does not match the account number. The name is almost right, just one letter different. Explain what verification of payee does and what the customer should do.Beginner

**Verification of payee** is a check that runs before a SEPA payment is sent. The bank compares the **payee name** the payer typed against the name registered to the **IBAN**, and it returns one of three results: a **match**, a **close match**, or **no match**. A close match means the name is almost right, often because of a spelling difference, a missing middle name, or a company trading name instead of its legal name. The customer should stop and check: is this the right person, is the IBAN copied correctly, and does the close match make sense? If the customer is sure the details are right, they can proceed, but they should know the bank has warned them. If the customer is not sure, they should contact the payee and confirm the name and IBAN before sending. A **no match** is a stronger warning: the name and the account do not belong together, and the payment is likely going to the wrong person or to a fraudster. Never ignore a no match. Verification of payee exists to stop **authorised push payment fraud** and to stop typing errors, and the few seconds it takes to check are worth far more than the hours it takes to chase a payment sent to the wrong account.

Read the full chapter →
Q80.A customer submits a SEPA credit transfer on Friday evening and expects the money to arrive the same day. Explain how SEPA value dates and cut-off times work, and when the beneficiary will actually be paid.Beginner

A standard **SEPA Credit Transfer**, or SCT, is not instant. It is processed on **business days**, and the value date, the day the beneficiary is credited, depends on when the payment is submitted and on the **cut-off time** of the payer bank. If the customer submits the payment on Friday evening after the cut-off, the bank will process it on the next business day, which is Monday, and the beneficiary will be credited on Monday, or Tuesday if the beneficiary bank takes a day to process it. The SEPA rule is that the payment must reach the beneficiary bank by the end of the next business day after it is accepted, so a Friday evening payment is not late, it is simply queued for Monday. If the customer needs the money to arrive on Friday, they should use **SEPA Instant**, which settles in seconds, 24 hours a day, including weekends. Tell the customer to check the bank cut-off time, which is usually published on the website, and to submit the payment before it if they want same day processing. The value date is the date the money is available to the beneficiary, not the date the customer clicked send, and understanding that difference avoids most complaints about SEPA timing.

Read the full chapter →
Q81.A corporate customer needs to pay a supplier 150,000 euro immediately, but their bank SEPA Instant limit is 100,000 euro. Explain the options and the risks of splitting the payment.Intermediate

The **SEPA Instant** scheme has a maximum amount per transaction, and many banks set their own lower limit, often **100,000 euro**, for risk and liquidity reasons. The customer has three options. First, ask the bank to raise the **limit** temporarily for this payment, which the bank may do after checking the customer and the beneficiary. Second, split the payment into two **SEPA Instant** payments, for example 100,000 euro and 50,000 euro. This works, but it creates a **reconciliation** problem, because the supplier receives two payments instead of one and must match both to the same invoice. Third, send the payment as a standard **SEPA Credit Transfer**, which has no scheme limit, but which will not arrive instantly and may take until the next business day. Splitting the payment also carries a **fraud risk**: if the supplier account is compromised, the customer has sent two payments instead of one, and both are irrevocable. Tell the customer to confirm the split with the supplier first, to include the same invoice reference on both payments, and to ask the bank about a temporary limit increase before splitting. The best option is usually the limit increase, because it keeps the payment as a single transaction with a single reference.

Read the full chapter →
Q82.A biller collects a SEPA Direct Debit and the customer bank returns it. The biller wants to know why. Explain the SDD R-transactions: return, refund, reversal, and reject, and what each one means for the biller.Intermediate

**R-transactions** are the exception messages in **SEPA Direct Debit**. Each one means something different, and the biller must handle them differently. A **reject** happens before the collection is processed, usually because the debtor account is closed, the IBAN is wrong, or the mandate is invalid. The biller receives the reject quickly and can fix the data. A **return** happens after the collection, because there were insufficient funds, or the debtor bank refused the debit. The biller can try to collect again, but should check with the debtor first. A **refund** is requested by the debtor: for an authorised collection, the debtor has **8 weeks** to ask for a refund, no questions asked, and the bank must return the money. A **reversal** is requested by the creditor bank, usually because the collection was made in error, for example a duplicate. The biller must understand that a refund is the debtor right, not a dispute, and that repeated refunds are a warning sign that the mandate or the collection process is wrong. The biller should track R-transactions by reason code, fix the root cause, and never keep collecting from an account that keeps returning the debit, because that damages the customer relationship and can lead to the mandate being cancelled.

Read the full chapter →
Q83.A bank in Sweden, which is in SEPA but does not use the euro, wants to offer SEPA Instant payments to its customers. Explain the challenges and what the bank must build.Advanced

Sweden is in **SEPA** but does not use the euro, which creates a specific challenge: the customer account is in **Swedish krona**, but the SEPA Instant payment must settle in **euro**. The bank must therefore offer a **currency conversion** as part of the payment, converting krona to euro at the point of sending, and it must show the customer the exchange rate and the converted amount before they confirm. The bank must also be **reachable** for SEPA Instant, which means connecting to a clearing system such as **TIPS** or the EBA Clearing RT1 system, and being available 24 hours a day, because instant payments never sleep. The bank must handle the **liquidity** in euro, holding enough euro in its settlement account to cover outgoing instant payments at any time, including weekends when the FX market is closed. The bank must also provide **verification of payee** for the euro IBAN, and it must handle **recalls** and **returns** in euro. The customer experience must be clear: the customer pays in krona, the beneficiary receives euro, and the exchange rate is shown upfront. The bank that gets this right can offer a genuinely useful service. The bank that gets it wrong will face complaints about rates, delays, and payments that fail because the euro liquidity ran out.

Read the full chapter →
Q84.A fraudster tricks a customer into sending a SEPA Instant payment to a mule account. The money is moved on within minutes. Explain why instant payments are attractive to fraudsters and what banks do to stop it.Advanced

**SEPA Instant** payments are attractive to fraudsters because they are **irrevocable** and they settle in **seconds**. Once the money is credited to the mule account, the fraudster can move it on to another account, withdraw it, or convert it, all before the victim realises they have been tricked. There is no time to stop the payment, because there is no clearing window to intervene in. Banks fight this in three ways. First, **verification of payee** checks the payee name against the IBAN before the payment is sent, and warns the customer if there is a mismatch. Second, **transaction monitoring** looks for mule account patterns: an account that receives money and immediately sends it on, an account with no normal activity that suddenly receives a large payment, or an account linked to other known mule accounts. Third, banks use **velocity controls** and **behavioural checks**, such as flagging a first time payment to a new payee, a payment that is unusual for the customer, or a payment made at an odd hour. When a bank detects a mule account, it freezes it and shares the intelligence with other banks. The victim bank should also try to recover the funds by contacting the beneficiary bank immediately, but recovery is rare once the money has moved. Prevention, through verification of payee and real time monitoring, is the only reliable defence.

Read the full chapter →
Q85.Your bank is choosing how to settle SEPA Instant payments: through TIPS or through EBA Clearing RT1. Explain the difference between the two and how the bank decides.Expert

**TIPS**, the TARGET Instant Payment Settlement service, is run by the **Eurosystem** and settles SEPA Instant payments in **central bank money**, in real time, 24 hours a day. Each payment is settled individually and immediately, with finality at the moment of settlement. **RT1**, run by **EBA Clearing**, is a clearing system that also settles in real time, but it uses a **prefunded** model: participating banks hold funds in a technical account, and payments are settled against those prefunded balances. The difference matters for **liquidity** and for **risk**. With TIPS, the bank needs liquidity in its central bank account, and settlement is in central bank money, which is the safest form of settlement. With RT1, the bank needs to prefund the technical account, and the prefunding must be managed carefully, because if the prefunded balance runs out, payments stop. The bank decision depends on its existing setup: a bank that is already a **direct participant** in TARGET services will find TIPS natural, while a bank that already uses EBA Clearing for other services may find RT1 easier. The bank should also consider **cost**, **resilience**, and **reach**: both systems reach all SEPA Instant participants, but the operational model, the liquidity management, and the incident handling are different. Many large banks connect to both, so that if one system has a problem, the other keeps payments flowing.

Read the full chapter →
Q86.Your bank still runs a legacy domestic payment format alongside SEPA. The board wants to retire the legacy format and move everything to ISO 20022. Explain the migration and the risks of running two formats in parallel.Intermediate

Migrating from a **legacy domestic format** to **ISO 20022** means changing the message format for every payment the bank sends and receives. The legacy format is usually a fixed length file or a proprietary message, while ISO 20022 uses **XML** with structured data, including structured addresses, purpose codes, and rich remittance information. The migration has three parts. First, the bank must **map** every field in the legacy format to the ISO 20022 equivalent, and decide what to do with fields that have no equivalent. Second, the bank must update its **customer channels**, because the data the customer provides must now be structured, and the bank must validate it before sending. Third, the bank must **test** with every counterparty, because a payment that is valid in the legacy format may be invalid in ISO 20022. Running two formats in parallel creates **reconciliation** risk, because the same payment can look different in each format, and it creates **operational** risk, because staff must know two systems. The bank should set a firm **retirement date** for the legacy format, migrate customers in waves, and keep the parallel run as short as possible. The longer the parallel run lasts, the more the bank pays in maintenance and the higher the chance of a payment being processed in the wrong format.

Read the full chapter →

Clearing and Settlement (18)

Q87.What is settlement risk?Intermediate

Settlement risk is the risk that one party to a payment or transaction does not deliver what it owes when it is due, even though the other party has already delivered its side. In payments, it is the risk that a bank credits its customer or releases goods or securities before it has actually received the funds from the sending bank, and then the sending bank fails to pay.

A simple example shows the problem. Bank A sends a payment instruction to Bank B, and Bank B credits its customer immediately in the expectation that Bank A will settle later that day. If Bank A becomes insolvent before settlement, Bank B has paid out money it will never receive. Bank B bears the loss, and its customer keeps the funds.

Settlement risk is largest in systems where there is a long gap between the payment instruction and the final settlement, such as deferred net settlement systems that settle once a day. It is smallest in real-time gross settlement systems, where settlement happens at the same moment as the payment, so there is no gap for a failure to fall into.

Banks and system operators manage settlement risk through several tools: settling in central bank money, which carries no credit risk; shortening the time between instruction and settlement; setting limits on how much a bank can owe; requiring collateral; and using payment versus payment or delivery versus payment mechanisms that make both sides settle at the same time. Reducing settlement risk is one of the main reasons central banks have promoted RTGS for high value payments.

Read the full chapter →
Q88.What is CHIPS netting?Intermediate

CHIPS netting is the process by which the Clearing House Interbank Payments System offsets payments between banks so that only the net amount needs to be settled at the end of the day. During the operating day, banks send payment instructions to CHIPS, which records them in a central queue. CHIPS does not settle each payment immediately. Instead, it keeps a running total of what each bank owes to every other bank. If Bank A owes Bank B 100 million dollars and Bank B owes Bank A 80 million dollars, the net position is 20 million dollars from A to B. CHIPS also uses a liquidity saving mechanism. It holds payments in a queue and releases them when an offsetting payment arrives, so that the net amount is smaller and less liquidity is needed. Each participant prefunds an account at the Federal Reserve Bank of New York, and CHIPS uses that prefunded balance to settle net positions. At the end of the day, CHIPS calculates the final net position for each bank and settles it by moving funds between the prefunded accounts. If a bank has a net debit, it must have enough prefunded balance to cover it. If it does not, CHIPS can use a loss sharing arrangement. Netting reduces the amount of liquidity banks need, because they do not have to fund every payment in full. The trade off is that settlement is not immediate for each payment, and banks face intraday exposure until the final net settlement.

Read the full chapter →
Q89.How does a bank manage cut-off times across multiple clearing systems?Intermediate

A large bank connects to many clearing systems: Faster Payments, CHAPS, BACS, SEPA, Fedwire, CHIPS and SWIFT. Each one has its own cut off time, the last moment a payment can be sent and still settle that day. The bank manages this with a cut off calendar. For each clearing system, the bank records the cut off time, the time zone and the value date rule. The payment hub reads this calendar when it routes a payment. If a payment arrives before the cut off, it is sent the same day. If it arrives after the cut off, the hub either holds it for the next day or rejects it, depending on the product rules. The customer is told the value date so they know when the beneficiary will receive the money. The complexity comes when a payment crosses time zones. A payment sent from London at 4pm for a US beneficiary may miss the Fedwire cut off in New York because of the time difference. The hub must convert the times correctly. The BA documents the cut off rules as a matrix: each clearing system, each currency, each cut off time and what happens after it. When a clearing system changes its hours, the BA updates the matrix and the hub configuration. Getting a cut off wrong means a payment settles a day late, which is a customer complaint and sometimes a financial loss.

Read the full chapter →
Q90.How does your bank actually connect to a clearing house? Explain the technical path from the payment hub to the clearing system.Expert

The bank does not send payments directly from the branch or the app to the clearing house. The **channel** captures the instruction and passes it to the **payment hub**. The hub is the single control point. It validates the instruction, checks sanctions and fraud, applies the charge option, and decides the clearing route. Then it formats the payment into the clearing system's message standard, for example **ISO 20022 pacs.008** for most modern clearing systems, or the local format the clearing house requires.

From the hub, the payment travels over a secure connection to the clearing house. For **SWIFT**, that connection is the SWIFT network, and the bank's **BIC** identifies it. For domestic clearing such as **CHAPS** or **Faster Payments**, the bank connects through the Bank of England or the Faster Payments central infrastructure, usually over a dedicated network link with encryption and mutual authentication. The clearing house validates the message, checks the sending bank's settlement account balance, and settles or queues the payment. The confirmation then travels back along the same path, and the hub updates the payment status. Every hop is logged so the bank can trace the payment end to end.

Read the full chapter →
Q91.The clearing house is down during a settlement window. What does the bank do with payments queued for that window?Advanced

The first step is to confirm the outage is real and not a problem on the bank's own side. The operations team checks the clearing house status page and contacts the clearing house service desk. Once confirmed, the **payment hub** holds all payments due for that window in the queue. Nothing is released, because there is nowhere to send it. The bank must not try an alternative route without checking, because the payment may already have been accepted by the clearing house before it went down.

The bank then communicates. Clients with time-critical payments are told the clearing house is down and given a revised estimate. Treasury is told, because the funding plan for the day changes. When the clearing house comes back, the bank releases the queued payments in priority order, usually high-value and time-critical first. The hub checks each payment is still valid, because some may have passed their value date or cut-off while waiting. If the outage runs past the settlement window, the value date moves to the next working day and the bank tells the affected clients. The bank also logs the incident, because a clearing house outage is a reportable operational event.

Read the full chapter →
Q92.Your bank has a large FX payment settling through CLS. How does CLS remove settlement risk, and what happens if one leg fails?Advanced

**CLS**, Continuous Linked Settlement, removes **Herstatt risk**, which is the risk that one side of an FX trade settles and the other side does not. The bank submits both legs of the FX payment to CLS. CLS holds both legs and settles them simultaneously, payment versus payment. If one leg cannot settle, neither leg settles. That is the core protection. The bank funds its CLS account in each currency before the settlement window, and CLS nets the flows so the bank only funds the net amount, not the gross.

If one leg fails, CLS does not settle the trade. The bank is told which currency is short and by how much. The bank then has to fund the short leg, usually by borrowing in the market or moving funds from another account. If it cannot fund in time, the trade is deferred to the next settlement cycle or unwound, and the bank faces a replacement cost because the FX rate has moved. The bank's treasury and operations teams monitor CLS funding continuously, because a shortfall in one currency can block settlement of several trades at once. The lesson is that CLS does not remove the need for funding, it removes the risk of paying one leg and never receiving the other.

Read the full chapter →
Q93.A payment is stuck in the RTGS queue because the bank does not have enough balance. How does queue resolution work, and what can the bank do to release it?Expert

When a bank sends a payment through **RTGS** and its **central bank settlement account** does not have enough balance, the payment does not fail. It sits in the **RTGS queue**. The central bank's queue resolution mechanism looks at all queued payments across all banks and tries to find a set that can settle together, because one bank's outgoing payment is another bank's incoming payment. If a group of queued payments can be settled by offsetting them against each other, the central bank releases them as a batch. This is called **gridlock resolution** or multilateral offset.

The bank can also act on its own. It can add funds to the settlement account, either by moving money from another account or by borrowing from the central bank's **intraday liquidity facility** against collateral. It can cancel lower-priority queued payments to free up the queue, or it can reorder the queue to release the most time-critical payment first. The operations team monitors the queue continuously and escalates to treasury when a payment has been queued for a long time. The worst outcome is a payment sitting in the queue past its cut-off, because then the value date is missed and the bank has to explain to the client why the payment did not settle on time.

Read the full chapter →
Q94.The bank receives a settlement confirmation from the clearing house. What does the bank do with it, and how does it update the payment status?Intermediate

The settlement confirmation arrives as a status message, usually a **pacs.002** with **ACSC** status, meaning the payment has been accepted and settled. The **payment hub** receives it and matches it to the original payment using the message reference and the **UETR**. The hub checks that the amount, currency, and value date match the original instruction. If they match, the hub updates the payment status to settled and posts the accounting entries, debiting the customer account and crediting the settlement account.

The hub then pushes the status update to the **channel**, so the customer can see the payment as completed. If the payment was a corporate payment, the hub may also send a confirmation through the corporate banking portal or an **MT900** confirmation message. If the confirmation does not match the original, for example the amount is different because charges were deducted, the hub raises an exception for the operations team to investigate. The settlement confirmation is the bank's proof that the money moved, so it is stored with the payment record and used later for reconciliation against the **camt.053** statement. Without the confirmation, the bank cannot be certain the payment settled.

Read the full chapter →
Q95.A payment is sent with the wrong settlement method in the pacs.008. What goes wrong downstream, and how do you fix it?Advanced

The **settlement method** in the **pacs.008** tells the clearing system how the payment should settle, for example through the central bank, through a correspondent, or through a clearing house. If it is wrong, the payment can go to the wrong settlement account or be rejected by the clearing system. The first sign is usually a **pacs.002** with an **RJCT** status, or the payment sitting in the hub with no settlement confirmation.

The operations team checks the pacs.008 against the static data for that corridor. Each corridor, meaning each currency and destination combination, has a defined settlement method, and the hub should have picked it automatically. If the static data is wrong, the fix is to correct the static data so every future payment on that corridor uses the right method. If the static data is right but the hub picked the wrong method, the fix is in the hub's routing logic. The failed payment itself must be repaired and resubmitted as a new instruction with a new message ID, keeping the same **UETR** so tracking stays continuous. The bank also checks whether other payments on the same corridor were affected, because a static data error usually hits more than one payment.

Read the full chapter →
Q96.A clearing house rejects a batch of payments for a formatting error. How does the bank find the error, fix it, and resubmit?Intermediate

When a clearing house rejects a batch, the first step is to read the rejection message carefully. It usually names the error, such as a schema failure, an invalid field, or a limit breach. The operations team pulls the rejected file and identifies which payments failed and which, if any, were accepted. The accepted ones are left alone, because resubmitting them would create duplicates.

The team then finds the root cause. If it is a **formatting error**, the fix is in the hub's message mapping for that clearing system. If it is a data error, such as an invalid **BIC** or a missing mandatory field, the fix is in the source data or the validation rules. The failed payments are corrected, revalidated, and resubmitted as new instructions with new message IDs, keeping the same **UETR** for tracking. The bank checks the value dates, because a rejected and resubmitted payment may miss its original value date, and the client must be told. The bank also adds a regression test so the same error is caught before submission next time, ideally at the hub's validation stage rather than at the clearing house.

Read the full chapter →
Q97.A customer payment is due to settle on a day the clearing house is closed for a holiday. What happens to the value date and the customer?Intermediate

When the clearing house is closed for a holiday, no settlement happens that day. The **payment hub** checks the clearing calendar before accepting the payment and warns the client that the value date will move. If the payment was already submitted, the hub holds it in the queue and releases it on the next working day. The value date becomes the next working day, and the customer is told the new date.

The bank must be careful with the customer promise. If the client was told the payment would settle on the holiday, that promise is now broken, and the bank should have caught it at submission. The channel should show the correct value date before the client confirms, not after. For standing instructions and scheduled payments, the bank's system should automatically move the value date to the next working day and tell the customer in advance. The operations team also watches the queue on the day before a holiday, because payment volumes spike as clients try to beat the closure, and the hub must process them all before the cut-off.

Read the full chapter →
Q98.Explain settlement finality. At what point can the bank be certain the money has moved and cannot be reversed by the clearing house?Intermediate

**Settlement finality** means the payment has settled and cannot be reversed by the clearing system. For **RTGS** payments, finality happens the moment the payment settles across the **central bank settlement account**. The sending bank's account is debited and the receiving bank's account is credited, and that movement is final. The receiving bank can then credit its customer knowing the funds are genuinely there.

For other systems, finality happens at different points. In **Faster Payments**, the beneficiary bank credits the customer immediately, but the interbank settlement is deferred, so the bank is taking a small risk until the net settlement cycle completes. In **CHIPS**, finality happens when the payment is released from the queue and settled through the prefunded account. In **SWIFT** correspondent payments, finality happens when the funds are credited to the beneficiary bank's account. The key point is that finality is a legal and operational concept, not just a technical one. Before finality, a payment can still be stopped or reversed. After finality, the only way to get the money back is a return or a recall, which needs the agreement of the receiving bank.

Read the full chapter →
Q99.The clearing system is down during the settlement window. Payments are queuing in the payment hub and the cut-off is approaching. How do you handle a clearing system outage?Advanced

A clearing outage means payments cannot settle, but they can still be accepted, validated, and queued. The first job is to protect the queue and keep customers informed. I confirm the outage through the clearing system status page and the **pacs.002** responses, because a missing response can look like an outage when it is actually a timeout. I check which payments are affected, separating those already settled from those still queued. For queued payments, I verify that the payment hub is holding them safely with their original value dates and instructions intact. I switch on **manual monitoring** of the queue, because automatic retry during an outage can create duplicates when the system comes back. I alert Treasury, because the outage changes the funding picture, and I alert the customer-facing teams with a clear message about what is delayed and when it is expected to clear. When the clearing system recovers, I release the queue in order, watching for duplicates and checking that each payment gets its **ACSC** confirmation. After the incident I run a root cause review and check whether the hub needs a better **store-and-forward** design, so queued payments survive an outage without manual intervention.

Read the full chapter →
Q100.How does a bank connect to a clearing house? What are the components of that connection, and what happens when it goes down?Advanced

A clearing house connection is not a single link, it is a set of components that must all work together. First, the **network connection** itself, usually SWIFT for cross border or a domestic network for local clearing. Second, the **message interface** that converts the hub's internal format to the clearing house format, ISO 20022 for modern clearing, MT for legacy. Third, the **security layer**: certificates, encryption and mutual authentication so the clearing house knows the message really came from your bank. Fourth, the **session management**: the connection must stay alive, handle logon and logoff, and recover from a dropped session without losing messages. Fifth, the **acknowledgement handling**: every message sent must get a response, and the system must track which messages are acknowledged and which are not. The design must include a **store and forward** mechanism, so if the clearing house is down, messages queue up safely and are sent when it comes back. You also need a **cut-off calendar** that knows every clearing window, holiday and maintenance period, so the hub never sends a payment when the clearing house is closed. Test the connection failure scenario regularly: kill the link, confirm messages queue, restore it, and confirm they all go through in order.

Read the full chapter →
Q101.How do cut-off times work across different clearing systems and time zones? What happens to a payment that arrives after cut-off?Intermediate

Cut-off times are the deadlines after which a payment cannot settle on the same day. Every clearing system has its own cut-off, and the hub must know them all. The design uses a **cut-off calendar** that stores the cut-off time for each clearing system, each currency, and each value date. When a payment arrives, the hub checks the current time against the cut-off for its route. If the payment arrives before cut-off, it goes for same day settlement. If it arrives after, the hub has two choices: queue it for the next business day, or reject it and tell the customer to resubmit. Most banks queue it and tell the customer the new value date. The tricky part is **time zones**. A payment from London to Tokyo crosses time zones, and the cut-off in Tokyo may have already passed when it is still morning in London. The hub must convert every cut-off to a common time zone, usually UTC, and compare against the current UTC time. You also need to handle **holidays**: if the destination country has a public holiday, the clearing system is closed and the value date moves to the next business day. The hub checks a holiday calendar before assigning a value date, because promising a value date that falls on a holiday is a broken promise to the customer.

Read the full chapter →
Q102.How does same-day settlement work? Walk through a high-value payment that is submitted, settled, and credited on the same day.Intermediate

Same-day settlement works because every part of the chain is aligned to the same clock. The customer submits the payment before the published **cut-off**, and the channel accepts it. The payment hub validates it immediately and sends the **pacs.008** to the clearing system. The clearing system processes it in its next settlement cycle. For a high-value system like **RTGS**, settlement is real time, so the funds move between the banks within minutes. For a batch system, the payment settles in the next batch window, which is still the same day if the cut-off was met. The beneficiary bank receives the instruction and the settlement, credits the customer account, and sends back a **pacs.002** with ACSC status. The sender gets confirmation the same day, and the **camt.054** notification arrives with the debit. The keys to making it work are a published cut-off that customers understand, a hub that processes fast enough to meet it, and a clearing system with enough cycles in the day. When the cut-off is missed, the value date shifts to the next business day, and the customer must be told. Same-day settlement is not magic, it is discipline around the clock.

Read the full chapter →
Q103.A corporate customer needs to send a 10 million pound payment today and it must settle today. Walk through how a high-value payment is processed cleanly.Expert

A high-value payment gets extra care at every stage, because the stakes are higher. The corporate customer submits the instruction, usually through a dedicated corporate channel, as a **pain.001**. The bank runs full validation, including sanctions screening, balance check, and a **four-eyes approval** if the amount exceeds the single-authoriser limit. The payment hub routes it to the high-value clearing system, such as **CHAPS** in the UK or **Fedwire** in the US, because these systems settle in real time with finality. The hub sends the **pacs.008** instruction, and the clearing system moves the funds between the banks settlement accounts immediately. The beneficiary bank receives the payment, credits the customer account the same day, and sends back a **pacs.002** with ACSC status. Treasury monitors the **Nostro position** throughout, because high-value payments move large amounts and the bank must have enough liquidity. The customer gets confirmation the same day, and the end-of-day **camt.053** statement shows the debit exactly as expected. The difference from a normal payment is the approval discipline, the real-time settlement, and the Treasury oversight, all of which exist because the amount justifies the extra control.

Read the full chapter →
Q104.How does the bank handle a partial acceptance, where the clearing house accepts some payments in a file and rejects others?Intermediate

**Partial acceptance** happens when the bank sends a file of payments to the clearing system and the clearing system accepts some and rejects others. The bank receives a status report, usually a **pacs.002** per payment, or a file-level response that lists the accepted and rejected items separately. The **payment hub** must handle each payment individually, not treat the whole file as accepted or rejected.

The accepted payments are processed normally. They settle, the status is updated, and the customer is told. The rejected payments are handled one by one. The hub reads the reason code on each rejection, classifies it as technical or business, and routes it to the right team for repair. The rejected payments are corrected and resubmitted as new instructions with new message IDs. The operations team checks the value dates, because the resubmitted payments may settle a day later than the original file. The team also investigates why the file had a mix of accepted and rejected items, because it usually means a data quality problem in the source system, and the same problem will affect the next file if it is not fixed. The bank tells the affected customers that their payments were delayed, not that the whole file failed.
