The bank holds a large balance in **Japanese yen**, but the urgent payments are in **US dollars**, and the yen cannot be spent on a dollar payment. It happens because liquidity is held in separate **nostro accounts** in different countries and different currencies, and moving it takes time, costs money, and depends on market hours. The yen balance may be trapped because the Japanese market is closed, because the bank has a **minimum balance** requirement with its correspondent, or because the funds are tied up in a **term deposit** that cannot be broken early. To free it up, the treasury team has three options. First, an **FX swap**: sell yen and buy dollars, which works if the FX market is open and the bank has a counterparty. Second, **borrow dollars** intraday from a correspondent bank, using the yen balance as evidence of creditworthiness. Third, **reprioritise** the dollar payments, delaying the less urgent ones until the dollar receipts arrive. The long term fix is better **liquidity forecasting** by currency, a **centralised treasury** that can see all balances in real time, and **standing FX facilities** so the bank can convert trapped balances quickly. Trapped liquidity is a sign that the bank is managing each currency separately instead of managing liquidity as a whole.

Read the full chapter →
Q165.It is month end and payment volumes are 40 percent higher than normal. The treasury team needs to fund the settlement account for the morning clearing window. Walk through how they prepare.Intermediate

Month end is the busiest day in payments, because **salaries**, **supplier payments**, and **tax payments** all fall on the same day. The treasury team prepares the day before. First, they take the **forecast**: the expected volume and value of outgoing payments, based on previous month ends and on the payment files already received from corporate customers. Second, they check the **opening balance** in the settlement account and calculate the shortfall. Third, they arrange **funding**: moving money from the bank own accounts, drawing on **intraday credit** from the central bank, or borrowing in the money market. Fourth, they set **limits and priorities**: they confirm which payments must settle in the first window, such as CHAPS house purchases and time critical corporate payments, and which can wait for a later window. Fifth, they brief **operations** on the plan, so everyone knows the funding is in place and what to do if volumes are even higher than forecast. During the morning, the team monitors the balance in real time and tops it up if needed. After the window, they review the forecast against the actual volumes and update the model, because a forecast that is wrong by 40 percent is a forecast that needs fixing before the next month end.

Read the full chapter →
Q166.A corporate customer notices that small charges are being deducted from their nostro account every month, and the balance is slowly falling. Explain what nostro charges are, why they appear, and how the customer forecasts them.Beginner

**Nostro charges** are the fees the correspondent bank deducts for holding and operating the **nostro account**. They include **account maintenance** fees, charges for each payment processed, fees for statements and reporting, and charges for investigations or repairs. The correspondent bank deducts them directly from the nostro balance, usually monthly, which is why the balance falls slowly even when no payments are going out. The customer should ask the correspondent bank for a **fee schedule**, which lists every charge and how it is calculated, and for a monthly **statement** that shows each deduction separately. To forecast the charges, the customer should take the expected number of payments, multiply by the per payment fee, add the monthly maintenance fee, and add a buffer for **exception charges**, such as investigation fees, which are higher and unpredictable. If the charges are higher than expected, the customer should check whether the account is being used efficiently: are payments being batched, are unnecessary investigations being raised, and is the account holding a larger balance than needed. The customer can also **negotiate** the fees with the correspondent bank, especially if volumes are growing, because correspondent banking is a competitive business and fees are not fixed forever.

Read the full chapter →
Q167.Several large payments are stuck in the RTGS queue because no bank has enough balance to settle. The queue is not clearing and the central bank intervenes. Explain RTGS gridlock and how queue resolution works.Expert

**Gridlock** happens in a **real time gross settlement** system when several banks are each waiting for an incoming payment before they can send their own outgoing payment, and nobody can move first. Bank A is waiting for money from Bank B, Bank B is waiting for money from Bank C, and Bank C is waiting for money from Bank A. No single bank is short of money overall, but each one is short right now, so the queue freezes. The central bank resolves gridlock with a **queue resolution** mechanism, also called a gridlock resolution. It looks at all the queued payments together, finds a set of payments that can be settled **simultaneously** if they are offset against each other, and settles them as a group. For example, if A owes B 10 million, B owes C 10 million, and C owes A 10 million, the central bank can settle all three at once with no net movement of money. Banks can also help by providing **intraday liquidity**, by reordering their queue to prioritise the payments that unblock others, or by splitting a large payment into smaller ones that can settle. The lesson for treasury teams is to monitor the queue early, to keep a **liquidity buffer**, and to communicate with the central bank, because a gridlock that is spotted early is resolved in minutes, while one that is left alone can freeze the whole system for hours.

Read the full chapter →
Q168.The treasury forecasting model predicted 500 million in outgoing payments today, but the actual volume is 700 million. The settlement account is underfunded. Explain what went wrong and how the team recovers and fixes the model.Advanced

A forecast that is wrong by **40 percent** usually has a specific cause, not a random error. The first step is to find it: did a large corporate customer send a payment file that was not in the forecast, did a **value date** change move payments from tomorrow to today, or did the model use the wrong day, such as treating a month end Monday as a normal Monday. The team recovers by **funding the gap** immediately: drawing on intraday credit from the central bank, borrowing in the money market, or moving funds from another account. They also **prioritise** the queue, settling the time critical payments first and delaying the rest until the funding arrives. Once the day is over, they fix the model. They compare the forecast against the actual payments, line by line, to find which customers or payment types were missed. They update the model to include **corporate payment files** received in advance, to handle **value date** changes, and to use a separate forecast for month end, quarter end, and year end, when volumes are always higher. They also set a **trigger**: if the actual volume exceeds the forecast by more than 10 percent by mid morning, the team escalates and arranges extra funding before the account runs dry. A forecast is only useful if it is checked and corrected, and a 40 percent error is a signal to rebuild it, not to ignore it.

Read the full chapter →

Reconciliation and Investigations (48)

Q169.What is a payment recall?Beginner

A payment recall is a request by the sending bank to cancel a payment that has already been sent and to return the funds. It is used when the payment was sent by mistake, for example to the wrong beneficiary, for the wrong amount, or in duplicate, or when the underlying transaction has been cancelled.

The recall is sent as a message through the same network that carried the original payment, usually a SWIFT message asking the beneficiary bank to return the funds. The sending bank must give a clear reason, such as wrong beneficiary or duplicate payment, and provide the original payment reference so the receiving bank can identify it.

Whether a recall succeeds depends on timing and on the beneficiary. If the funds have not yet been credited to the beneficiary's account, the beneficiary bank can usually stop the payment and return the money. If the funds have already been credited and the beneficiary has withdrawn or used them, the beneficiary bank cannot simply take the money back. It must ask the beneficiary for consent to return the funds, and the beneficiary can refuse.

That is why recalls are not guaranteed. They work best when raised quickly, within hours of the original payment, and when the error is clear. A recall is also different from a fraud report: if the payment was the result of fraud, the bank will follow its fraud process alongside the recall, and may involve law enforcement. The practical lesson is to check payment details carefully before sending, because undoing a payment is far harder than getting it right the first time.

Read the full chapter →
Q170.What is a payment return?Beginner

A payment return is when a payment that was sent to a beneficiary bank is sent back to the sender because it cannot be applied. Unlike a recall, which is initiated by the sender, a return is usually initiated by the beneficiary bank or an intermediary bank that cannot complete the payment.

The most common reasons for a return are incorrect beneficiary details, such as a wrong account number or a name that does not match the account, a closed or blocked account, or missing information that the beneficiary bank needs to process the credit. Compliance reasons can also cause a return: if the payment fails a sanctions or anti money laundering check at the receiving bank, it may be returned rather than credited.

When a payment is returned, the funds travel back through the chain to the sending bank, which credits the sender's account. The returned amount may be less than the original because intermediary banks may have already deducted their fees, and because a currency conversion may have happened at a different rate on the way back.

A return message should explain the reason, often with a standard return reason code, so the sender can fix the problem and resend the payment correctly. If returns happen repeatedly on the same corridor or beneficiary, it is a sign that the payment details need to be corrected at the source, such as verifying the beneficiary's account details before sending. Keeping accurate beneficiary records is the simplest way to avoid returns.

Read the full chapter →
Q171.What is a nostro account reconciliation?Intermediate

Nostro account reconciliation is the daily process of matching every entry on a nostro account statement from the correspondent bank against the bank own internal records, to prove that the two agree. The bank downloads the statement from, say, Wells Fargo for its US dollar nostro account, and compares each debit and credit with its own ledger. Items that match are cleared. Items that do not match become breaks, and each break must be investigated. Common breaks include a payment debited by the correspondent but not yet recorded internally, a charge of USD 20 deducted without a matching instruction, a value date difference, or a credit that arrived a day later than expected. Reconciliation matters because a nostro account is real money held abroad. An unreconciled difference can hide a duplicate payment, a fraud, a misapplied credit, or a liquidity shortfall. Most banks reconcile daily, and many now reconcile intraday for their largest accounts. The process uses the account statement, usually an MT940 or MT950, plus the bank own payment records. Unmatched items are aged, and old breaks are escalated to operations managers because they can affect the bank balance sheet and its regulatory reporting. Good reconciliation also feeds liquidity forecasting, since the reconciled balance is the true amount available for new payments that day.

Read the full chapter →
Q172.What is a recall (camt.056) and when is it used?Intermediate

A recall is a request by the sender bank to the beneficiary bank to return a payment that has already been sent, and in ISO 20022 it is carried by the camt.056 message, the FI to FI Payment Cancellation Request. A recall is used when the sender has made a mistake, for example sending a duplicate payment, sending the wrong amount, sending to the wrong beneficiary, or sending a payment that was based on fraud. It is also used when the sender customer asks the bank to stop a payment after it has left the bank. The camt.056 must reference the original payment, including its UETR, its end to end identification, and its original instruction details, so the beneficiary bank can find the payment. It must also give a reason for the recall, such as duplicate payment or wrong beneficiary. The beneficiary bank is not obliged to return the funds automatically. It must check whether the funds are still in the beneficiary account, whether the beneficiary consents, and whether any legal reason prevents the return. In the worked example, if the French company realised it had sent USD 367,574.90 twice, BNP Paribas would send a camt.056 to Banco Santander, through the correspondent chain, asking for one payment to be returned. The recall does not move money by itself. It is a request, and the actual return happens only if the beneficiary bank agrees and sends a pacs.004.

Read the full chapter →
Q173.What is a payment repair?Intermediate

A payment repair is the manual work done to fix a payment that cannot be processed automatically because it has an error, missing data, or an unclear instruction. When a payment arrives at a bank and fails straight through processing, it is moved to a repair queue, where an operations analyst reviews it and decides what to do. Common repairs include fixing a wrong account number, adding a missing beneficiary address, correcting a wrong currency code, clarifying a vague remittance reference, or splitting a payment that exceeds a limit. The analyst may need to contact the sender bank for the correct details, using an MT195 query or a camt.028 status request. The repair must be done before the payment cut off, or the payment will be delayed to the next day. Repairs are expensive, because they take staff time and they slow the payment down, and they are often charged back to the sender bank or to the customer. Banks therefore measure their repair rate, which is the percentage of payments that need manual repair, and they work to reduce it by improving customer instructions, by validating account numbers before release, and by using structured data in ISO 20022, which leaves less room for free text errors. A payment that cannot be repaired, for example because the beneficiary cannot be identified at all, is returned to the sender with a pacs.004 and a reason code, rather than being held indefinitely.

Read the full chapter →
Q174.What is a payment amendment and how is it processed?Intermediate

A payment amendment is a change to a payment instruction after it has been sent but before it has been finally settled, for example correcting a beneficiary name, changing an account number, updating a remittance reference, or changing the value date. Amendments are needed when the sender spots an error, or when the beneficiary asks for a correction, and they are processed through a formal request, not by editing the original message. In the MT system, an amendment is usually sent as an MT195 query with the corrected details, or as a new instruction that cancels and replaces the old one. In ISO 20022, an amendment can be sent as a camt.056 cancellation request followed by a new pacs.008, or as a pacs.008 amendment where the scheme allows it. The bank that receives the amendment must check whether the payment can still be changed. If the payment is still with the sender bank, the change is easy. If it is already with a correspondent, the correspondent must be asked to apply the change, and it may charge a fee. If the payment has already been credited to the beneficiary, an amendment is no longer possible, and the sender must use a recall instead. Amendments are treated as urgent, because a payment with the wrong beneficiary details may be returned or credited to the wrong person. Customers should therefore check payment details carefully before release, because an amendment after release is slower, more expensive, and less certain than getting it right first time.

Read the full chapter →
Q175.How does a reconciliation API work? How do a bank and its corporate partner compare their payment records at end of day?Advanced

A **reconciliation API** lets the bank and its partners compare their records automatically. The flow is: at end of day, the hub generates a **reconciliation file** listing every payment it processed, with the payment ID, the amount, the currency, the status, and the settlement reference. The partner downloads the file through an API endpoint and compares it against their own records. Any payment in the hub file but not in the partner's records is a **missing payment** on the partner's side. Any payment in the partner's records but not in the hub file is a payment the hub never received. Any payment in both but with a different amount or status is a **mismatch**. The API also supports **intraday reconciliation**: the partner can query the status of a specific payment at any time through the status enquiry endpoint. The reconciliation file is usually in **CSV or JSON** format, and it is available for download for at least 90 days. The most important design point is that the reconciliation data must come from the same **source of truth** as the payment processing, not from a separate reporting database that could be out of sync.

Read the full chapter →
Q176.How does a bank reconcile payments at end of day?Intermediate

Reconciliation is the daily check that every payment the bank sent actually settled, and every payment it received actually arrived. The reconciliation team starts with three lists: what the payment hub sent, what the clearing system confirmed and what the core banking system posted to customer accounts. They match these three lists against each other. A payment that appears on all three lists is clean. A payment that is on the hub list but not on the clearing list is a problem: it was sent but clearing has no record of it. A payment that is on the clearing list but not on the core banking list is also a problem: clearing settled it but the customer account was not updated. The team investigates each break. Common causes are a timing difference, the payment settled after the reconciliation cut off, or a genuine error like a wrong account number. Nostro reconciliation is done the same way: the bank's own ledger is matched against the statement from the nostro agent bank. Any difference is a break that must be resolved before the next business day. Reconciliation is not a nice to have. It is how the bank knows its books are right, and regulators expect it to be done daily with breaks cleared within a set time.

Read the full chapter →
Q177.What happens when a payment is sent to the wrong account at a large bank?Intermediate

A payment sent to the wrong account is one of the hardest problems in payments because the money has already moved. First, the bank checks what happened: was the account number wrong, did the customer type it incorrectly, or did the bank map it wrong. Second, the bank contacts the receiving bank and asks for the money back. This is a recall, sent as a camt.056 cancellation request. Third, the receiving bank checks whether the funds are still in the account. If the beneficiary has already spent the money, the receiving bank cannot return it. If the funds are still there, the receiving bank asks the beneficiary for consent to return the money. The beneficiary can refuse, and in that case the sending bank has to take legal action or accept the loss. Fourth, the bank tells the customer what is happening and sets realistic expectations: a recall can take days or weeks, and it may not succeed. The bank also checks whether its own validation could have caught the error, for example by checking that the beneficiary name matches the account number. Confirmation of payee, which checks the name against the account before the payment is sent, prevents many of these cases. The BA needs to know this flow because it shapes the validation and confirmation requirements for any new payment product.

Read the full chapter →
Q178.It is end of day and the bank's central bank account does not reconcile. The balance is off and sign-off is due. What do you check, and what happens if you cannot find the break?Advanced

At the end of the day, the bank must prove its **central bank settlement account** balance matches what the central bank says it is. The operations team pulls the central bank statement, usually a **camt.053** or the central bank's own statement, and compares it line by line against the bank's own ledger. Every **RTGS** payment, every receipt, and every liquidity movement must appear in both. The team checks the opening balance, each transaction, and the closing balance.

If the balance does not match, the team finds the break. The most common causes are a payment that settled in the central bank system but was not posted in the bank's ledger, a duplicate posting, or a timing difference where a payment settled after the bank's end-of-day cut-off. Each break is investigated, the root cause is found, and the ledger is corrected. The reconciliation must be signed off before the bank closes the day, because an unreconciled central bank account means the bank does not know its true cash position. If the break cannot be resolved the same day, it is logged, owned by a named person, and escalated to the operations manager.

Read the full chapter →
Q179.A cross-border payment is rejected before settlement and the receiving bank sends back a pacs.002 with RJCT status and a reason code. No funds have moved. What do you do?Beginner

A **pacs.002** with RJCT status is a pre-settlement rejection, so the first fact I establish is that no money has moved. That single fact decides the whole path, because this is repair and resubmit, not a return. I read the **reason code** carefully, because it tells me exactly what failed. Then I classify the failure as technical or business. A technical failure means a schema error, a bad format, or an invalid field, and the fix sits with the sending system. A business failure means a sanctions flag or a regulatory restriction, and the fix sits with compliance. I confirm there is no settlement by checking that no **ACSC** status exists for this payment. Then I repair at the source, fixing the instruction data or the originating system, not just this one payment. I resubmit as a new instruction with a new message ID, but I keep the same **UETR** so tracking stays continuous. I also check whether the same defect affects other payments in the batch or from the same source. Finally I feed the root cause back into the validation rules, so the next bad payment fails earlier, ideally at initiation, before it ever leaves the bank.

Read the full chapter →
Q180.The instructed amount and the settled amount differ on a cross-border payment. The payment engine validated the instruction and sent a pacs.008, but the clearing layer settled a different amount. How do you investigate?Advanced

The engine and the clearing layer apply different rules, so the instructed amount and the settled amount can legitimately differ. My job is to find exactly which rule changed it, and whether that rule was supposed to apply. I start from the **pacs.008** the engine sent and compare the instructed amount against what the clearing layer actually settled, so I know the size and direction of the difference. Then I check **fees and charges** applied downstream, starting with the charge option, OUR, SHA or BEN, and any correspondent deductions taken between instruction and settlement. I check **value dating and cut-off rules**, because if the payment missed a cut-off the value date shifts and the FX conversion may have happened at a different rate. I look for a format or rule-mapping issue at the handoff, such as a wrong settlement method or a wrong charge bearer default. I pull the **clearing confirmation and the pacs.002 chain** to pinpoint the exact hop where the amount changed. I fix it at the source, usually a mapping correction or a static data fix, not a one-off adjustment. Then I add a **regression test** for the same corridor and charge option, asserting the settled amount matches the expected amount every release.

Read the full chapter →
Q181.A customer is waiting for a 125,000 pound international payment. The sender confirms it left, the beneficiary bank says it never arrived. There is no rejection, no return, no confirmation. How do you investigate?Expert

When nobody can say where the money is, I prove what happened before I act. A blind re-send would risk a duplicate, which is worse than a delay. I first classify the investigation, because a payment that clearly failed needs a different approach from one where nobody can yet prove what happened. I pull the **UETR** and check the **gpi Tracker** for the last confirmed hop, because the last successful hop tells me where to look. Then I ask three questions. Is the payment sitting with an **intermediary**, is it in a **compliance review**, or is it stuck in a **queue**. I check **pacs.002 statuses and camt.054 notifications** for silent progress the customer cannot see. I contact the intermediary with structured references, the UETR, the EndToEndId and the amount, not a vague message asking where the money is. I do not re-send until the original is accounted for. And I keep both the sender and the expectant beneficiary updated at every step, because uncertainty needs communication most. A customer who hears nothing assumes the worst, so regular updates are part of the fix.

Read the full chapter →
Q182.A duplicate payment has gone out. The retry fired after a timeout and the system sent the same payment twice. The customer has been paid twice. What is your response?Beginner

The first move is to **stop the bleed**. I freeze the retry and payout batch immediately so no more duplicates go out while I investigate. Then I identify the full population, every payout that went twice, matched by reference or **idempotency key**. I reverse the duplicates systematically and track the **recovery rate** until every case is closed. Then I find the root cause. In most duplicate cases the retry fired after a timeout, and an idempotency gap turned the retry into a second payment. The system believed the first attempt had failed, but it had actually succeeded. I fix it permanently by putting **idempotency keys on every payout**, so a repeated request is recognised, not re-executed. I add real-time reconciliation that flags double credits the moment they happen. I also add a release gate, so retry-logic changes get **failure-injection tested** before they reach production. Finally I own it openly with customers. I say what happened, what I am doing, and when it will be fixed. Trust recovers faster than silence, and a duplicate payment is exactly the kind of incident where honest communication matters most.

Read the full chapter →
Q183.A payment was sent to the wrong account because the IBAN was typed incorrectly. The funds have settled and the beneficiary bank has credited the wrong person. What do you do?Expert

A payment sent to the wrong IBAN is not a failed payment, it is a successful payment to the wrong person. That distinction matters, because the recovery is a recall, not a retry. I start by confirming settlement, an **ACSC** status on the pacs.002 chain, which tells me the funds have actually moved. Then I send a **camt.056 cancellation request** down the chain to the beneficiary bank, asking for the funds back. The beneficiary bank checks whether the funds are still available and whether there is any fraud concern on the account. The decision comes back in a **camt.029**, accept or reject, with a reason. Only on accept does a **pacs.004** move the money back along the return chain. On reject, the sender has no payment-rail path left, and the only remaining option is a commercial claim outside the rails. Speed matters here. The faster the camt.056 goes out, the better the odds the funds are still there. I also set the customer expectation clearly on timing and charges before initiating, because returns are slower than people assume. And I feed the lesson back into initiation controls, so beneficiary details are validated before the payment is released.

Read the full chapter →
Q184.A customer wants to recall a payment that has already been credited to the beneficiary. The sender bank sends a camt.056, the beneficiary bank answers with a camt.029, and only then does a pacs.004 move the funds. Walk through this process.Advanced

A recall after credit is a request, not a command. The beneficiary bank decides, and the money only moves if it accepts. The sender bank sends a **camt.056 cancellation request** down the chain to the beneficiary bank. The beneficiary bank checks two things. Are the funds still available in the account, and is there any fraud concern. The decision comes back in a **camt.029**, accept or reject, with a reason code. Only on accept does a **pacs.004** move the money back along the return chain, hop by hop, in reverse order. On reject, the sender bank has no rail-based path left, and the customer must pursue a commercial claim. I keep the customer informed at every stage, because a recall can take days and silence creates escalations. I also make sure the **UETR and references** are linked between the original payment and the return, so both legs reconcile automatically. As a business analyst I build the recall **status model** around the real states, requested, pending, accepted, rejected, so operations always knows where a recall stands and what happens next. Speed is everything here, so the camt.056 must go out the moment the customer asks.

Read the full chapter →
Q185.A payment times out with no response. The bank sent a pacs.008, the network received it, but no pacs.002 came back within the SLA. Do you retry it?Advanced

No. A timeout means I do not know the outcome, and a blind retry can double-pay. I **freeze the payment** and block any automatic retry until the true state is established. Then I investigate with the **UETR, EndToEndId, and TxId** across the gpi Tracker and the internal hop logs. I check for late responses, because a pacs.002, pacs.004, or pacs.009 may have arrived after the timeout was declared. I reconcile against **camt.054 notifications and statements**, because the statement shows whether funds actually moved, regardless of what the status says. I map the possible outcomes. The payment could have failed, it could still be in flight, it could be delivered, it could be settled, or it could have been rejected with the response lost. I act only on the true state. I resubmit only if the payment truly failed. If it settled incorrectly, I switch to a recall or a return. The design lesson is that every **timeout path needs a defined investigation flow**, never a blind retry, and this belongs in the requirements. A system that retries on timeout without checking state will eventually double-pay a customer, and that is a far worse outcome than a delay.

Read the full chapter →
Q186.A pacs.004 return was expected three days ago but it never arrived. The original payment settled, the beneficiary bank said it would return the funds, and now there is silence. What do you do?Advanced

A return that never arrives is an open item, and open items age badly. I start by confirming the original payment settled, using the **ACSC** status on the pacs.002 chain. Then I check whether the return was actually initiated. I look for the **pacs.004** in the message logs, and I check the gpi Tracker with the original UETR to see if a return leg exists. If no pacs.004 was ever sent, I contact the beneficiary bank with a structured query, giving the full references, the original amount, and the date the return was promised. I ask for the return status and the expected value date. If the beneficiary bank says the return was sent, I check the intermediary hops, because a return can stall at any correspondent in the chain. I also check the **Nostro account** and the camt.054 notifications, because the funds may have arrived without the status message. If the return is genuinely lost, I escalate through the correspondent banking team and raise a formal investigation. Throughout, I keep the customer updated, because a missing return is a customer funds issue. I also log the case against the beneficiary bank, because a pattern of slow returns is a relationship issue, not just an operations issue.

Read the full chapter →
Q187.A corporate customer calls, angry, because a 500,000 euro payment to a supplier has not arrived after two days. The supplier is threatening to stop deliveries. How do you handle this complaint?Beginner

The customer is angry because they have no information, not just because the money is late. So the first job is to get facts fast and communicate them. I take the payment reference and the **UETR** and check the **gpi Tracker** immediately, because the last confirmed hop tells me where the payment is. I read the **pacs.002 chain** to see the latest status, whether it is accepted, pending, rejected, or settled. I check whether the payment is held in **sanctions screening**, stuck on a beneficiary name mismatch, or waiting at an intermediary. Once I know the state, I call the customer back with a clear answer. I say where the payment is, why it is there, and what happens next, with a realistic time. I do not guess. If the payment is held at the beneficiary bank, I raise a **camt.029 investigation query** to get the exact reason. If it needs to be returned, I start the **pacs.004** flow. If it is simply slow, I explain the corridor timing honestly. After the payment resolves, I follow up with the customer to confirm the supplier received it. Then I check whether the delay was avoidable, for example a missing field or a late submission, and I feed that back into the initiation controls so the next payment does not hit the same problem.

Read the full chapter →
Q188.The beneficiary bank credited a customer account, then discovered the account was closed. The beneficiary bank itself initiates the return. Who sends the pacs.004 and how does it work?Advanced

The beneficiary bank discovered the problem, so it becomes the return originator and sends the **pacs.004** itself. It does not wait for the sender to ask. The trigger is found post-credit, a closed account, a frozen account, or a similar problem discovered after the funds landed. The beneficiary bank initiates the pacs.004, and the return travels the **chain in reverse**, with each intermediary validating and passing it on. **Return charges** may be deducted at hops along the way, so the sender gets back the original amount minus charges. **Status reporting** on the return leg flows through pacs.002 updates, keeping every party informed. The original sender's books must match the return against the original payment using the **UETR**, so the two legs reconcile automatically. Operations needs the same **maker-checker discipline** on returns as on outward payments, because a return is a real movement of funds and an error here creates a second problem. The lesson for a business analyst is that returns can be initiated from either end of the chain, and the system must handle a beneficiary-initiated return just as cleanly as a sender-initiated one.

Read the full chapter →
Q189.A customer says the money left their account but the beneficiary never received it. Walk through your investigation step by step.Beginner

The payment was debited but the credit never arrived, so first confirm the debit actually happened by checking the **core banking posting**. Then check the **pacs.002** chain. If the clearing house returned an ACSC, settlement happened and the problem is downstream, likely at the beneficiary bank. If the pacs.002 shows RJCT, the payment was rejected before settlement and the funds should be returned automatically. If there is no pacs.002 at all, the payment is stuck between the hub and the clearing house. The most common cause is a **timeout** where the hub sent the message but never received an acknowledgement, so it does not know whether the clearing house got it. In that case you must not resend blindly, because that creates a duplicate. Instead, send a **status enquiry** to the clearing house using the UETR. Once you know the true status, act on it. If settled, chase the beneficiary bank. If rejected, return the funds. If never received, resend with the same UETR. Always keep the customer informed at each step and give a realistic time for resolution. The worst thing you can do is tell the customer to wait without knowing where the payment is.

Read the full chapter →
Q190.How do you reconcile payments between the payment hub, the core banking system and the clearing house? What are the common breaks?Advanced

Reconciliation between the hub and the core is a **three way match**. At end of day, you compare three sources: the **payment hub ledger** (every instruction the hub accepted), the **core banking postings** (every debit and credit the core recorded), and the **clearing house confirmations** (every payment the clearing house settled). The three must agree. Start with the hub ledger as the source of truth for what was initiated. For each payment, check that the core has a matching debit. Then check that the clearing house has a matching settlement. Any payment in the hub but not in the core is a **posting failure**. Any payment in the core but not in the hub is an **unauthorised posting**. Any payment in the hub and core but not in clearing is a **settlement failure**. Run the reconciliation automatically every night and produce a **break report** listing every mismatch with the amount, the UETR and the age. Operations clears the breaks the next morning. The reconciliation must also check amounts, not just counts, because a payment can exist in all three systems with a different amount in one of them. That is the most dangerous break because it hides in a count match.

Read the full chapter →
Q191.Walk through a clean reconciliation day. How does a bank prove that its books match the clearing confirmations and the bank statements?Intermediate

Clean reconciliation means the books agree, and it works because the comparison happens continuously, not once a month. The payment hub records every payment it sends, with the amount, the value date, and the status. The clearing system sends back a **pacs.002** confirmation for each payment, and the hub matches it against the original instruction. The correspondent bank sends a **camt.053** statement at end of day, and the reconciliation engine matches each statement line against the hub ledger. Any line that does not match becomes a **break**, and the break is assigned to an owner with a deadline. In a clean operation, the break rate is near zero, because the hub, the clearing confirmations, and the statements all derive from the same payment data. The breaks that do appear are small and old, and they are cleared the same day. The reconciliation team reviews the **break aging report** every morning, and any break older than one day gets escalated. The key is that reconciliation is an **early-warning system**, not month-end admin. A bank that reconciles daily catches problems while they are small, and a bank that reconciles monthly discovers them when they are large.

Read the full chapter →
Q192.Walk through a clean end-of-day. How does the camt.053 statement get reconciled against the bank's books before the next business day?Intermediate

A clean end-of-day works because the statement and the books are compared the same day, not the next morning. The correspondent bank sends a **camt.053** statement at the end of the business day, listing every debit and credit on the Nostro account. The reconciliation engine takes the statement and matches each line against the payment hub ledger. Every payment the hub sent should appear as a debit on the statement, and every payment received should appear as a credit. The engine matches them by amount, value date, and reference. Lines that match are closed automatically. Lines that do not match become **breaks**, and each break gets an owner and a deadline. In a clean operation, the break count is zero or near zero, and the closing balance on the statement matches the **Nostro ledger** exactly. The reconciliation team reviews the result before the next business day starts, so the bank opens the new day with clean books. The key is the **timing**. A bank that reconciles the same day catches errors while the evidence is fresh. A bank that waits until month end is investigating from memory, and memory is a poor witness.

Read the full chapter →
Q193.A company pays a supplier overseas and the supplier reconciles the payment against the invoice on the same day. How does full remittance data make that possible?Beginner

A clean cross-border payment with full remittance data works because the beneficiary can reconcile it without a phone call. The customer sends a **pain.001** with the full remittance information, the invoice number, the purchase order, and the payment reference, all in the structured fields. The bank sends the **pacs.008** with the remittance data intact, and the intermediary banks pass it through without stripping it. The beneficiary bank receives the payment, credits the account, and includes the **remittance information** in the credit notification to the beneficiary. The beneficiary's accounts team matches the payment against the open invoice using the invoice number, and closes the invoice the same day. The sender gets a **pacs.002** with ACSC status, confirming the payment settled. The end-of-day **camt.053** shows the debit, and the beneficiary statement shows the credit with the reference. What makes it clean is the **remittance data surviving the journey**. In a poor flow, the reference is stripped at an intermediary and the beneficiary cannot match the payment. In a clean flow, the structured remittance data travels end to end, and reconciliation is automatic. A payment the beneficiary can reconcile same day is a payment that builds trust.

Read the full chapter →
Q194.A pacs.002 comes back with ACCP status. What does that mean, and what does the bank do with it?Beginner

**ACCP** means the payment has been accepted by the clearing system or the next bank in the chain, and it is being processed. It does not mean the money has settled yet. It means the payment passed validation, the account exists, and the payment is on its way. When the **payment hub** receives a **pacs.002** with ACCP, it matches the message to the original payment using the reference and the **UETR**, checks the amount and currency, and updates the payment status from submitted to accepted.

The hub then pushes the status to the **channel**, so the customer can see the payment is accepted and in progress. No accounting entries change at ACCP, because no money has moved yet. The hub keeps waiting for the next status, which should be **ACSC** once the payment settles. If ACCP is the last status the bank ever receives, and no ACSC follows within the expected time, the operations team chases it, because an accepted payment that never settles is a problem. The key point is that ACCP is a progress update, not a settlement confirmation, and the bank must not tell the customer the payment is complete at this stage.

Read the full chapter →
Q195.A pacs.002 comes back with RJCT. Walk me through the handling step by step.Intermediate

**RJCT** means the payment has been rejected before settlement, and no money has moved. That is the most important fact, because it means the fix is repair and resubmit, not a return. The first step is to read the **pacs.002** carefully. It carries a reason code that tells the bank exactly what failed, for example an invalid account number, a sanctions flag, or a formatting error.

The operations team classifies the failure as technical or business. A technical failure, such as a schema error or an invalid field, is fixed in the hub's message mapping or the source data. A business failure, such as a sanctions flag or a regulatory restriction, goes to compliance. The team confirms no settlement happened, then repairs the instruction at the source and resubmits it as a new payment with a new message ID, keeping the same **UETR** so tracking stays continuous. The team also checks whether the same defect affects other payments in the batch or from the same source. Finally, the customer is told the payment was rejected and why, in plain language, and given a revised timeline. The root cause is fed back into the hub's validation rules so the next bad payment fails earlier, ideally at initiation.

Read the full chapter →
Q196.The payment shows ACSC in the hub but the customer says they have not received the money. How do you investigate?Intermediate

The first step is to trust the **ACSC** status but verify it. ACSC means the clearing system confirmed settlement, so the funds left the bank. The operations team pulls the settlement confirmation and checks the amount, currency, value date, and beneficiary account against the original instruction. If everything matches, the bank's side is correct, and the problem is at the beneficiary bank or in the customer's expectation.

The team then checks the **SWIFT gpi** tracker, if the payment went through gpi, to see whether the beneficiary bank confirmed credit. If the tracker shows the payment was credited, the customer may be looking at the wrong account or the credit may not have appeared yet because of the beneficiary bank's own processing times. If the tracker shows the payment is still with the beneficiary bank, the team contacts the beneficiary bank directly and asks for the credit status. The team also checks whether the payment was recalled or returned after settlement, which would explain why the customer cannot see it. The customer is told what the bank found and when the credit should appear, and if the beneficiary bank cannot confirm the credit, the team opens a formal investigation with a **camt.056** or an **MT199** message.

Read the full chapter →
Q197.How does the bank reconcile its payment ledger against the camt.053 statement from its account servicer?Intermediate

The **camt.053** is the account statement the bank receives from its account servicer, usually a correspondent bank or the central bank. It lists every debit and credit on the account for the period, with references. The reconciliation team loads the camt.053 into the reconciliation system and matches each line against the bank's own **payment ledger**. A match needs the same amount, currency, value date, and reference.

Most items match automatically. The unmatched items fall into two groups. First, items on the statement that are not in the ledger, such as a credit the bank was not expecting, or a charge deducted by the correspondent. Second, items in the ledger that are not on the statement, such as a payment the bank sent but the servicer has not yet posted, which is usually a timing difference. Each unmatched item is investigated. The team checks the payment record, the settlement confirmation, and the correspondent's messages. When the root cause is found, the ledger is corrected or the item is explained. The reconciliation must balance before the team signs off, and any item that cannot be explained is logged and owned by a named person.

Read the full chapter →
Q198.A camt.054 debit notification arrives but there is no matching payment in the hub. What do you do?Advanced

A **camt.054** is a debit or credit notification. It tells the bank that money has moved on its account, and it arrives separately from the statement. When a camt.054 debit arrives with no matching payment in the hub, the first step is to check whether it is a charge, a fee, or a settlement adjustment, rather than a customer payment. Correspondent banks deduct charges, and the central bank deducts fees, and those appear as debits with no matching customer instruction.

If it is not a charge, the team checks the reference on the camt.054 against the payment records, the settlement confirmations, and the **nostro** account entries. The debit may relate to a payment that was processed through a different system, or a payment that was settled but the hub did not record correctly. The team also checks whether the debit is a duplicate of an entry already posted, because a duplicate camt.054 would create a double debit. Once the debit is identified, the team posts it to the correct account or corrects the hub record. If the debit cannot be identified after investigation, it is posted to a **suspense account** and owned by a named person until it is resolved. The bank never ignores an unexplained debit, because it means money has left the account.

Read the full chapter →
Q199.The bank sent 1,000 payments today but only received 995 pacs.002 responses. How do you chase the missing five?Beginner

The **payment hub** tracks every payment it sends and expects a **pacs.002** response for each one. At the end of the settlement window, the hub runs a check that lists every payment still waiting for a response. The operations team works through the list. For each missing response, the team checks whether the payment actually settled by looking at the clearing confirmation and the **camt.053** statement. Sometimes the payment settled but the pacs.002 was lost in transit, and the bank can update the status from the statement instead.

If there is no settlement confirmation either, the team checks the **SWIFT gpi** tracker to see where the payment is. If the tracker shows the payment is with an intermediary, the team contacts that bank. If the tracker shows nothing, the team sends an investigation message, usually an **MT199** or a **camt.056**, to the next bank in the chain asking for the status. The team also checks whether the clearing system had an outage that delayed the responses. The missing responses are chased the same day, because a payment with no status is a payment the bank cannot explain to the customer, and it may also be a payment that never settled.

Read the full chapter →
Q200.A duplicate pacs.002 arrives for a payment that is already ACSC. How does the bank handle it without double-posting?Beginner

A duplicate **pacs.002** is not unusual. The clearing system or an intermediary may send the same status twice, especially after a retry or a system recovery. The **payment hub** must handle it without double-posting. The hub matches each incoming pacs.002 to the payment using the message reference and the **UETR**, and checks the current status of the payment. If the payment is already **ACSC** and the duplicate pacs.002 also says ACSC, the hub recognises it as a duplicate and discards it. No accounting entries are posted a second time.

The hub uses the status sequence to decide. A status can only move forward, from accepted to settled, never backward. If a duplicate arrives with an older status, for example an ACCP after an ACSC, the hub ignores it because the payment has already moved past that stage. The hub logs the duplicate for audit, so the bank can show it was received and correctly discarded. The danger is a hub that does not check for duplicates, because it would post the settlement twice, credit the customer twice, or double-count the payment in reconciliation. The duplicate check is a basic control, and it should be tested in every release.

Read the full chapter →
Q201.The customer channel still shows the payment as pending, but the hub shows ACSC. How do you fix the mismatch and what do you tell the customer?Intermediate

This is a status synchronisation problem between the **payment hub** and the **channel**. The hub is the system of record, so the ACSC status in the hub is correct. The channel, which is what the customer sees, has not received the update. The first step is to confirm the hub status is genuinely ACSC by checking the settlement confirmation. Then the operations team checks the interface between the hub and the channel. The status update may have failed, the channel may have been down when the update was sent, or the channel may be showing a cached status.

The team forces a status refresh from the hub to the channel, so the customer sees the correct status. The team also checks whether other payments are affected, because a broken hub-to-channel interface usually affects more than one payment. The customer is told the payment has settled, even if the channel took time to catch up, and the bank apologises for the confusion. The root cause is fixed so the interface does not fail again. The key point is that the customer should never have to call the bank to find out a payment settled, because the channel is supposed to tell them automatically.

Read the full chapter →
Q202.A reconciliation break appears: the ledger shows a debit the clearing confirmation does not have. How do you find the root cause?Advanced

The first step is to confirm the break is real and not a timing difference. The team checks the value date and the settlement time. If the debit is in the ledger but the clearing confirmation has not arrived yet, it may simply be that the confirmation is still in transit, and the break will clear itself. If the confirmation should have arrived by now, the team investigates.

The team pulls the original payment instruction and checks the amount, currency, and reference against the ledger entry. The most common causes are a **reference mismatch**, where the clearing confirmation carries a different reference from the ledger, a **duplicate posting** in the ledger, or a payment that was sent through a different route from the one recorded. The team also checks the **camt.053** statement to see whether the debit appears there. If it appears on the statement but not in the clearing confirmation, the payment settled through a different channel. If it appears in neither, the payment may not have settled at all, and the team checks the **pacs.002** status. Once the root cause is found, the ledger is corrected, and the team checks whether the same error affects other payments. The break is documented, because reconciliation breaks are reviewed by audit.

Read the full chapter →
Q203.A payment is rejected with reason code AC01 (incorrect account number). What is the repair process and how do you stop it happening again?Intermediate

**AC01** means the account number is incorrect. The **pacs.002** carries this reason code, and it tells the bank the beneficiary account number in the instruction does not match any account at the beneficiary bank. The payment was rejected before settlement, so no money moved. The first step is to confirm the rejection and tell the customer the payment did not go through.

The operations team then checks the account number against the source. The error usually comes from the customer typing the number wrong, from a stale beneficiary record in the bank's system, or from a data migration that corrupted the account number. The team corrects the account number at the source, not just on this one payment, and validates it against the beneficiary bank's format rules. The payment is then resubmitted as a new instruction with a new message ID, keeping the same **UETR**. The team also checks whether other payments to the same beneficiary are affected. To stop it happening again, the bank should validate the account number at the point of entry, for example by checking the **IBAN** checksum or by confirming the beneficiary details with the customer before the first payment.

Read the full chapter →
Q204.The camt.053 shows a credit the bank was not expecting. How do you identify what it is and post it correctly?Advanced

An unexpected credit on the **camt.053** means money arrived in the bank's account that the bank was not expecting. The reconciliation team must identify it before it can be posted correctly. The first step is to read the statement line carefully. It carries a reference, a value date, an amount, and sometimes a remittance description. The team searches the **payment hub** and the **nostro** records for a matching payment using the reference and the amount.

The most common explanations are a return of a payment the bank sent, a refund from a correspondent, an interest payment, or a payment from a client that was not expected that day. If the team finds the match, the credit is posted to the correct account and the payment record is updated. If no match is found, the team contacts the account servicer and asks for more detail, and checks whether the credit relates to a payment that is still being investigated. If the credit still cannot be identified, it is posted to a **suspense account** and owned by a named person until it is resolved. The bank never treats an unexplained credit as income, because it may belong to a customer or may need to be returned.

Read the full chapter →
Q205.How does the bank reconcile nostro accounts using MT950 or camt.053, and what are the common breaks?Expert

**Nostro reconciliation** is the daily check that the bank's own record of its **nostro account**, the account it holds with a correspondent bank in a foreign currency, matches the correspondent bank's record. The bank receives a statement, usually an **MT950** or a **camt.053**, from the correspondent and compares each line against its own nostro ledger. A match needs the same amount, currency, value date, and reference.

The common breaks are timing differences, where a payment is recorded in the bank's ledger but has not yet appeared on the correspondent's statement, charges deducted by the correspondent that the bank did not expect, and **value date** mismatches where the two sides record the same payment on different days. Each break is investigated. The team checks the payment record, the settlement confirmation, and the correspondent's messages. Charges are verified against the agreed fee schedule and posted. Timing differences are monitored and should clear within a day or two. If a break does not clear, it is escalated. Nostro reconciliation matters because the nostro balance is the bank's cash in that currency, and if the balance is wrong, the bank may think it has funds it does not have, or refuse payments it could have made.

Read the full chapter →
Q206.A value date mismatch appears between the pacs.008 the bank sent and the settlement confirmation. How do you resolve it?Advanced

A **value date** mismatch means the bank expected the payment to settle on one date but the settlement confirmation shows a different date. The first step is to check the original instruction. The **pacs.008** carries the requested execution date, and the hub should have applied the correct value date based on the clearing calendar and the cut-off. If the hub applied the wrong value date, for example because it used the wrong calendar or ignored a holiday, the fix is in the hub's value date logic.

If the hub was right, the mismatch may come from the clearing system. The payment may have missed the cut-off and been pushed to the next working day, or the beneficiary bank may have applied a different value date. The operations team checks the **pacs.002** and the settlement confirmation to find where the date changed. The customer is told the actual value date, because it affects when the beneficiary can use the funds and whether interest or late payment charges apply. The team also checks whether the value date mismatch affects the accounting, because the bank's ledger posts the payment on the value date, and a wrong value date means the ledger is wrong for that day. The root cause is fixed so the same corridor does not produce the same mismatch again.

Read the full chapter →
Q207.The bank receives a pacs.002 with a status it does not recognise. What is the handling?Intermediate

When a **pacs.002** arrives with a status the hub does not recognise, the hub should not crash and it should not ignore the message. It should park the message in an exception queue and alert the operations team. The team reads the raw pacs.002 and identifies the status code. It may be a new status introduced by the clearing system, a proprietary status from an intermediary, or a code the hub's mapping table does not cover.

The team checks the clearing system's documentation to understand what the status means and whether it represents an acceptance, a rejection, or a settlement. The team then updates the payment status manually in the hub, so the customer can see the correct status, and tells the customer what happened. The hub's status mapping table is updated so the same status is recognised automatically next time. The team also checks whether other payments received the same unrecognised status, because a new status usually affects a group of payments, not just one. The lesson is that the hub must be able to handle unknown statuses gracefully, because clearing systems change their codes and the bank cannot afford to lose track of a payment because of a code it did not expect.

Read the full chapter →
Q208.An investigation is opened with a camt.056 for a payment the beneficiary says never arrived. Walk through the investigation.Advanced

When a beneficiary says a payment never arrived, the bank opens a formal investigation. The first step is to check the bank's own records. The **payment hub** shows the status, and the settlement confirmation shows whether the funds left the bank. If the payment shows **ACSC**, the funds did leave, and the investigation moves to the next bank in the chain.

The bank sends a **camt.056** cancellation request or an investigation message, usually an **MT199**, to the next bank, asking for the status of the payment and whether it was credited. Each bank in the chain responds in turn, and the bank traces the payment hop by hop until it finds where it stopped. The bank also checks the **SWIFT gpi** tracker, which may show the payment's location faster than the formal investigation. The customer is kept informed at each step, because an investigation can take days and the customer needs to know the bank is actively chasing it. If the payment is found sitting at an intermediary, the bank asks for it to be released or returned. If the payment was credited to the wrong account, the bank starts a recall. The investigation is closed only when the payment is found or the funds are returned.

Read the full chapter →
Q209.A reconciliation item sits in the suspense account for three days. What is the process to clear it, and who owns it?Intermediate

A **suspense account** is where the bank parks money it cannot yet explain. When a reconciliation item sits in suspense for three days, it is already overdue. The reconciliation team owns the item and must clear it. The first step is to re-investigate. The team checks the payment record, the settlement confirmation, the **camt.053** statement, and any messages from the correspondent or the clearing house. The team also checks whether the item is a duplicate, a charge, or a timing difference that should have cleared.

If the item can be identified, it is posted to the correct account and removed from suspense. If it cannot be identified, it is escalated to the operations manager, who assigns it to a named person with a deadline. The item is reported in the daily reconciliation summary, so management can see how many items are in suspense and how old they are. The bank sets an age limit, usually a few days, after which the item must be escalated to senior management. The key point is that money in suspense is money the bank cannot account for, and it is an audit and a control issue. A growing suspense balance means the bank's reconciliation process is not working, and that is a finding, not just an inconvenience.

Read the full chapter →
Q210.The bank's auto-reconciliation matches 98 percent of items. What happens to the other 2 percent, and how are they worked?Intermediate

**Auto-reconciliation** matches most items automatically, usually 95 to 99 percent, because most payments match on amount, currency, value date, and reference. The remaining 2 percent do not match, and they are the ones that need human attention. The reconciliation system puts the unmatched items in an exceptions queue, and the reconciliation team works through them. Each exception is one of a few types. A timing difference, where the item will match tomorrow when the other side posts it. A reference mismatch, where the two sides used different references for the same payment. A charge or a fee that one side recorded and the other did not. Or a genuine error, where a payment was posted wrongly or not at all.

The team investigates each exception by checking the payment record, the settlement confirmation, and the statement. Timing differences are monitored and should clear within a day. Reference mismatches are corrected by updating the matching rules. Charges are posted. Genuine errors are corrected and the root cause is found. The team reports the exception count and the age of the oldest exception every day, because a growing exceptions queue means the reconciliation process is falling behind. The goal is not 100 percent auto-matching, which is unrealistic, but a small, well-managed exceptions queue where every item has an owner and a deadline.

Read the full chapter →
Q211.A customer is charged a fee that does not match the charge option on the pacs.008. How do you investigate and correct it?Advanced

The charge option on the **pacs.008** tells the banks in the chain who pays the fees. **OUR** means the sender pays all charges, **SHA** means the sender and the beneficiary share them, and **BEN** means the beneficiary pays them all. When the customer is charged a fee that does not match the charge option, the first step is to check the pacs.008 and confirm what was instructed. Then the team checks the **camt.053** statement and the correspondent's messages to see what was actually deducted.

The most common cause is a correspondent bank deducting a fee that was not in the agreed schedule, or the beneficiary bank deducting a fee when the charge option said OUR. The team compares the deduction against the fee schedule agreed with the correspondent. If the deduction is wrong, the team raises a claim with the correspondent and asks for a refund. If the deduction is correct but the customer was not told, the issue is communication, and the bank should have explained the charges upfront. The customer is told what was charged, why, and whether a refund is due. The team also checks whether other payments on the same corridor were affected, because a fee error usually repeats. The charge option must be applied consistently, because a wrong charge is a customer complaint and a potential regulatory issue.

Read the full chapter →
Q212.How does end-of-day reconciliation sign-off work, and what happens if the team cannot sign off?Advanced

**End-of-day reconciliation sign-off** is the formal confirmation that the bank's books balance for the day. The reconciliation team checks that every payment sent and received is accounted for, that the **nostro** accounts reconcile to the correspondent statements, that the **central bank settlement account** matches the central bank's record, and that the **suspense account** contains no unexplained items beyond the agreed limit. Each reconciliation is reviewed and signed by the team lead, and the sign-off is recorded.

If the team cannot sign off, it means there is an unresolved break. The team identifies the break, quantifies it, and escalates to the operations manager. The manager decides whether the break is material. A small timing difference that will clear tomorrow may be accepted with a note. A large unexplained difference cannot be accepted, and the bank must keep working until it is resolved or a clear explanation is documented. The bank does not close the day with an unreconciled material break, because that means the bank does not know its true cash position. The sign-off is a control, and audit reviews it, so the team documents every break, its cause, and its owner, even when the break is resolved the same day.

Read the full chapter →
Q213.A pacs.002 arrives after the bank has already sent a pacs.004 return for the same payment. How do you resolve the conflict?Expert

This is a conflict that should not happen, but it does. A **pacs.004** return means the bank already sent the money back, but a **pacs.002** arriving afterwards says something about the original payment's status. The **payment hub** must handle this carefully. The hub checks the sequence. If the pacs.004 was already sent and the return is in progress, the pacs.002 is usually a late status update on the original payment, and it does not change the fact that the return is underway.

The operations team checks whether the pacs.002 status contradicts the return. For example, if the pacs.002 says the original payment was **RJCT**, meaning it never settled, then the return should not have been sent, because there was nothing to return. In that case the team stops the return if possible and investigates why the return was initiated. If the pacs.002 says **ACSC**, confirming the original settled, then the return is valid and the pacs.002 is just late information. The team updates the payment record to show both the original settlement and the return, so the full history is visible. The team also checks whether the return amount matches the original, because charges may have been deducted. The lesson is that messages can arrive out of order, and the hub must use the business state, not just the message arrival order, to decide what happened.

Read the full chapter →
Q214.A duplicate payment is sent because the channel submitted it twice. How does the bank detect it, stop the second one, and recover the funds if it settled?Advanced

A duplicate payment usually happens when the **channel** submits the same instruction twice, for example because the customer clicked submit twice, or because the channel retried a submission after a timeout without checking whether the first one went through. The **payment hub** should catch it. The hub checks each incoming instruction against recent payments using the customer, the amount, the beneficiary, and the reference. If it finds a match within a short window, it blocks the second submission as a suspected duplicate and alerts the operations team.

If the duplicate was not caught and both payments settled, the bank must recover the funds. The team confirms the duplicate by checking the payment records and the **camt.053** statement. The bank then contacts the beneficiary bank and asks for the duplicate to be returned, usually through a **pacs.004** return or a recall with a **camt.056**. The beneficiary bank will return the funds if they are still available. The customer is told what happened and that the duplicate is being recovered. The team also fixes the root cause, which is usually a missing duplicate check in the channel or the hub. The duplicate check should compare the full instruction, not just the amount, and it should cover a window of at least 24 hours, because duplicates can arrive hours apart.

Read the full chapter →
Q215.How does the bank reconcile charges and fees deducted by correspondent banks against what was instructed in the pacs.008?Expert

When a payment travels through correspondent banks, each bank in the chain can deduct a fee. The **pacs.008** carries the charge option, **OUR**, **SHA**, or **BEN**, and the instructed amount. The bank reconciles the charges by comparing three things. First, what was instructed in the pacs.008. Second, what the correspondent deducted, as shown on the **camt.053** statement and the **camt.054** notifications. Third, what the beneficiary actually received, as shown on the **gpi tracker** or the beneficiary bank's confirmation.

If the deductions match the charge option and the agreed fee schedule, the reconciliation is clean. If a correspondent deducted more than agreed, the team raises a claim and asks for a refund. If the beneficiary received less than expected, the team traces the deductions hop by hop through the gpi tracker to find where the extra fee was taken. The team also checks whether the charge option was applied correctly at each hop, because a bank in the chain may have misread the option. The customer is told the full fee breakdown when they ask, because transparency on charges is a regulatory expectation. The team reviews the fee schedule with each correspondent regularly, because fees change and the bank's reconciliation must reflect the current schedule.

Read the full chapter →
Q216.A payment is sent twice by mistake. How do you handle it?Intermediate

A duplicate payment is serious because the beneficiary has been paid twice and the bank may not get the second payment back easily. First, I confirm it is a real duplicate: same amount, same beneficiary, same reference, sent twice. I check whether both payments settled or only one did. Second, I stop any further duplicates: I check if the source system is sending the payment twice, if a retry loop is firing, or if an operator resubmitted manually. I make sure the root cause is fixed before more duplicates go out. Third, I start the recovery for the duplicate: the bank sends a recall request to the beneficiary bank asking for the second payment back. The beneficiary bank checks if the funds are still available and asks the beneficiary for consent. Fourth, I tell the customer what happened honestly: the payment was sent twice by mistake, we have asked for the second payment back, and here is the realistic timeline. Fifth, I investigate the root cause properly: was it a system retry without an idempotency check, was it a file sent twice, was it a manual error. I make sure the fix addresses the root cause, not just this one duplicate. For example, adding an idempotency key so the system recognises a retry of the same payment and does not process it twice. A duplicate payment is embarrassing but it is recoverable if handled quickly and honestly.
