Fraud AML and Sanctions (17)

Q217.What is sanctions screening?Beginner

Sanctions screening is the process of checking every party and detail in a payment against lists of people, companies, countries, and vessels that governments have sanctioned. If a payment involves a sanctioned person or country, the bank must not process it, or must process it only under a specific licence. Screening happens before the payment is released, and it is one of the most important controls in a bank, because a single missed sanction can lead to fines running into billions and serious reputational damage.

The screening engine compares the payment message against sanctions lists, such as the OFAC list in the United States, the EU consolidated list, and the UN list, plus the bank's own internal lists. It checks the sender and receiver names, and sometimes addresses, account numbers, and the payment narrative. Because names can be spelled differently or transliterated from other scripts, the engine uses fuzzy matching, which catches close matches rather than only exact ones. A payment that matches is stopped for a human analyst to review.

Screening applies to far more than just the customer. A bank must screen its customers at onboarding and on an ongoing basis, screen every payment it processes, and screen related parties such as directors and beneficial owners. It also has to keep up with lists that change frequently, sometimes daily, as governments add or remove names. The challenge is that screening generates a huge number of alerts, most of which turn out to be false positives, so banks invest heavily in tuning their engines and in trained analysts who can clear alerts quickly without letting a real sanction slip through.

Read the full chapter →
Q218.How does a bank handle a sanctions hit on a payment?Intermediate

When a payment hits a sanctions list, the system stops it automatically before it leaves the bank. No one can override this by hand. The payment goes to a sanctions queue where a compliance analyst reviews it. The analyst checks the name, the address and the details of the payment against the sanctions list to decide if it is a true match or a false positive. A false positive is common: a customer name that is similar to a sanctioned person but is not the same person. In that case the analyst clears the payment and releases it, and records the decision. A true match is different. If the payment is to a sanctioned person or country, the payment is blocked and the bank must not release it. The bank reports the blocked payment to the regulator and keeps a record. The customer is told the payment could not be processed, but the bank does not always explain the sanctions reason in detail. The BA needs to know this flow because sanctions screening sits in the middle of the payment journey, and any new payment product must pass through it. The screening must be fast enough not to delay normal payments, but thorough enough to catch real hits.

Read the full chapter →
Q219.A payment is sent to a bank in a country under sanctions screening. It is held at the clearing stage. Walk through what happens next.Intermediate

When a payment is held at the clearing stage for **sanctions screening**, it means a name, a country, or a word in the payment matched a sanctions list or a screening rule. The payment does not fail, it is held for review. The bank's compliance team receives the alert and investigates. They check the names against the sanctions lists, look at the full payment details, and decide whether the match is real or a false positive, for example a common name that happens to match a listed person.

If it is a false positive, compliance clears the payment and releases it, but the value date may have moved, and the client must be told. If the match is real, the payment is blocked and cannot proceed. The bank must not tell the client the specific reason if that would amount to **tipping off**, so the message to the client is kept generic. The bank reports the blocked payment to the relevant authority as required. The operations team also checks whether other payments from the same client or to the same beneficiary are affected. The key point is that a sanctions hold is a compliance decision, not an operations decision, and operations must not release the payment without compliance approval.

Read the full chapter →
Q220.A payment is held mid-flight because the beneficiary name fuzzy-matches a sanctions list. It could be a real hit or a false positive. What happens next?Advanced

The payment is held immediately and no funds move while the review is open. That is the first rule, because a held payment can be released but a released payment cannot be un-sent. The analyst escalates to the **compliance officer** with the match evidence attached, including which list matched, the match score, and the payment details. Then comes **true-match verification**. The compliance team compares the beneficiary details against the list entry, name, date of birth, address, nationality, to decide whether this is the same person or just a similar name. If it is a false positive, the payment is released and the decision is documented. If it is a true match, the payment is blocked, and if the activity meets the reporting threshold, a **SAR, Suspicious Activity Report**, is filed. Every step is documented, because the decision trail is what regulators will ask for. The lesson is that the **screening-to-escalation-to-SAR workflow** is the real control, not the alert itself. An alert is only a trigger. What matters is how fast the review happens, how well it is documented, and whether genuine payments get released quickly while real hits stay blocked.

Read the full chapter →
Q221.Screening flags the ultimate beneficiary details as doubtful, but not definitively wrong. Do you reject the payment immediately or investigate first?Advanced

When the data is doubtful but not definitively wrong, I ask before I kill the payment. I park it, request the information, and decide on facts. An instant reject could kill a legitimate payment, and a wrongly rejected payment damages the customer relationship. I send a **request for additional information** back up the chain to the sender bank, asking for the specific detail that is unclear. I **park the payment** with a clear status so it is visible in the queue, not lost in a pile. I give the sender a **bounded window** to respond, because open-ended parks become forgotten parks. If clean information arrives, I release the payment. If it confirms a problem, I reject or return depending on whether settlement has happened. If the deadline passes with no response, I apply the **default rule** in policy, reject pre-settlement, return post-settlement. As a business analyst I design the **aging, escalation, and default action** for parked payments, because without those controls they pile up silently. Every parked payment needs an owner, a deadline, and a defined outcome, or the queue becomes a graveyard of forgotten payments.

Read the full chapter →
Q222.A letter of credit worth 28 million dirhams is delayed eight working days because sanctions screening fuzzy-matched a common surname. There is no fraud and no real risk, just bad screening logic. How do you fix false positives without missing real hits?Advanced

About 95 percent of sanctions alerts are false positives, but every one still delays real business. The client in this case faced **cash-flow strain** because a legitimate letter of credit sat parked for eight working days on a common surname match. I fix it by **triaging by risk**. Exact matches and high-risk corridors get senior review first. Common-name matches go through a fast lane with a clear checklist. I **fine-tune the matching rules**, adjusting fuzzy-match thresholds per corridor and per name frequency, instead of one global setting that treats every name the same. I use **AI-assisted matching** to cut noise while keeping true-hit detection strong. I keep **watchlists current**, because stale lists generate stale alerts. And I measure the **false-positive rate and average hold time** as KPIs of the screening flow, reporting them to management. A screening system that catches everything but delays every legitimate payment is not working. The goal is a system that releases clean payments fast, holds genuinely risky ones, and gives operations a clear, fast path to resolve the grey area in between.

Read the full chapter →
Q223.A 500,000 dollar wire is blocked when the beneficiary name fuzzy-matches the OFAC SDN list. The analyst escalates to compliance, the payment is held, and a SAR is filed. Walk through what happens.Intermediate

The payment is held immediately when **screening flags** the beneficiary name as a fuzzy match against the SDN list. No funds move while the review is open. The analyst **escalates to the compliance officer** with the match evidence attached, including the list entry, the match score, and the full payment details. Then comes **true-match verification**. The compliance team compares the beneficiary against the list entry, checking name, date of birth, address, and nationality, to decide whether this is the same person or just a similar name. If it is a false positive, the payment is released. If it is a true match, the payment stays blocked, and the bank must not release it under any circumstances. If the activity meets the reporting threshold, a **SAR, Suspicious Activity Report**, is filed with the authorities. **Every step is documented**, because the decision trail is what regulators will ask for. The lesson is that the **screening-to-escalation-to-SAR workflow** is the real control, not the alert. The alert is only a trigger. What matters is how fast the review happens, how well it is documented, and whether the bank can prove it followed its own process.

Read the full chapter →
Q224.Transaction monitoring flags multiple accounts. The pattern is small inward transfers from unrelated sources, funds moved out within minutes of credit, minimal balance retention, and common device linkage. What is this and how do you respond?Expert

This is a **mule account network**. The red flags are clear. Small-value inward transfers from unrelated sources, rapid outward movement within minutes of credit, minimal balance retention, and common device or IP linkage across accounts. One account with this pattern is a case. Linked accounts with the same pattern are a network. I act fast. A **debit freeze** on the suspect accounts stops the flow immediately, because every hour of delay is more money moved. I run **EDD, enhanced due diligence, and KYC reviews** on every flagged account to understand who they are and whether the activity is legitimate. I **recalibrate the detection rules** so the pattern is caught earlier next time, tightening the thresholds on rapid outward movement and shared device signals. I **escalate to investigations** with full evidence for regulatory reporting, because a mule network is a money laundering concern. And I balance **friction and flow**. The rules must catch mules without punishing genuine customers. A rule that freezes every account with a fast outward transfer will create more complaints than it prevents fraud, so the thresholds need tuning against real customer behaviour, not just against the fraud pattern.

Read the full chapter →
Q225.Where does sanctions screening fit in the payment flow, and how do you design it so it does not slow down real time payments?Advanced

Sanctions screening sits in the payment flow between validation and routing, and it must be fast enough not to break real time payments. The flow is: the channel sends the instruction to the hub, the hub extracts the **debtor name, creditor name, and any address fields**, and sends them to the screening engine. The engine compares them against sanctions lists and returns a result: clear, potential match, or confirmed match. If clear, the payment continues. If potential match, the payment goes to a **manual review queue** and an analyst checks it. If confirmed match, the payment is **blocked** and reported. The design challenge is speed. Screening must return in under a second for real time payments, so the hub calls the screening engine synchronously but with a short timeout. If the screening engine is slow or down, the hub must decide: hold the payment, or let it through and screen it afterwards. Most banks hold it, because sending an unscreened payment is a regulatory breach. The screening result is stored with the payment record so auditors can see exactly what was checked and when. Always screen on the **structured data**, not free text, because free text matching produces too many false positives.

Read the full chapter →
Q226.Transaction monitoring flags an account that receives several small transfers from unrelated people, then sends the full amount abroad within an hour. Explain the pattern, what it suggests, and what the bank does next.Advanced

This is a classic **money mule** pattern. The account receives multiple small **inward transfers** from people who have no connection to the account holder, and then sends the money out almost immediately, usually to an account abroad. The small amounts are designed to stay below the **monitoring thresholds**, and the speed is designed to move the money before the bank can react. The pattern suggests the account holder is either a willing mule, paid to move criminal money, or an unwitting mule, tricked into receiving and forwarding money, often through a fake job advert or a romance scam. The bank must act quickly: **freeze** the account to stop further movement, review the full transaction history, check whether the account holder has other accounts, and check whether the sending accounts are also linked to fraud. The bank must file a **suspicious activity report** with the financial intelligence unit, and it must consider whether to close the account and report the holder to law enforcement. The bank should also contact the account holder and ask them to explain the transactions, but it must not reveal that a report has been filed. The key point is speed: a mule account that is left open for a day can move a large amount of criminal money, so the monitoring alert must be acted on the same day it fires.

Read the full chapter →
Q227.A sanctions list is updated at midday and a new name is added. Several payments are already in flight that involve that name. Explain what the bank must do with the payments that are already moving.Intermediate

When a **sanctions list** is updated, the new entry applies **immediately**. The bank must screen all payments against the updated list, including payments that are already in flight. The first step is to identify which payments are affected: the bank checks the **payment queue** for payments sent but not yet settled and payments received but not yet credited. Any payment that matches must be **held**, which means stopping it before it settles or before it is credited to the beneficiary. If the payment has already settled and the funds have been credited, the bank cannot take the money back through the payment system, but it must report it to the **sanctions authority**. If the payment is still in flight, the bank must block it and hold the funds in a **blocked account**, and it must not release them without permission from the sanctions authority. The bank must also check whether it has a **relationship** with the sanctioned person, such as an account, and if so, it must freeze the account. The operations team should have a process for list updates: the list is loaded as soon as it is published, the queue is rescreened automatically, and the compliance team is notified of any hits within minutes. A bank that pays a newly sanctioned person because it did not update its list in time is in breach, and the excuse that the payment was already in flight does not protect it.

Read the full chapter →
Q228.A customer calls in tears. They were tricked by a fraudster posing as their bank into sending 15,000 pounds to a criminal account. Explain how the bank handles the case, what the customer can expect, and what the bank does to try to recover the money.Intermediate

This is **authorised push payment fraud**, where the customer was tricked into authorising the payment themselves. The bank must act with **empathy** first: the customer is a victim, and the first thing they need is to be believed and to be told what will happen next. The bank must immediately contact the **receiving bank** and ask it to freeze the criminal account, because the fraudster moves the money within hours. The bank must also raise a **fraud case**, record all the evidence, such as the phone number the fraudster used and the messages they sent, and report the fraud to the police and to the industry fraud database. Under the **PSR reimbursement rules**, the sending bank must reimburse the customer in most cases, with the cost split between the sending and receiving banks, unless the customer acted with gross negligence. The customer should expect a decision within **five business days** and a clear explanation of the outcome. The bank should also review whether its own controls failed: did **confirmation of payee** warn the customer, did the bank show a fraud warning before the payment was confirmed, and did transaction monitoring flag the payment as unusual. The lesson is that prevention matters most, but when prevention fails, a fast, kind, and honest response is what the customer remembers.

Read the full chapter →
Q229.A customer makes cash deposits of 9,500 pounds every few days, always just below the 10,000 pound reporting threshold. Explain what the bank suspects, how it investigates, and what happens if the suspicion is confirmed.Advanced

The bank suspects **structuring**, which is the deliberate splitting of transactions to avoid a **reporting threshold**. The threshold exists so that large cash transactions are reported to the authorities, and a customer who consistently deposits just below it is likely trying to avoid that report. The pattern is suspicious because there is no normal business reason to deposit 9,500 pounds repeatedly instead of the full amount. The bank investigates by looking at the customer **profile**: what is their normal activity, what is their source of income, and does the cash make sense for their business. The bank also looks at the **timing** and the **pattern**: are the deposits always just below the threshold, do they happen at different branches, and is the money then moved on quickly. If the investigation cannot explain the pattern, the bank must file a **suspicious activity report** with the financial intelligence unit, and it must consider whether to close the account or to restrict it. The bank must never tell the customer that a report has been filed, because that is **tipping off** and it is a criminal offence. The customer may be asked for information about the source of funds as part of normal due diligence, but the bank must not reveal that monitoring has flagged them. Structuring is a crime in itself, even if the underlying money is legitimate, because it is an attempt to evade the reporting rules.

Read the full chapter →
Q230.A payment is held because the beneficiary name fuzzy matches a sanctions list entry. The name is a common one, like Mohammed Khan, and the customer is angry about the delay. Explain fuzzy matching, why the payment was held, and how it gets released.Beginner

**Fuzzy matching** is the technique sanctions screening systems use to catch names that are spelled differently, transliterated from another alphabet, or entered with a typo. The system does not look for an exact match. It looks for names that are **similar enough** to be the same person, and it scores the similarity. A common name like Mohammed Khan will match many entries on a sanctions list, because the list contains many people with that name, and the system cannot tell them apart from the name alone. The payment was held because the system flagged a **possible match**, and the bank must investigate before it releases the payment. The compliance team compares the **full details**: the date of birth, the address, the nationality, and the passport number, against the sanctions listing. If the details clearly show it is a different person, the bank documents the decision and releases the payment. If the details are missing, the bank asks the sending bank for more information. Tell the customer that the delay is caused by the name being common, not by anything they did wrong, and that providing full identifying details with the payment, such as the date of birth and address, speeds up the check. The bank cannot skip the check, because releasing a payment to a sanctioned person carries fines of millions of dollars.

Read the full chapter →
Q231.A bank trade finance team notices that the invoice value for a shipment of electronics is three times the market price, and the goods are shipped through three countries for no clear reason. Explain trade based money laundering and how the bank responds.Expert

**Trade based money laundering** is the use of international trade to move criminal money across borders by disguising it as legitimate business. The techniques include **over invoicing**, where the invoice value is inflated so that extra money moves with the shipment, **under invoicing**, where the value is reduced, and **phantom shipments**, where the goods do not exist at all. In this case, the invoice is three times the market price and the goods take an unnecessarily complex route, which are both red flags. The bank responds by **enhancing its due diligence**: it asks for the underlying trade documents, the purchase order, the shipping documents, the insurance certificate, and the customs declaration, and it checks whether the documents are consistent with each other. It also checks the **market price** of the goods, the **reputation** of the buyer and seller, and whether the trade route makes commercial sense. If the documents do not add up, the bank must refuse to process the payment, file a **suspicious activity report**, and consider whether to exit the relationship. Trade based money laundering is hard to detect because the paperwork often looks genuine, so the bank must train its trade finance team to spot **price anomalies**, unusual routes, and counterparties with no real business history. The bank that processes a trade payment without checking the underlying trade is financing crime.

Read the full chapter →
Q232.A customer adds a new payee to their online banking, then immediately sends a large payment to that payee. The bank transaction monitoring flags it. Explain what the bank suspects and what controls should have stopped it.Advanced

The bank suspects **account takeover**. A fraudster has gained access to the customer account, added a new payee, which is an account the fraudster controls, and then sent a large payment to it. The pattern is a red flag because genuine customers rarely add a payee and send a large payment in the same session. The controls that should have stopped it include **strong customer authentication** when the payee is added, a **cooling off period** where a new payee cannot receive a large payment for 24 hours, **confirmation of payee** to check the payee name against the account, and **behavioural monitoring** that flags a payment that is unusual for the customer, such as a new device, a new location, or a much larger amount than normal. When the monitoring flags the payment, the bank should **hold** it, contact the customer through a trusted channel, such as a phone call to the number on record, and ask them to confirm the payment. The bank must not use the contact details the fraudster may have changed. If the customer confirms they did not make the payment, the bank must freeze the account, reverse the payment if possible, and help the customer secure their account, including resetting passwords and checking for malware. The lesson is that payee creation is a high risk event and it needs stronger controls than a routine payment.

Read the full chapter →
Q233.A customer wants to send a large payment to a cryptocurrency exchange. The bank compliance team is unsure whether to allow it. Explain the risks, what the bank should check, and how it makes the decision.Expert

A payment to a **cryptocurrency exchange** carries specific risks. Cryptocurrency can be used to move money quickly and anonymously, which makes it attractive for **money laundering**, **fraud**, and **sanctions evasion**. The bank must check several things before it allows the payment. First, is the exchange **regulated** and does it carry out **customer due diligence** on its own users. A regulated exchange in a reputable jurisdiction is lower risk than an unregulated exchange in a high risk country. Second, what is the **purpose** of the payment: is the customer investing, trading, or paying for goods, and does the amount make sense for their profile. Third, has the customer been **scammed**: many cryptocurrency frauds start with a fake investment advert, and the victim is told to send money to an exchange. The bank should ask the customer about the source of the opportunity and warn them about common scams. Fourth, does the payment breach the bank **risk appetite**: some banks block all cryptocurrency payments, while others allow them with limits and enhanced checks. The decision should be documented, and if the bank allows the payment, it should monitor the account for further payments to the same exchange. If the bank refuses, it should explain why to the customer, because a blanket refusal without explanation damages trust. The bank must balance the customer right to spend their money with its obligation to prevent financial crime.

Cards and Acquiring (16)

Q234.Walk through a clean card payment, from the customer tapping the card to the merchant being settled. What happens at authorisation, clearing, and settlement?Intermediate

A card payment has three stages, authorisation, clearing, and settlement, and in a clean flow each one happens on time. The customer taps their card, and the merchant sends an **authorisation request** to the acquiring bank. The acquirer routes it through the card scheme to the issuing bank. The issuing bank checks the balance, the card status, and the fraud rules, then approves the transaction and places a hold on the funds. The customer sees the transaction immediately. At the end of the day, the merchant sends a **clearing file** with all the day transactions. The scheme nets the amounts between banks and calculates the settlement. The issuing bank transfers the funds to the acquiring bank, and the acquirer credits the merchant, minus the **interchange and scheme fees**. The customer statement shows the purchase, and the merchant statement shows the credit. What makes it clean is the separation of the stages. Authorisation is instant, clearing is batched, and settlement is netted. Each stage has its own controls, and the scheme rules make sure every participant knows their role. A card payment that works well is one the customer never thinks about, because the tap just works.

Read the full chapter →
Q235.A customer taps their card at a cafe and the terminal declines it, even though they have plenty of money in the account. The customer is embarrassed and angry. How do you investigate the decline and what do you tell the customer?Beginner

Start with the **authorisation response code**, because it tells you exactly why the issuer said no. A code like **05 do not honour** is a generic issuer decline, **51** means insufficient funds, **54** means an expired card, and **91** means the issuer is temporarily unavailable. Ask the merchant for the code from the terminal receipt or the acquirer log before you guess anything. Next, check the **card status** in the issuer system. The card may be blocked, reported lost, frozen in the app, or restricted after a fraud alert, and none of that shows up as a balance problem. Also check **velocity controls**, because several contactless taps in a short period can trigger a PIN request or a temporary block. If the issuer was unavailable, the decline is a system issue, not a customer issue, and the fix sits with the issuer or the network. Tell the customer plainly what happened, in plain language, and give them a next step: try the chip and PIN, use another card, or call the number on the back of the card. Never blame the merchant terminal until you have the response code, and never tell the customer the payment went through when it did not.

Read the full chapter →
Q236.A merchant receives a chargeback 60 days after a sale. The reason code says the cardholder did not authorise the transaction, but the merchant has signed delivery proof and a photo of the goods being handed over. How does the merchant fight the chargeback, and what are the chances?Intermediate

The merchant fights it through **representment**, which is the formal reply to a chargeback sent through the acquirer to the card scheme. The acquirer has a strict deadline, usually **30 to 45 days** from the chargeback date, and missing it means the money is lost automatically, so the first step is to confirm the deadline and start the clock. The merchant must submit **compelling evidence**: the signed delivery note, the photo, the order details, the delivery address matching the cardholder address, and any messages between the merchant and the customer. For a card present sale, the **EMV chip data** and the terminal receipt showing the card was present are strong evidence that the cardholder was there. The issuer reviews the evidence and either accepts it, which returns the funds, or rejects it and sends the case to **pre-arbitration**. Be honest with the merchant: representment works best when the evidence proves the cardholder received the goods, but it does not always win, because the issuer may still side with its customer. The lesson is to keep delivery proof for every high value sale and to record the authorisation code, the terminal ID, and the card entry method for every transaction.

Read the full chapter →
Q237.A small retailer has not received card settlement for two days. Takings were normal, the terminal shows the sales went through, but no money has arrived in the bank account. Walk through how you find the problem.Intermediate

Start by checking whether the terminal **batched and closed** for those two days. Card payments are authorised in real time, but they are only sent for clearing when the terminal closes its **batch**, usually at end of day. If the batch was never closed, the money is sitting authorised but uncleared, and closing the batch releases it. Next, ask the acquirer to confirm it received the **clearing file** and check the **settlement account** details on the merchant account. A changed bank account, a closed account, or a wrong sort code means the acquirer tried to pay and the payment bounced. Also check whether the acquirer placed a **hold or reserve** on the account, which happens when risk flags appear, such as a sudden spike in refunds or a large transaction that looks unusual. If the batch closed and the account is correct, ask for the **settlement reference** and trace it through the acquirer settlement report against the merchant bank statement. Give the retailer a clear timeline: what was checked, what was found, and when the money will arrive. Most cases turn out to be an unclosed batch or a bank detail problem, and both are fixed in a day once found.

Read the full chapter →
Q238.An online shopper starts a purchase, gets a 3-D Secure challenge on their phone, fails it twice, and abandons the checkout. The merchant loses the sale and blames the bank. Explain what happened and how the merchant reduces abandoned checkouts without increasing fraud.Intermediate

The shopper hit **3-D Secure**, the extra authentication step that asks the cardholder to confirm the payment, usually through their banking app or a one time passcode. Failing it twice means the issuer could not verify the shopper, so the payment was not authenticated and the merchant correctly did not proceed. Under **PSD2 strong customer authentication** rules, the issuer must challenge payments that look risky, and the merchant cannot skip that step. The merchant can reduce abandonment by using **frictionless flow** wherever possible, which means the issuer checks risk signals in the background and approves the payment without a challenge. Merchants should also send rich **transaction data** with each payment, such as the device details, the delivery address, and the purchase history, because better data means fewer challenges. **Exemptions** help too: low value payments, recurring payments, and trusted beneficiaries can skip authentication when the rules allow. Tell the merchant that every abandoned checkout is not a lost customer. Some shoppers return and complete the purchase, and the ones who do not are often the riskiest. The right balance is fewer challenges for genuine customers and firm challenges for anything that looks like fraud.

Read the full chapter →
Q239.Your bank stores card numbers for one-click checkout. The team wants to move from stored PANs to network tokens. Explain what changes, what the risks are, and how you migrate without breaking existing customers.Advanced

Moving to **network tokens** means replacing the stored **PAN**, the 16 digit card number, with a token issued by the card scheme, such as Visa or Mastercard. The token works like the card number for payments, but it is useless if stolen, because it only works with the merchant it was issued for and can be suspended without reissuing the card. The migration starts with the **token requestor** setup: the bank or its processor registers with the scheme, agrees the token rules, and builds the token vault that maps each token back to the real PAN. Existing customers are migrated by requesting a token for each stored PAN, and the checkout is updated to send the token and the **cryptogram**, a one time code that proves the token is genuine. The biggest risks are **token lifecycle** events: when a card is reissued, lost, or expires, the token must be updated automatically, or the customer payment fails. You also need a **fallback** for acquirers that do not yet accept tokens, which means keeping the PAN path available during the transition. Test the full journey with real scheme sandboxes, including reissue, expiry, and suspension, before moving any live customer. Done well, tokens cut fraud and cut the scope of **PCI DSS** compliance, because the merchant no longer holds real card numbers.

Read the full chapter →
Q240.A customer taps their card several times during the day and suddenly the terminal asks for a PIN. They have never been asked for a PIN on contactless before. Explain why this happens and what the customer should do.Beginner

This is the **contactless cumulative limit** doing its job. Under **strong customer authentication** rules, a card can only be used contactless for a certain total value, or a certain number of taps, before the terminal must ask for a **PIN** to prove the person holding the card is the real cardholder. In the UK the single tap limit is **100 pounds**, and the cumulative limit means that after several taps the card needs a PIN even if each individual tap was small. The limit resets once the PIN is entered correctly. The terminal is not broken, the card is not blocked, and the customer has done nothing wrong. Tell the customer to simply insert the card and enter the PIN, and contactless will work again straight away. If the PIN is entered wrong three times, the card locks and the customer must contact the issuer. This check exists to limit the damage if a card is lost or stolen, because a thief can only make a few small contactless payments before the PIN stops them. It is a security feature, not a fault, and it applies to every card, not just this customer's.

Read the full chapter →
Q241.A customer pays by card while on holiday abroad and later complains that the amount taken from their account is higher than the price on the receipt. The shop offered to charge them in their home currency. Explain what happened and what the customer should have done.Beginner

The shop offered **dynamic currency conversion**, known as DCC, which means the card payment is converted into the customer home currency at the point of sale, using the exchange rate set by the merchant or their acquirer. That rate is almost always worse than the rate the card scheme, Visa or Mastercard, would apply, and it often includes an extra **markup** of 3 to 5 percent. The customer accepted the conversion, probably without realising the cost, and the higher amount is the result. The right choice is almost always to pay in the **local currency** and let the card scheme do the conversion, because scheme rates are close to the wholesale rate and the issuer charges are transparent. Tell the customer to check the terminal screen before entering the PIN: if it offers a choice of currencies, always choose the local one. If the customer was not given a choice, or the DCC was applied without consent, the issuer can raise a dispute with the acquirer, because the rules require the customer to be offered the choice clearly. The lesson for the customer is simple: abroad, always pay in the local currency and decline the conversion offer.

Read the full chapter →
Q242.A card scheme raises its interchange rates. The acquirer passes the increase to merchants, and a large retailer threatens to leave. Explain what interchange is, why the merchant pays it, and how the acquirer handles the negotiation.Intermediate

**Interchange** is the fee the merchant bank, the acquirer, pays to the cardholder bank, the issuer, on every card transaction. It is the largest part of the **merchant service charge**, the total fee the merchant pays to accept cards, and it is set by the card scheme, not by the acquirer. The acquirer cannot remove it, it can only decide how much of its own margin to add on top. When the scheme raises interchange, the acquirer cost rises on every transaction, so passing it on is normal, but the merchant sees only a higher bill. Explain to the merchant that interchange varies by **card type**, **merchant category**, and **transaction type**: a premium rewards card costs more to accept than a standard debit card, and a card not present transaction costs more than a chip and PIN sale. The acquirer should show the merchant the breakdown, interchange, scheme fees, and acquirer margin, so the increase is transparent. The negotiation options are to move the merchant to **interchange plus pricing**, where they see the real cost, to review the merchant category code, because a wrong code can inflate interchange, and to look at routing, such as encouraging debit or domestic scheme cards where they are cheaper. Losing the merchant over a scheme increase helps nobody, so transparency is the acquirer best tool.

Read the full chapter →
Q243.An authorisation is approved at the till, the customer leaves with the goods, but the merchant settlement for that day is short by exactly that amount. The clearing file has no record of the transaction. What went wrong and how do you fix it?Advanced

The authorisation and the clearing are two separate steps, and this case shows the second step failed. The card was authorised in real time, which is why the customer left with the goods, but the transaction was never **presented for clearing**. In a **dual message** system, the authorisation holds the funds and the clearing message, the presentment, actually moves the money. If the terminal batch was interrupted, the network dropped the presentment, or the acquirer host rejected the record, the clearing file has no entry and the merchant is never paid. First, pull the **authorisation log** from the terminal or the acquirer and confirm the approval code, the amount, and the card details. Then check the **batch totals**: the terminal batch total should match the acquirer received total, and the difference will be exactly this transaction. The fix is a **late presentment**, where the acquirer submits the transaction for clearing with the original authorisation details, as long as it is still within the scheme presentment window, usually a few days. If the window has passed, the merchant must ask the issuer for a **goodwill settlement** or accept the loss. Tell the merchant to reconcile batch totals against acquirer totals every single day, because a one day delay in spotting a missing presentment is the difference between an easy fix and a lost sale.

Read the full chapter →
Q244.A customer subscription payment fails the month after their card is reissued with a new expiry date. The customer did not update the card details with the merchant. Explain why the payment failed and how it should have worked.Beginner

The payment failed because the merchant tried to charge the **old card details**. A reissued card has a new expiry date and sometimes a new card number, and the stored details the merchant holds are now out of date. The subscription should have kept working through the **account updater** service, run by Visa and Mastercard. When a card is reissued, the issuer sends the new details to the scheme, and merchants enrolled in the updater service receive the new card number and expiry date automatically, before the next payment is due. If the merchant is not enrolled, or the updater feed failed, the payment is attempted with stale details and the issuer declines it. The fix is for the merchant to enrol in the **account updater** service and to build a **retry and dunning** flow: when a recurring payment fails, tell the customer immediately, give them a simple way to update the card, and retry a few days later. The customer should also be told to update card details with important merchants whenever a new card arrives. This is one of the most common reasons subscriptions fail, and it is entirely preventable with the updater service and a clear message to the customer.

Read the full chapter →
Q245.A merchant is charged more for card acceptance than expected. When you investigate, you find the merchant category code on the account is wrong. Explain what a merchant category code is, why it matters, and how you fix it.Intermediate

The **merchant category code**, or MCC, is a four digit code that describes what type of business the merchant is, such as a supermarket, a restaurant, or an airline. The code is set when the merchant account is opened, and it drives two things: the **interchange rate** the merchant pays, because different business types have different rates, and the **risk rules** applied to the account, because some categories, like travel or electronics, carry higher chargeback risk. A wrong MCC can mean the merchant pays a higher interchange rate than they should, or that their transactions are treated as higher risk and held for review. To fix it, the acquirer must confirm the merchant real business activity, check the scheme **MCC list** for the correct code, and update the merchant account. The acquirer should also check whether the wrong code affected past charges and whether a **rebate** is due. Tell the merchant to check their MCC whenever their business changes, for example if a shop starts selling online as well as in store, because the code must match the main activity. Getting the MCC right is a small admin fix that can save a merchant real money every month.

Read the full chapter →
Q246.A fraudster uses a stolen card at a terminal. The chip fails to read, the terminal falls back to the magnetic stripe, and the transaction goes through. Who bears the loss, and what should the merchant and the acquirer have done?Advanced

This is an **EMV fallback** transaction, where the chip could not be read and the terminal used the **magnetic stripe** instead. The magnetic stripe is easy to copy, which is why the industry moved to chip, and fallback transactions are a known fraud route. Under the **liability shift** rules, the party that has not adopted EMV bears the loss. If the merchant terminal is chip enabled but the card chip was faulty, the issuer usually bears the loss. If the merchant terminal is old and cannot read chips at all, the merchant bears the loss, because the merchant did not upgrade. If the terminal was deliberately set to allow fallback when it should not, the acquirer bears responsibility for the configuration. The merchant should have a clear rule: fallback is only allowed when the chip is genuinely unreadable, and staff should ask for **ID** or an alternative payment when a fallback happens. The acquirer should monitor fallback rates by merchant, because a high fallback rate is a warning sign of either faulty terminals or deliberate fraud. The long term fix is to retire magnetic stripe acceptance entirely and to move to **contactless and mobile wallets**, which cannot be skimmed the way a stripe can.

Read the full chapter →
Q247.A customer returns goods to a shop and the refund is issued to a card that has since expired. The customer worries the money is lost. Explain where the refund goes and what the customer should expect.Beginner

The money is not lost. When a refund is issued to an **expired card**, the issuer routes it using the card account behind the card number, not the plastic card itself. The card number stays linked to the same account even after the expiry date passes, so the refund lands in the account that the old card belonged to. If the customer has been issued a **replacement card**, the refund usually appears on the new card statement, because the issuer maps the old card number to the new one. If the account itself is closed, the issuer cannot post the refund and will return it to the merchant, who must then pay the customer by another method, such as a bank transfer or a cheque. Tell the customer to check the statement for the account the old card belonged to, and to allow **five to ten working days**, because refunds take longer than purchases to appear. If nothing arrives after ten days, the customer should ask the merchant for the **refund authorisation code** and give it to the issuer, who can trace the refund through the scheme. The key point is that expiry affects the plastic card, not the account, and the money follows the account.

Read the full chapter →
Q248.A new online merchant wants to start accepting card payments. The acquirer asks for business details, trading history, and a reserve. The merchant thinks this is unnecessary paperwork. Explain why the acquirer does this and what the merchant should expect.Intermediate

The acquirer is doing **merchant underwriting**, which is the risk check every acquirer must do before letting a business take card payments. Card payments carry a risk the acquirer takes on: if the merchant takes money and then fails to deliver the goods, or goes out of business, the acquirer must refund the cardholders through **chargebacks**. The acquirer therefore checks the business model, the trading history, the expected volumes, and the **chargeback risk** before agreeing terms. For a new business with no history, or a high risk category such as travel or electronics, the acquirer will usually ask for a **reserve**, which is a percentage of each settlement held back for a period, often 90 to 180 days, to cover future chargebacks. The merchant should expect questions about what they sell, how they deliver, their refund policy, and their website, and they should expect the process to take days, not minutes. Tell the merchant that a thorough underwriting protects them too: it sets realistic terms, avoids sudden account freezes later, and builds a relationship where the acquirer understands the business. A merchant that refuses underwriting is a warning sign, and no reputable acquirer will onboard them without it.

Read the full chapter →
Q249.Explain the difference between single message and dual message card clearing, and why a merchant might be paid at a different time depending on which system their acquirer uses.Expert

In a **dual message** system, a card payment has two separate steps. The **authorisation** message checks the funds and holds the amount, and hours later a **clearing** message, the presentment, actually moves the money. Visa and Mastercard credit cards mostly work this way, and the merchant is paid after the clearing file is processed, usually the next working day. In a **single message** system, the authorisation and the clearing happen in one message, so the money moves at the same time as the approval. Many debit card systems work this way, and the merchant can be paid faster, sometimes the same day. The difference matters for **settlement timing** and for **reconciliation**: in a dual message system the merchant must match authorisations to presentments, and a missing presentment means no payment even though the sale was approved. In a single message system there is nothing to match, because each message is both the approval and the payment. The merchant experience also differs on **refunds and adjustments**: a dual message system can adjust the cleared amount, for example adding a tip, while a single message system usually needs a separate transaction. When a merchant asks why one acquirer pays faster than another, the answer is often that one uses single message clearing and the other uses dual message, and neither is wrong, they are just different designs.

Payment Operations (26)

Q250.What is a payment exception queue?Intermediate

A payment exception queue is the worklist where payments that cannot be processed automatically are held for manual handling by operations staff. Payments land in the exception queue for many reasons: a sanctions screening alert, a failed validation such as an invalid account number, a missing beneficiary address, a limit breach, a liquidity shortfall, or a technical error such as a rejected message from a clearing system. Each item in the queue shows the payment details, the reason it failed, and the actions available: repair and resubmit, release, return to sender, or escalate. Operations teams work the queue in priority order, guided by service level agreements based on value date and cut-off times, because a payment that misses its cut-off may settle a day late. Good exception handling design includes clear reason codes, the ability to see the full payment history, four-eyes approval for high-value repairs, and automatic escalation when an item ages beyond its SLA. The exception queue is also a source of management information: recurring reasons point to upstream problems, such as a channel that accepts invalid IBANs or a mapping error. For a BA, the exception queue is a core functional area: you define the queue structure, the workflow states, the repair screens, and the reporting that helps operations and product teams reduce exception volumes.

Read the full chapter →
Q251.What is a payment operations dashboard?Beginner

A payment operations dashboard is a real-time view of payment processing health that lets operations teams see what is happening and act quickly when something goes wrong. It typically shows volumes by payment type, channel, and currency; the straight through processing rate; the size and ageing of exception queues; payments approaching cut-off times; settlement and nostro balances; and the status of connections to clearing systems. Good dashboards use traffic-light indicators: green for normal, amber for warning, and red for breach, so an operator can spot a problem at a glance. They also support drill-down: clicking on a red exception count shows the underlying payments and their failure reasons. Dashboards serve different audiences: operators need live queues and alerts, team leads need staffing and SLA views, and management needs trends and cost metrics. They are usually built on data from the payment hub, enriched with reference data and fed by streaming or near-real-time updates. For a BA, dashboard requirements cover the metrics to display, the data sources, refresh frequency, alert thresholds, user roles, and the actions an operator can take from the dashboard, such as reprioritizing a queue or pausing a payment type. A well-designed dashboard turns a flood of payment data into decisions.

Read the full chapter →
Q252.What is a payment test case?Beginner

A payment test case is a documented scenario that verifies a specific behavior of a payment system, with defined inputs, expected results, and pass or fail criteria. A good test case starts with a clear objective, for example verifying that a SEPA payment with an invalid IBAN is rejected with the correct error code. It specifies the preconditions, such as the test account setup and reference data; the test steps, such as entering the payment details and submitting; the test data, including amounts, currencies, and dates; and the expected result, such as the exact error message and the payment status. Payment test cases cover happy paths, such as a standard domestic payment settling on time, and edge cases, such as a payment on a bank holiday, a payment above a limit, a payment to a sanctioned country, and a payment with a special character in the beneficiary name. They also cover non-functional aspects such as performance under load and correct handling of duplicate messages. Test cases are organized into test suites by payment type and are traced back to requirements so that every requirement has at least one test. For a BA, writing test cases is a core skill: it forces you to think through the requirement completely, and the test cases you write are often the basis for user acceptance testing with the business.

Read the full chapter →
Q253.How does a large bank handle peak volumes on a salary day or month end?Intermediate

A large bank plans for peak days weeks in advance. The operations team looks at the calendar and knows which days will be heavy: month end, salary days, tax payment deadlines and the days before a public holiday. First, they check capacity. The payment hub, the core banking system and the clearing interfaces all have throughput limits, and the team confirms they can handle the expected volume. Second, they staff up. More people are put on the exceptions queue and the helpdesk because more payments means more failures. Third, treasury pre-funds the nostro accounts with extra liquidity, because more payments going out means more money leaving the accounts. Fourth, the bank may ask large corporate clients to send their files early so the payments can be spread across the day rather than arriving in one burst. During the peak, operations watches the queues in real time. If a queue is building up, they can prioritise urgent payments and hold lower priority ones. After the peak, the team runs a full reconciliation to make sure every payment settled and every exception was caught. The key lesson is that peak days are not a surprise. They are planned like an event, with a runbook and named owners for each step.

Read the full chapter →
Q254.How are payments operations teams structured in a large bank?Intermediate

In a large bank like BNY Mellon or Goldman Sachs, payments operations is split into teams by function, not by product. The intake team receives payment files and instructions from channels and checks they are complete. The processing team monitors the payment hub and makes sure payments flow through without getting stuck. The exceptions team investigates payments that fail validation, get rejected by clearing or come back with an error. The reconciliation team matches what the bank sent against what clearing confirmed, and matches the nostro accounts against the ledger. The investigations team handles customer queries about missing or delayed payments. The treasury operations team manages liquidity and funding. Above these teams sits a duty manager who owns the day and makes decisions when something goes wrong. The BA sits alongside these teams. The BA writes the requirements when a new payment type is added, documents the exception handling rules and helps operations when a defect is found. The structure matters because each team has a clear owner and a clear handoff. A payment that fails does not sit in a gap between teams. It has a named owner at every stage.

Read the full chapter →
Q255.What happens when a payment is stuck in a queue at a large bank?Intermediate

A payment gets stuck in a queue when it cannot move to the next step. The most common reasons are a missing field, a failed validation, a sanctions hold or a system that is down. The payment hub holds the payment in a queue and flags it for the operations team. The operations team looks at the queue regularly during the day. They open the payment, read the error or the hold reason and decide what to do. If it is a data problem, they fix the data or send it back to the channel team to fix at source. If it is a sanctions hold, they pass it to the compliance team for review. If it is a system problem, they raise it with engineering and wait for a fix. While the payment is stuck, the customer may call to ask where their money is. The investigations team checks the payment status and gives the customer a realistic time. The payment is not lost. It is sitting in the hub waiting for someone to act. The risk is that a stuck payment misses its value date, which means the beneficiary gets the money late. That is why large banks monitor their queues in real time and have a target for how quickly each queue must be cleared.
