Q256.How does a large bank test a payment change before it goes live?Advanced

Testing a payment change in a large bank has several layers because a defect can stop real money. First, the engineers run unit tests on the code they wrote. Second, the QA team runs system integration tests in a test environment that mirrors production, checking that the payment hub talks correctly to the core banking system, the sanctions screening and the clearing interfaces. Third, the BA writes end to end test scenarios based on real payment flows: a normal payment, a payment with a missing field, a payment that gets rejected, a payment that hits sanctions, a payment that needs to be returned. These scenarios are run with test data that looks like real customer data. Fourth, operations run user acceptance testing. They process payments the way they would on a normal day and confirm the system behaves as expected. Fifth, the bank runs a dress rehearsal of the cutover, following the exact steps that will be used on the go live night. If the change touches a clearing system, the bank may also test with the clearing house in their test environment. Only when all layers pass does the change get approved for production. The BA owns the test scenarios and the acceptance criteria, and signs off that the change is ready.

Read the full chapter →
Q257.What is the role of a payments operations manager during a system outage?Advanced

When a payment system goes down, the operations manager becomes the incident owner. The first job is to assess the impact: which payments are affected, how many, and whether customers are impacted. The manager opens an incident, calls the engineering team and the duty manager, and starts a bridge call. Second, the manager decides whether to stop taking new payments or to queue them. Stopping intake prevents a backlog building up, but it means customers cannot pay. Queuing keeps the intake open but risks a large backlog when the system comes back. Third, the manager communicates. The manager updates the business, the helpdesk and the customer communications team so that customers get a consistent message. Fourth, the manager works with engineering on the fix and tracks the recovery step by step. Fifth, once the system is back, the manager oversees the catch up: the queued payments are released in priority order, urgent payments first, and the team checks that reconciliation matches. Finally, the manager leads the post incident review: what failed, why, what should change. The BA supports this by documenting the impact, writing the incident report and turning the lessons into requirements for a fix.

Read the full chapter →
Q258.How does a bank handle a failed file from a corporate client?Intermediate

A corporate client sends a payment file, usually a bulk file with hundreds or thousands of payments. The bank's file gateway receives the file and checks it. First, it checks the file format: is it a valid file, does it have the right structure, are the headers correct. If the format is wrong, the whole file is rejected and the client is told to fix it and resend. Second, it checks each payment inside the file: is the account number valid, is the amount present, is the currency supported. Payments that fail this check are rejected individually, and the good payments in the file still go through. Third, it checks for duplicates: has this file been sent before, are there duplicate payments inside it. The bank sends a response file back to the client listing which payments were accepted and which were rejected, with a reason code for each rejection. The operations team monitors file intake and calls the client if a large file fails, because a failed salary file means employees do not get paid. The BA needs to know this flow because corporate file processing is a common requirement, and the error handling and response file format are part of the design.

Read the full chapter →
Q259.How does a large bank measure payment performance and what are the key metrics?Intermediate

A large bank tracks payment performance with a small set of metrics that everyone watches. The first is the straight-through processing rate: the percentage of payments that go through without manual intervention. A high STP rate means the system is working well. The second is the average processing time: how long from instruction to settlement. For instant payments this is measured in seconds, for cross border it is measured in hours. The third is the exception rate: the percentage of payments that land in a repair or investigation queue. A rising exception rate signals a data quality or system problem. The fourth is the reconciliation break rate: how many payments fail to match at end of day. The fifth is the on time settlement rate: the percentage of payments that settle on the promised value date. The sixth is the customer complaint rate for payments, which tells the bank how the experience feels from the outside. These metrics are reported daily to operations management and weekly to senior management. When a metric moves in the wrong direction, the team investigates the root cause and fixes it. The BA uses these metrics to make the case for change: if the exception rate is rising, the BA can show the cost and propose a fix.

Read the full chapter →
Q260.A corporate customer submits a payment one minute after the cut-off. The channel accepts it, but the clearing system rejects it because the settlement window has closed. The customer expects same-day value. What do you do?Intermediate

A cut-off is a contract between the bank, the clearing system, and every downstream batch. When a payment misses it, the channel and the clearing system disagree, and the customer is caught in between. I first check the **pacs.002** status to confirm the rejection and the reason. If the payment was rejected pre-settlement, no funds have moved, so I can repair and resubmit for the next value date. I tell the customer plainly that the value date has shifted to the next business day, and I explain why, because a customer who understands the cut-off will plan around it next time. Then I look at the root cause. Was the cut-off published clearly in the channel, did the customer submit late, or did the bank change its cut-off without telling the customer. If the bank changed its cut-off, that is a **coordination failure**, and I raise it with the partner team so the change is communicated properly. I also check whether other payments from the same customer or channel hit the same issue, because a cut-off problem is rarely a single payment. Finally I review the cut-off configuration in the payment hub, making sure the channel window, the clearing window, and the published customer cut-off all agree, so the channel never accepts a payment the clearing system cannot settle.

Read the full chapter →
Q261.Customers report duplicate debits, but no alerts fired. The root cause is a messaging failure, the broker acknowledged a message before replication finished, then died, and the retry charged again. How do you debug this?Expert

The failure is in the interaction between systems, not in any single component, which is why no alert fired. Each part behaved as designed. The producer used **acks equals 1**, so only the leader broker acknowledged the message. The broker died before replication finished, so the message was lost. But the payment had already been charged, and the system believed it had failed, so the retry charged a second time. I debug it by tracing the full flow, from the payment request through the message broker to the debit posting, and I look for the gap between what the system believed and what actually happened. The fix has three parts. First, use **acks equals all and idempotent producers**, so a message is only acknowledged after full replication. Second, put **dedup keys on every payment**, so a repeated message is recognised, not re-executed. Third, use the **transactional outbox pattern**, writing the business record and the event atomically, so they cannot diverge. I keep **reconciliation as the backstop**, because it must catch double debits even when messaging fails. And I chaos-test broker failures before production, because messaging guarantees only hold if you verify them.

Read the full chapter →
Q262.A payment timeout keeps recurring but the network is healthy and the servers look fine. Where do you look for the root cause?Advanced

The timeout is the symptom, not the cause. I stop fixating on where the error surfaced and start from where the message was created. I trace the **full end-to-end lifecycle** hop by hop, with timestamps and message copies at every step. In this kind of case the real culprit is often a small deviation from **message standards** upstream, not an infrastructure problem. A field that is slightly out of spec, a format that is almost right, or a value that is technically valid but unexpected. Small deviations **compound downstream**. A tolerant receiver today becomes a hard failure after the next release, when the receiving system tightens its validation. I validate messages against the **standard at every boundary**, not just at entry, because a message can be corrupted or transformed at any hop. I keep an **investigation playbook**, timestamps, message copies, hop-by-hop tracing, every time, so the next incident starts from evidence instead of guesses. The standing lesson is that the **most visible error is rarely the root cause**. A timeout that keeps coming back is telling you to look earlier in the chain, not harder at the place where it surfaced.

Read the full chapter →
Q263.A release passes QA, staging, and a small rollout. Hours after full release, volumes spike and failures spike with them. What went wrong?Advanced

Testing never hit the fringe edge case. The root cause was one parameter that everyone assumed was always populated, but in a small number of real cases it came back empty. QA, staging, and a small rollout all passed because the edge case only appeared at full volume. The cascade was fast. **Partner API calls failed**, reconciliation mismatched, and war rooms opened with stakeholders. Recovery needs calm coordination across engineering, operations, and partner support, without blame. The first job is to stop the failures, then fix the code, then fix the **assumption**. I validate every input, especially the ones labelled always present, because those are the ones nobody checks. I add **contract tests** with the partner covering empty and null variants of every field, so the next release catches the gap before production. And I communicate proactively throughout, because **rebuilding partner trust** takes longer than the technical fix. A partner who hears nothing during an incident assumes the worst. A partner who gets regular, honest updates will work with you through the fix.

Read the full chapter →
Q264.Payments fail intermittently, but only during peak hours. The system is fine at all other times. How do you find the root cause?Advanced

I run the **5-Why chain** from the symptom down. The payments time out, so why. Processing is slow, so why. Database queries are lagging, so why. Server load is high, so why. The servers are not sized for peak traffic. That chain points at capacity, not code. **Peak-only failures mean capacity**. All-day failures mean code or data. I fix the root, not the symptom. I add **database indexing** on the slow queries, increase server capacity, and add **load balancing** so traffic spreads evenly. Then I **monitor after the fix** to confirm the failures actually stopped, not just moved to a different time of day. I **document the RCA** so the next incident starts from evidence instead of guesses. And I add **peak-load testing** to the release cycle for every payment service, so capacity is proven before production, not discovered by customers during the busiest hour. The pattern to remember is simple. If it only breaks when it is busy, it is a capacity problem. Fix the capacity, prove it with a load test, and monitor it in production.

Read the full chapter →
Q265.A payment left the channel but never arrived at the clearing house. The customer is asking where their money is. How do you trace it and what do you tell them?Advanced

Start by checking the **pacs.002** status reports. If the clearing house sent an ACSC, the payment settled and the problem is in the feedback loop. If there is no pacs.002, the payment never reached the clearing house. Next, check the **payment hub logs** for that UETR. The hub records every hop: received from channel, validated, sent to clearing. Find the last hop that succeeded. Then check the **clearing interface**. The message may be stuck in the outbound queue because the clearing house connection dropped, or the interface may have rejected it for a format error. Also check the **cut-off**. If the payment arrived after the clearing cut-off, it sits in a queue until the next window and the status looks frozen. Once you find the break, fix the cause, not just this payment. If it is a connection drop, restart the interface and replay the queue. If it is a format error, fix the mapping and resubmit. Always notify the customer with the real status, not a generic message. And add monitoring on the **age of unacknowledged payments** so the next stuck payment raises an alert within minutes, not hours.

Read the full chapter →
Q266.A corporate customer sends a bulk file with 5,000 salary payments. Walk through how the file is processed without errors, from receipt to settlement.Beginner

A clean bulk file starts before the file even arrives. The corporate customer prepares a **pain.001** file with hundreds or thousands of payments, and the bank publishes a clear file specification so the customer knows the exact format. When the file arrives, the hub validates the file structure first, checking the header, the record count, and the control totals. Then it validates each payment inside, the account numbers, the amounts, the beneficiary details, and the sanctions lists. If every payment passes, the hub processes the whole file as a batch, sending each payment to the clearing system and tracking the **pacs.002** status on each one. The hub generates a **pain.002** report telling the customer which payments were accepted and which were rejected, with a reason for each rejection. The accepted payments settle on the promised value date, and the customer gets a single **camt.054** summary plus the individual credits. The signs of a healthy bulk flow are a high first-time acceptance rate, clear rejection reasons when something fails, and a customer who can reconcile the file against the bank statement without calling operations. A bulk file that processes cleanly is a sign that the file specification, the validation, and the customer onboarding all work together.

Read the full chapter →
Q267.A customer submits a payment at 3 PM and the cut-off is 4 PM. Walk through how the payment meets the cut-off and settles on the same value date.Beginner

Meeting the cut-off works because the whole chain is aligned to the same clock. The customer submits the payment before the published **cut-off time**, and the channel accepts it. The payment hub validates it immediately and sends the **pacs.008** to the clearing system before the clearing cut-off. The clearing system processes it in the current settlement cycle, and the beneficiary bank credits the account on the same **value date**. The customer sees the credit the same day, and the sender gets a **pacs.002** with ACSC status. The keys to making it work are a published cut-off that the customer can see in the channel, a hub that processes fast enough to meet it, and a clearing system with enough cycles. The bank also builds in a **buffer**, so the internal cut-off is a few minutes before the clearing cut-off, giving the hub time to process the last payments. If the customer submits after the cut-off, the channel tells them immediately that the value date is the next business day, so there is no surprise. A payment that meets the cut-off is a promise kept, and a bank that keeps its cut-off promises earns customer trust.

Read the full chapter →
Q268.A corporate customer sends a payment file that passes validation on the first attempt. What does the bank do to make first-time-right files the norm?Beginner

A file that passes validation the first time is a sign that the customer onboarding and the file specification both work. The corporate customer prepares the file using the bank's **published specification**, which defines the exact format, the mandatory fields, and the validation rules. Before sending the file, the customer runs it through the bank's **pre-validation tool**, which checks the format and flags any errors. The customer fixes the errors and sends the file. The bank hub validates the file structure, checking the header, the record count, and the control totals, and then validates each payment, the account numbers, the amounts, and the beneficiary details. If everything passes, the hub accepts the whole file and sends a **pain.002** acceptance for every payment. The payments settle on the promised value date. The customer gets a single confirmation, and the **camt.054** notifications match the file. What makes it clean is the **feedback loop**. The customer knows the rules before they send, they can test the file before they send, and they get a clear answer when they send. A file that fails validation is not a failure, it is a signal that the specification or the onboarding needs work.

Read the full chapter →
Q269.Walk through a clean bulk salary run. How does an employer pay 5,000 employees on payday with every payment landing on time?Beginner

A clean salary run works because the file, the funding, and the timing are all agreed in advance. The employer sends a **pain.001** file with every employee payment, the account numbers, the amounts, and the value date, which is payday. The bank validates the file, checking each payment against the account details and the sanctions lists. The bank checks that the employer account has **enough funds** to cover the total, and if not, it alerts the employer before the value date. On payday, the bank releases the file, sending each payment to the clearing system. The clearing system settles them, and each employee bank credits the salary to the employee account. The employer gets a **pain.002** confirmation showing every payment was accepted, and the end-of-day statement shows the total debit. Each employee sees their salary in their account on payday, on time, in full. What makes it clean is the **advance preparation**. The file arrives days before payday, the funding is confirmed, and the validation happens early, so any problem is fixed before the value date. A salary run that works is one that nobody notices, because the money simply arrives.

Read the full chapter →
Q270.A production incident hits during a release. What is your role?Advanced

My role in a production incident is to own the business impact and the communication, while engineering owns the technical fix. First, I find out what is affected: which payments, how many customers, whether money is stuck or just delayed. I write this down clearly so everyone is working from the same facts. Second, I join the incident bridge and stay on it, translating between engineering and the business. When engineering says the message queue is backed up, I turn that into the business impact: 200 payments are delayed and the oldest is 45 minutes old. Third, I help the operations manager decide the priority: which payments to release first when the system comes back, usually the urgent and high value ones. Fourth, I draft the customer message in plain language so the helpdesk and the communications team give customers a consistent update. Fifth, after the incident, I lead the business side of the post incident review: what was the customer impact, what did we learn, what requirement or control needs to change so it does not happen again. I do not try to fix the code. My value is making sure the business knows what is happening and the fix addresses the real problem.

Read the full chapter →
Q271.How do you prioritise when five payment issues land at once?Intermediate

I triage by impact first, then by urgency. I look at all five issues and ask three questions about each one: how many customers are affected, is money stuck or at risk, and is there a deadline like a cut off or a regulatory report. The issue that affects the most customers and has money at risk comes first. I am explicit about the order and I tell the stakeholders what I am working on and what is queued. I do not try to do all five at once. I pick the top one, work it until it is stable or handed to the right owner, then move to the next. For each issue I identify the owner: is it a data fix I can do, an engineering defect, or an operations problem. I delegate what is not mine. I also look for a common cause: five issues landing at once sometimes share one root cause, like a bad deployment or a file that failed. If I find a common cause, fixing that fixes several issues at once. I keep a simple tracker: the issue, the impact, the owner, the status and the next update time. I update the stakeholders at the times I promised, even if the update is that there is no change yet. People can wait if they know when they will hear from you.

Read the full chapter →
Q272.A payment is failing in production and nobody knows why. Walk me through your investigation.Advanced

I start with the facts, not guesses. First, I find a failing payment and get its reference number and UETR. I check the payment hub to see where it stopped and what error was recorded. I look at the message that was sent and the response that came back. If the response is a pacs.002 rejection, I read the reason code: it tells me exactly what failed. Second, I check whether the failure is isolated or widespread. I look at the same time window and see if other payments failed the same way. If many failed, it is likely a system or configuration issue. If only one failed, it is likely a data issue with that payment. Third, I check the recent changes: was there a deployment, a configuration change or a reference data update around the time the failures started. Fourth, I check the upstream and downstream systems: did the channel send the payment correctly, did the hub receive it, did clearing accept it. I narrow it down hop by hop until I find the exact point of failure. Fifth, I work with engineering on the fix and with operations on the workaround for the affected payments. I document the investigation so the next person does not start from zero. A structured investigation saves hours compared to guessing.

Read the full chapter →
Q273.A user acceptance test fails on the last day before go-live. What do you do?Advanced

I would not sign off a go live with a failing test on the last day. First, I find out what failed and how serious it is. Is it a defect that stops payments, or a minor display issue. If it stops payments or risks wrong payments, the go live must be delayed or the scope reduced. I would explain this to the stakeholders with the evidence: the failing test, the impact and the risk of going live with it. Second, I look for a workaround: can the affected payment type be excluded from the first release, can operations handle it manually for a short period, can we go live for a limited set of customers. Third, I work with engineering on the fix and the retest: how long will the fix take, can it be tested properly in the time available, and is there a risk the fix breaks something else. Fourth, I update the go live plan: the revised scope, the revised date or the agreed workaround, and the communication to customers if they are affected. Fifth, I record the decision and who made it. A go live is a business decision, not a BA decision, but the BA must make sure the decision is made with full information. Going live with a known defect that affects payments is how banks end up with a production incident on day one.

Read the full chapter →
Q274.A test environment does not match production. How do you handle it?Intermediate

A test environment that does not match production is a common and dangerous problem, because a test can pass and the change can still fail in production. First, I identify the differences: is the data different, is the configuration different, is a system missing or a different version. I document the gaps precisely so everyone knows what the test did and did not cover. Second, I work with engineering to close the gaps that matter most: the configuration of the payment hub, the reference data, the clearing system simulators and the test data. I prioritise the gaps that affect the payment flow being tested. Third, for the gaps that cannot be closed quickly, I note them as test limitations and I plan additional checks: a dress rehearsal in an environment closer to production, a controlled pilot with a small volume of real payments, or extra monitoring after go live. Fourth, I make sure the go live decision accounts for these limitations. If a critical part of the flow was never tested in a production like environment, the stakeholders need to know that before they approve the release. Fifth, I raise the environment gap as a problem to fix, not just for this change but for future changes. A test environment that cannot be trusted wastes everyone's time.

Read the full chapter →
Q275.How do you prepare for a payment system cutover weekend?Advanced

A cutover weekend is planned in detail because the bank cannot afford to get it wrong. The preparation starts weeks before. I write the cutover plan with every step, who does it, how long it takes and what the rollback is. I run a dress rehearsal in a test environment following the exact steps, and I time each step to confirm the plan fits in the window. I prepare the test scenarios for the go live validation: a set of payments that will be run immediately after cutover to prove the system works. I confirm the communications plan: who is told, when and by whom, including customers if they are affected. On the weekend, I am on the bridge call from the start. I track each step against the plan and note any deviation. After each major step, we run a validation check before moving to the next. Once the system is live, we run the validation payments and check that they settle correctly and reconciliation matches. I stay on the bridge until the first real payments have settled and the operations team confirms they are comfortable. Only then is the cutover declared complete. The next business day I am available early to support operations. A good cutover is boring: nothing unexpected happens because everything was rehearsed.

Regulatory Frameworks (16)

Q276.What controls does a large bank put around payments to manage risk?Advanced

A large bank layers controls around payments because the risk is real money leaving the bank. The first control is authentication: the person giving the instruction must prove who they are, through a password, a token or a biometric. The second is authorisation: the payment must be approved by someone with the right limit, and large payments need two approvers. The third is sanctions screening: every payment is checked against sanctions lists before it is released, and a hit stops the payment automatically. The fourth is fraud detection: the bank looks for unusual patterns, a new beneficiary, a large amount, a payment at an odd hour, and holds the payment for review. The fifth is limits: each customer and each channel has a daily limit, and payments above it need extra approval. The sixth is reconciliation: every payment is matched against what clearing confirmed, and any gap is flagged the same day. The seventh is audit: every action on a payment is logged, who did it, when and why, so the bank can trace any payment end to end. These controls are not optional. They are required by regulators, and the bank is audited on them. A BA needs to know these controls because every new payment feature must fit inside them.

Read the full chapter →
Q277.A stakeholder wants a change that breaks a regulatory rule. What do you do?Advanced

I would not agree to it, but I would not just say no either. First I would understand what the stakeholder actually needs. Often the request that breaks a rule is a shortcut to a genuine business need, and there is a compliant way to meet that need. I would explain the rule in plain language: what the regulation says, why it exists and what happens if the bank breaks it, including fines and reputational damage. I would bring the evidence, the exact regulation and the control that would fail. Then I would propose an alternative. For example, if the stakeholder wants to skip a sanctions check to speed up payments, I would suggest ways to make the check faster, like improving the screening rules to reduce false positives, rather than removing the check. I would involve compliance early so the stakeholder hears the same message from them, not only from me. If the stakeholder still pushes, I would escalate through the proper governance route and record the decision. The key is that a BA does not silently build something that breaks a rule. The BA protects the bank and the customer, and finds a way to deliver the business outcome within the rules.

Read the full chapter →
Q278.A regulatory change lands with a tight deadline. How do you respond?Advanced

A regulatory change with a tight deadline is a common situation in payments. First, I read the regulation and the regulator's guidance to understand exactly what must change and by when. I do not rely on a summary from someone else. Second, I assess the impact: which payment types are affected, which systems, which customer journeys and which reports. I map the change to the current process and identify the gaps. Third, I bring the right people together: compliance to confirm the interpretation, operations to confirm the operational impact, engineering to estimate the build and testing effort, and the business to confirm the customer impact. Fourth, I build a plan working backwards from the deadline: design, build, test, user acceptance, cutover and the buffer for problems. If the deadline is not achievable with the full scope, I propose a phased approach: the minimum compliant change by the deadline, and the fuller improvement after. Fifth, I communicate the plan to senior management with the risks spelled out: what happens if we miss the deadline, what is the regulatory exposure. Sixth, I track the delivery daily and escalate the moment something slips. Regulatory deadlines do not move, so the plan must be realistic from day one and the team must know the deadline is fixed.

Read the full chapter →
Q279.How do you handle a situation where the business and compliance disagree?Intermediate

When the business and compliance disagree, the BA is in the middle and has to help both sides reach a decision that is compliant and workable. First, I make sure I understand both positions precisely. The business usually wants speed or simplicity for the customer. Compliance wants the control that protects the bank and meets the regulation. I write down both positions and the underlying reason for each, so the conversation is about the reasons, not the positions. Second, I check the regulation itself, not someone's interpretation of it. I read the rule and the guidance, and I ask compliance to point to the specific requirement. Third, I look for a solution that meets the regulatory requirement and still works for the business. Often there is a middle ground: a control that is less disruptive but still compliant, a phased approach, or a manual control for a short period while the automated control is built. Fourth, if no middle ground exists, the regulatory requirement wins, because the bank cannot choose to break a rule for convenience. I explain this to the business clearly and help them understand the consequence of non compliance. Fifth, I document the decision and the reasoning so it can be audited. The BA does not decide compliance questions. The BA makes sure the decision is informed and recorded.

Read the full chapter →
Q280.A customer tries to pay online and the bank asks them to approve the payment in their banking app. The customer complains that this is an extra step and asks why it is needed. Explain strong customer authentication under PSD2 and when the bank can skip it.Intermediate

**Strong customer authentication**, or SCA, is a requirement under **PSD2**, the European payment services law. It means the customer must prove their identity using at least two of three factors: something they know, such as a password, something they have, such as their phone, and something they are, such as a fingerprint. The bank asks for approval in the app because the app combines something the customer has with something they know or are. SCA applies to most electronic payments, including online card payments and account access. The bank can skip it in specific cases called **exemptions**: low value payments below 30 euro, recurring payments after the first one, payments to a **trusted beneficiary** the customer has whitelisted, and low risk payments where the bank transaction risk analysis shows the payment is safe. Explain to the customer that SCA exists because online fraud was growing fast and passwords alone were not enough. It is an extra step, but it stops a fraudster who has stolen the card number from completing a payment, because they do not have the customer phone or fingerprint. The bank should make the app approval as quick as possible, because a slow or confusing step is what makes customers complain.

Read the full chapter →
Q281.Your bank operates in the euro area. The Instant Payments Regulation now requires you to offer SEPA Instant payments and to check the payee name before sending. Explain what the regulation requires and what your bank must build to comply.Intermediate

The **Instant Payments Regulation** requires banks in the euro area to offer **SEPA Instant Credit Transfer**, or SCT Inst, so that customers can send and receive euro payments within **10 seconds**, 24 hours a day, every day of the year. The bank must also offer instant payments at a price no higher than a standard credit transfer, which means it cannot charge a premium for speed. The second requirement is **verification of payee**. Before the payer confirms the payment, the bank must check that the payee name matches the account number, the IBAN, and warn the payer if there is a mismatch or a close match. This check stops **authorised push payment fraud**, where a customer is tricked into paying a fraudster, and it stops payments to the wrong account because of a typing error. To comply, the bank must build real time payment processing that never sleeps, instant settlement through **TIPS** or another clearing system, and a verification of payee service that responds in milliseconds. The bank must also update its customer journeys, because the payment is **irrevocable** once sent, and the customer needs to understand that before they confirm. Non compliance means regulatory fines and, more importantly, customers who cannot pay instantly when every other bank can.

Read the full chapter →
Q282.Your bank payment platform goes down for four hours during a busy morning. The regulator asks for a report under the operational resilience rules. Explain what DORA requires, what the bank must show, and how the operations team prepares for this.Advanced

**DORA**, the Digital Operational Resilience Act, requires financial firms in the EU to be able to withstand, respond to, and recover from technology disruptions. A four hour payment outage is exactly the kind of incident DORA covers. The bank must report the incident to the regulator within a strict timeline, usually an **initial notification within 4 hours** and a fuller report within 72 hours, describing what happened, which services were affected, how many customers were impacted, and what was done to recover. The bank must also show that it had identified payment processing as a **critical business service**, that it had set an **impact tolerance**, meaning the maximum disruption it can accept, and that it had tested its recovery plan. The operations team prepares by running **resilience testing**, including failover tests where the backup system takes over, and by keeping a clear **incident log** from the first minute, so the report is based on facts, not memory. The team should also have a **communication plan** for customers and for correspondent banks, because silence during an outage makes the damage worse. DORA is not about never having an outage. It is about proving the bank knew the risk, had a plan, executed it, and learned from it.

Read the full chapter →
Q283.A customer is tricked by a fraudster into sending 20,000 pounds to a criminal account. The customer reports it to the bank the same day. Under the UK PSR rules on authorised push payment fraud, who pays, and what does the bank have to do?Intermediate

Under the **PSR reimbursement rules**, the sending bank must reimburse the customer for **authorised push payment fraud**, where the customer was tricked into authorising the payment. The cost is split **50/50** between the sending bank and the receiving bank, unless the receiving bank can show it did not meet its obligations. The customer must be reimbursed within **five business days** of the claim, and the maximum reimbursement is **85,000 pounds**. The bank must first check whether the customer acted with **gross negligence**, which is a very high bar, or whether the claim is fraudulent, because those are the only reasons to refuse. The bank must also try to recover the funds by contacting the receiving bank immediately and asking it to freeze the criminal account. The receiving bank must act quickly, because fraudsters move the money within hours. Explain to the customer that they should report the fraud immediately, keep all evidence, such as the messages from the fraudster, and that the bank will handle the claim. The lesson for the bank is that prevention matters more than reimbursement: **confirmation of payee** checks, fraud warnings before the customer confirms, and transaction monitoring are what stop these payments in the first place.

Read the full chapter →
Q284.The SWIFT CBPR+ migration deadline has passed and MT messages are no longer accepted for cross border payments. A small bank in your network is still sending MT103 messages. What happens to those messages and what must the bank do?Advanced

When the **CBPR+ migration** deadline passes, the SWIFT network stops accepting **MT103** messages for cross border payments and requires **ISO 20022** messages, such as the **pacs.008**. An MT103 sent after the deadline is **rejected** by the network, and the sending bank receives a rejection notice. The payment does not travel, the beneficiary is not paid, and the sending bank must fix the problem before the customer payment can go through. The small bank must complete its migration: build or buy the ability to create and receive **pacs.008** messages, map its internal data to the ISO 20022 structure, including **structured addresses** and purpose codes, and test against the **CBPR+ usage guidelines**. It must also update its customer channels, because the data the customer provides must now be richer and more structured. If the bank cannot migrate in time, its options are to use a **correspondent bank** that has migrated, to use a payment service provider that converts the messages, or to stop offering cross border payments until it is ready. The regulator and the bank board need to know, because offering a payment service the bank cannot deliver is a conduct risk. The migration was announced years in advance, so a bank that misses it has a planning failure, not a technical surprise.

Read the full chapter →
Q285.A payment is blocked because the beneficiary name matches a name on the OFAC sanctions list. The customer says it is a different person with the same name. Explain what happens next and why the bank cannot simply release the payment.Beginner

**OFAC**, the US Office of Foreign Assets Control, maintains the **SDN list**, a list of people and entities that US persons and banks must not deal with. When a payment matches a name on the list, the bank must **block** it, which means holding the funds and not releasing them, while it investigates. The customer saying it is a different person is not enough, because the bank must prove it. The compliance team compares the **full details**: the date of birth, the address, the nationality, the passport number, and any other identifiers, against the listing. If the details clearly show it is a different person, the bank documents the decision and **releases** the payment. If the details are unclear, or if the payment involves a sanctioned country, the bank must keep the payment blocked and may need to report it to OFAC. The bank cannot simply release the payment on the customer word, because if it turns out to be the sanctioned person, the bank faces **fines** running into millions of dollars and criminal liability for its staff. The customer should be told honestly that the check is required by law, that it protects the bank and the customer, and that providing full identifying details speeds up the release.

Read the full chapter →
Q286.A customer asks why the bank needs their full address for a cross border payment, and whether the bank is sharing their personal data. Explain the GDPR position and what the bank must do with payment data.Intermediate

Under **GDPR**, the bank can only collect and use personal data when it has a **lawful basis**. For a cross border payment, the lawful basis is that the data is necessary to perform the contract, the payment instruction, and to comply with a **legal obligation**, because payment regulations require the bank to include the payer name, account, and address in the payment message. The bank must include this data in the **pacs.008** or MT103, because the receiving bank and the intermediary banks need it for **sanctions screening** and reconciliation. The bank must tell the customer what data it collects and why, in its **privacy notice**, and it must only share the data that is necessary for the payment. The bank must also protect the data with **encryption** and access controls, and it must not keep it longer than necessary. The customer has rights under GDPR, including the right to see their data and to ask for corrections, but they do not have the right to have the payment data deleted while the bank is legally required to keep it for **record keeping**, usually five to ten years. Explain to the customer that the address is not the bank being nosy. It is required by law, it travels only to the banks that need it, and it is what stops the payment being blocked for missing information.

Read the full chapter →
Q287.Transaction monitoring flags a customer who has received several cash deposits just below the reporting threshold, then sent the money abroad. Explain what the bank suspects, what it must do, and what it must never tell the customer.Advanced

The bank suspects **structuring**, which is the deliberate splitting of transactions into smaller amounts to avoid a reporting threshold. It is a classic **money laundering** technique: the criminal breaks a large sum into deposits just below the threshold, so no single transaction triggers a report, then moves the money abroad where it is harder to trace. The bank must investigate the pattern: who is the customer, what is their normal activity, what is the source of the cash, and does the behaviour make business sense. If the investigation cannot explain the pattern, the bank must file a **suspicious activity report**, or SAR, with the financial intelligence unit, and it must consider whether to continue the relationship. The bank must never tell the customer that a SAR has been filed, or that they are under investigation. This is called **tipping off**, and it is a criminal offence, because it warns the criminal to move the money or destroy evidence. The bank can ask the customer for information about the source of funds as part of normal due diligence, but it must not reveal that monitoring has flagged them. The case should be handled by the **financial crime** team, not by the branch, and the branch should follow the team instructions exactly, even if that means delaying a payment while the review is done.

Read the full chapter →
Q288.The Bank of England migrates CHAPS to ISO 20022. A corporate customer asks what changes for them. Explain the migration, what the customer must do, and what improves once it is live.Intermediate

The **Bank of England** migrated **CHAPS**, the UK high value payment system, to **ISO 20022** message formats. The change means CHAPS payments now use the same structured data standard as the rest of the world, instead of the older MT format. For the corporate customer, the main change is in the **data** they must provide. The payment instruction now needs a **structured address**, with separate fields for street, town, and postcode, instead of free text. It also needs a **purpose code** that says what the payment is for, and richer **remittance information** so the beneficiary can reconcile it. The customer must update their payment files, their treasury system, and their templates to provide this data, and they must test with their bank before the migration date. Once live, the customer gets better **reconciliation**, because the beneficiary receives structured data they can match automatically, better **sanctions screening**, because the structured address is easier to check, and better **straight through processing**, because fewer payments need manual repair. The payment itself does not get faster or slower. CHAPS is still a real time gross settlement system with same day finality. What changes is the quality of the data travelling with it.

Read the full chapter →
Q289.An Indian company wants to pay a supplier in Germany. The payment is delayed because the bank asks for FEMA documentation. Explain what FEMA is, why the bank asks, and what the company should prepare.Advanced

**FEMA**, the Foreign Exchange Management Act, is the Indian law that governs how money moves in and out of India. It requires that cross border payments are made for a **permitted purpose**, that the amount is genuine, and that the transaction is reported to the **Reserve Bank of India** through the bank. The bank asks for documentation because it is the **authorised dealer** and it is legally responsible for checking that the payment complies with FEMA before it releases the funds. For a supplier payment, the company should prepare the **invoice**, the **purchase order**, the **shipping documents** if goods are involved, and the **FEMA declaration** stating the purpose of the payment. If the payment is for services, the bank may also ask for the **service agreement** and evidence that the service was delivered. The bank checks the documents against the payment instruction: the beneficiary name must match the invoice, the amount must match, and the purpose code must be correct. If anything does not match, the bank must hold the payment and ask for clarification. Tell the company to keep the documents ready before they instruct the payment, because a payment held for FEMA checks can take days to release, and the supplier will not wait.

Read the full chapter →
Q290.A bank receives a payment instruction where the beneficiary information is missing. The payment cannot be processed. Explain the travel rule and what the bank must do.Beginner

The **travel rule** requires that certain information about the payer and the payee **travels with** the payment, from the sending bank all the way to the beneficiary bank. Under the EU **Funds Transfer Regulation**, the payer information must include the name, the account number, and the address, and the payee information must include the name and the account number. When a payment arrives with the beneficiary information missing, the receiving bank cannot complete its **sanctions screening**, because it does not know who the money is going to, and it cannot reconcile the payment, because it does not know who to credit. The bank must not process the payment as it stands. It should contact the **sending bank** and ask for the missing information, using an MT199 or the gpi Case Resolution tool, and it should hold the payment while it waits. If the sending bank cannot provide the information, the bank must **reject** the payment and return the funds. The travel rule exists to stop criminals hiding behind incomplete payment messages, and every bank in the chain is responsible for enforcing it. A bank that processes payments with missing beneficiary data is breaching the regulation and risks a fine.

Read the full chapter →
Q291.Your bank has identified its payment platform as a critical business service under the operational resilience rules. The board asks what impact tolerance means and what happens if it is breached. Explain it in plain language.Expert

**Impact tolerance** is the maximum disruption the bank is willing to accept for a **critical business service** before the harm to customers, to the market, or to the bank itself becomes unacceptable. For a payment platform, the board might set a tolerance of **two hours**: the platform can be down for up to two hours, but beyond that, customers cannot pay, businesses cannot settle, and the damage is severe. The tolerance is not a target, it is a limit. The bank must be able to **recover** within the tolerance, which means the backup systems, the recovery procedures, and the people must all be ready to restore service inside two hours. If the tolerance is breached, the bank must notify the **regulator**, explain what happened, what the impact was, and what it will do to prevent a repeat. The board must also review whether the tolerance was realistic and whether the investment in resilience was enough. Setting the tolerance is a board decision, not a technology decision, because it is about how much harm the bank will accept. A tolerance of two hours for payments means the bank must invest in **real time replication**, tested failover, and a recovery team that can act in minutes, not hours. If the bank cannot meet its own tolerance, it must either invest more or reduce the service it offers.

Business Analyst and Product Owner (13)

Q292.What is a payment workshop and what questions do you ask?Intermediate

A payment workshop is a facilitated session where a BA brings business stakeholders, operations staff, and technical teams together to define requirements for a payment change. It is more effective than one-to-one interviews for payments because a payment flow crosses many teams, and a workshop surfaces disagreements early. A typical workshop starts with the current state: how does the payment flow work today, and where does it break? Then it moves to the future state: what should change, and what does success look like? Key questions include: which payment types and channels are in scope, and which are out of scope? What are the cut-off times and value dating rules? What validation should happen at the channel versus the hub? What happens when screening flags a payment, and who decides whether to release it? What are the fee and charging rules? What reports and reconciliations are needed? What are the non-functional requirements, such as volumes, performance, and availability? Good workshops use process flows on a whiteboard, real payment examples, and edge cases such as a payment on a public holiday. The BA's job is to keep the discussion focused, capture decisions and open actions, and turn the output into requirements. A well-run workshop can resolve in hours what would take weeks of email.

Read the full chapter →
Q293.How does a BA work with engineering and operations in a large bank?Intermediate

A BA in a large bank is the bridge between the business and the engineers. The work starts with operations. The BA sits with the operations team and watches how they process payments today, where they struggle and what they need. The BA writes down the current process, the pain points and the requirements for the new system. Then the BA works with engineering. The BA explains the business requirement in a way engineers can build: the data fields, the validation rules, the expected behaviour when something fails. The BA writes user stories, acceptance criteria and test scenarios. During development, the BA answers questions from engineers and makes decisions when the requirement is unclear. During testing, the BA works with operations to run user acceptance testing and confirms the system does what the business asked for. After go live, the BA stays with operations for the first weeks to catch issues and fix them. The BA does not write code and does not process payments. The BA makes sure the thing that gets built is the thing the business actually needs, and that operations can use it on a busy Monday morning without calling the BA for help.

Read the full chapter →
Q294.How is a change delivered in a large bank: release, testing and cutover?Advanced

Change in a large bank follows a strict path because a mistake can stop payments for thousands of customers. First, the change is designed and the requirements are written and signed off by the business, operations and risk. Second, the engineers build it in a development environment. Third, the change goes to a test environment where the QA team runs functional tests, regression tests and performance tests. The BA writes the test scenarios based on real payment flows, including the unhappy paths like a rejected payment or a missing field. Fourth, the change goes to user acceptance testing where operations run it with real scenarios and confirm it works. Fifth, the change is scheduled for a release window, usually a weekend or an overnight slot when volumes are low. The cutover plan lists every step, who does it, how long it takes and what the rollback is if something goes wrong. On the night, the team follows the plan step by step and checks the system after each step. After go live, the team monitors the first payments closely and has a war room open for the first hours. The release is only declared complete when the first batch of payments has settled cleanly and reconciliation matches.

Read the full chapter →
Q295.How does a large bank onboard a new corporate client onto its payment platform?Intermediate

Onboarding a corporate client onto a payment platform is a project that takes weeks, not days. First, the bank does due diligence: it checks the client's identity, its business, its owners and its risk profile. This is the know your customer process, and it must be complete before the client can send a payment. Second, the bank sets up the client's static data: the accounts, the users, the approval limits, the payment types the client can use and the file formats they will send. Third, the bank and the client agree on the connectivity: will the client send files through a secure portal, an API or a direct host to host connection. Fourth, the bank runs a test phase where the client sends test files and the bank confirms they are processed correctly. The client also tests the response files and the online screens. Fifth, the bank and the client agree a go live date and a cutover plan. On the day, the client sends its first live file and the bank monitors it closely. The BA is involved throughout: writing the onboarding requirements, documenting the client configuration, running the test scenarios and supporting the go live. A smooth onboarding means the client can pay its suppliers and staff from day one without a problem.

Read the full chapter →
Q296.What is the role of a business analyst in a payments transformation programme?Intermediate

A payments transformation programme in a large bank replaces old systems with new ones, often moving from legacy mainframe payment engines to a modern payment hub. The BA is central to this work. First, the BA documents the current state: how payments work today, which systems are involved, where the manual workarounds are and what breaks. Second, the BA works with the business to define the future state: what should the new hub do, which payment types will it support, what are the target STP rates and exception handling rules. Third, the BA writes the requirements for the new system in a form engineers can build from, including the data model, the validation rules, the message formats and the reconciliation needs. Fourth, the BA supports testing, writing the test scenarios and running user acceptance testing with operations. Fifth, the BA manages the migration: which customers move when, how the old and new systems run side by side, and how the bank cuts over without stopping payments. Sixth, the BA handles the change impact: training for operations, new procedures and updated customer communications. Transformation programmes run for years and cost millions, and the BA is the person who makes sure the business need stays clear while the engineers build. Without a good BA, the programme builds the wrong thing.

Read the full chapter →
Q297.You have two conflicting requirements from operations and engineering. How do you resolve it?Advanced

I would start by bringing both sides into the same room with the facts in front of them. Operations wants the payment to be processed a certain way because that is how their team works today. Engineering wants a different way because it is simpler to build or fits the system architecture better. I would first check whether the conflict is real or a misunderstanding. Often operations describes a need and engineering hears a different requirement. I would write down both requirements side by side and trace each one back to its source: is it a regulatory rule, a customer promise, an operational need or a preference. Regulatory and customer promises are not negotiable. Preferences can be discussed. Then I would look for a solution that meets the non negotiable part of both sides. For example, operations may need a manual override for a specific payment type, and engineering may not want to build a custom screen. The compromise might be a controlled override through an existing tool with proper audit logging. I would document the agreed solution, get both sides to sign off, and make sure the acceptance criteria are clear. If no compromise is possible, I escalate with a recommendation and the trade offs spelled out, so the decision maker can choose with full information.

Read the full chapter →
Q298.How do you gather requirements for a new payment product?Beginner

I start by understanding the problem the product is solving, not the solution someone has already imagined. I talk to the business sponsor and ask: who is the customer, what payment are they making, what goes wrong today, what does good look like. Then I talk to operations, because they process the payments today and they know where the pain is. I watch them work and note the manual steps, the workarounds and the exceptions. Then I talk to the customers if possible, or read the customer complaints and the helpdesk tickets to see what customers actually struggle with. I also look at the existing systems and data: what payment types exist, what volumes, what the failure rates are. From all of this I write the requirements, starting with the user stories: as a customer I want to do this so that I get that benefit. I add the acceptance criteria, the validation rules, the error handling and the non functional requirements like performance and security. I validate the requirements by walking them through with operations and engineering, using a real example payment end to end. I keep the requirements in a place everyone can see, and I update them when the team learns something new. Requirements gathering is not a single meeting. It is a continuous conversation until the product goes live.

Read the full chapter →
Q299.How do you explain a complex payment failure to a non-technical stakeholder?Intermediate

I start with the outcome, not the technical detail. I would say: the payment did not reach the beneficiary on time, and here is what that means for the customer. Then I explain the cause in plain terms, using an analogy if it helps. For example, I might say: think of the payment like a letter. The letter was written correctly, but the post office could not read the address because one line was missing, so the letter was returned. In the same way, our system rejected the payment because a required field was blank, and the payment was sent back to us. I would then explain what we are doing about it: we have fixed the missing information, we have resent the payment, and the beneficiary should receive it by tomorrow. I would also say what we are changing so it does not happen again, for example adding a check that stops the payment from being sent when a required field is blank. I avoid jargon completely. I do not say pacs.002 or RJCT. I say the payment was rejected and returned. I check that the stakeholder understood by asking them to repeat back what will happen next. The goal is that the stakeholder leaves the conversation knowing what happened, what it means for them and what happens next.

Read the full chapter →
Q300.How do you handle a requirement that keeps changing?Intermediate

Changing requirements are normal in payments because the business learns as the build progresses. I handle it by making the change process visible and controlled. First, I understand the change: what is different, why is it needed, and what is the impact on what is already built. I write the change down as a change request with the old requirement, the new requirement and the reason. Second, I assess the impact with engineering: how much work to change it, does it affect testing already done, does it affect the go live date. Third, I take the impact to the decision maker, usually the product owner, with a clear recommendation and the cost of the change. Fourth, once approved, I update the requirements, the test scenarios and the acceptance criteria, and I tell everyone affected. I do not let changes happen by a verbal comment in a meeting, because then nobody knows what the current requirement is. I keep a single source of truth for requirements and I version it. Small changes that do not affect the design can be absorbed quickly. Large changes that affect the architecture need proper approval. The key is that change is expected and managed, not feared and hidden.

Read the full chapter →
Q301.A vendor delivers a payment component late. What do you do?Advanced

First, I assess the impact: what is delayed, who is affected and whether there is a workaround. I tell the stakeholders immediately so they hear it from me, not from a missed deadline. Second, I understand the reason for the delay from the vendor: is it a resource problem, a technical blocker or a scope misunderstanding. I ask for specifics, not a vague new date. Third, I look at the options. Can we descope the component and use a manual workaround for the first release. Can we use a different vendor component. Can we reorder the work so other parts of the build continue while we wait. Fourth, I replan with engineering: what is the new realistic date, what is the critical path and what can be done in parallel. Fifth, I manage the stakeholders: I give them the revised date with the reason and the mitigation, and I update them regularly until the component arrives. Sixth, when the component does arrive, I make sure the testing is thorough because a late component is often a rushed component. I do not accept a vendor date without evidence, and I do not hide a delay. The stakeholder would rather hear a bad date early than a good date that turns out to be wrong.

Read the full chapter →
Q302.How do you validate that a payment requirement is complete?Intermediate

I validate a requirement by testing it against real examples. First, I take a real payment and walk it through the requirement end to end: does the requirement cover every step, every field, every decision point and every error. If I find a step with no requirement, the requirement is incomplete. Second, I test the unhappy paths: what happens when a field is missing, when the amount is zero, when the currency is unsupported, when the beneficiary bank rejects the payment. If the requirement only describes the happy path, it is incomplete. Third, I check the non functional side: performance, security, audit, reconciliation and reporting. A requirement that says what the system should do but not how fast, how secure or how it is audited is incomplete. Fourth, I review it with operations: I read the requirement to them and ask if they could do their job with only this document. If they have questions I cannot answer from the document, the requirement needs more work. Fifth, I review it with engineering: can they build from it without guessing. If they are guessing, the requirement is incomplete. A complete requirement is one that a developer can build from and an operator can use without calling the BA.

Read the full chapter →
Q303.How do you work with a difficult stakeholder?Intermediate

I start by understanding what the stakeholder actually cares about, not what they are demanding. A difficult stakeholder is often someone under pressure from their own manager or client, and the demand is a symptom of that pressure. I listen without interrupting and I repeat back what I heard so they know I understood. Then I separate the person from the problem: I focus on the requirement and the facts, not on the tone. I bring evidence: the data, the process, the options and the trade offs. Evidence is hard to argue with. I also find common ground: we both want the payment to work and the customer to be happy, and I say that out loud. I give the stakeholder choices, not a single yes or no, because people accept a decision better when they chose it. If the relationship is still difficult, I involve their manager or a neutral party early, before it becomes a conflict. I keep every agreement in writing so there is no dispute later about what was decided. I stay calm and professional even when the stakeholder is not, because losing my temper would damage the working relationship and make the next conversation harder. Over time, consistent delivery and honest communication turn most difficult stakeholders into allies.

Read the full chapter →
Q304.How do you document a payment flow for both business and technical readers?Intermediate

I write two versions of the same flow, because business and technical readers need different things. For the business reader, I write a simple step by step flow in plain language: the customer gives the instruction, the bank checks it, the bank sends it, the beneficiary receives it. I use a diagram with boxes and arrows, and I label each box with what happens and who does it. I include the timing: when the payment is sent, when it settles and when the customer is told. For the technical reader, I write the same flow but with the detail: the message types, the field names, the validation rules, the API calls, the error codes and the expected responses. I include a table of the data fields with the format, whether each field is mandatory and what happens when it is missing. I keep both versions linked so a reader can go from the business flow to the technical detail and back. I validate the document by asking a business user to read it and explain the flow back to me, and asking an engineer to build from it. If either of them cannot, the document needs work. Good documentation is not long. It is clear, and it answers the reader's question without them having to ask someone else.

Payments Career and Interview Preparation (16)

Q305.Tell me about a time you found a defect in a payment flow.Beginner

I found it during user acceptance testing, before go live, which is exactly when you want to find it. We were testing a new payment type and the test scenario was a payment with a special character in the beneficiary name. The payment hub rejected it, which was correct, but the error message that came back to the user was a raw system code that meant nothing to anyone in operations. The payment was stuck and nobody could tell why without calling engineering. I traced the flow: the hub rejected the payment, the rejection reason was passed to the front end without translation, and the front end displayed the code as it was. I raised it as a defect with the evidence: the test case, the screenshot of the error, and the expected behaviour, which was a clear message saying the beneficiary name contains an unsupported character. I worked with engineering to map the common rejection codes to plain language messages. We retested with five different invalid inputs and confirmed each one now showed a clear message. The lesson I took from it is that a defect is not only a wrong calculation. A message the user cannot understand is also a defect, because it stops operations from doing their job.

Read the full chapter →
Q306.Tell me about a time you had to say no to a stakeholder.Beginner

I had a stakeholder who wanted a new payment feature built in two weeks, but the design needed six weeks because it touched the sanctions screening and the reconciliation. I said no to the two week date, but I did not leave it there. First, I understood why two weeks mattered: the stakeholder had promised a client a date. I explained clearly what was involved and why two weeks was not safe: the sanctions change needed compliance sign off, the reconciliation needed testing, and skipping those steps risked a regulatory breach. I showed the work broken down so the stakeholder could see it was not padding. Then I offered a phased option: in two weeks we could deliver a limited version for a small set of clients with manual controls, and the full version in six weeks. The stakeholder agreed because it met the client commitment without taking on the risk. The lesson is that saying no is not the end of the conversation. It is the start of finding a safe alternative. A BA who always says yes builds things that fail. A BA who says no with a reason and an alternative builds trust, and stakeholders come back to that BA because they know they will get an honest answer.

Read the full chapter →
Q307.Tell me about a time you improved a payment process.Beginner

I noticed that the exceptions team was spending a large part of their day manually correcting payments that failed because the beneficiary account number had a space or a dash in it. The payment hub rejected these as invalid, and an operator had to open each one, remove the space and resubmit it. I counted the volume: about 200 payments a day were failing for this reason, taking roughly two hours of operator time. I proposed a simple fix: strip spaces and dashes from the account number field at the point of entry, before validation. The rule was safe because spaces and dashes carry no meaning in an account number. I wrote the requirement, got it approved and worked with engineering to implement it. We tested it with the common variations: spaces, dashes, mixed. After go live, the failure rate for this reason dropped to near zero, and the operators got two hours a day back. The improvement was small in technical terms but large in operational terms. That is what I look for: the small friction that happens hundreds of times a day and adds up to real cost. A BA does not need to redesign the whole system to add value. Fixing a repeated manual task is often the highest value work.

Read the full chapter →
Q308.Tell me about a time you had to learn a new payment system quickly.Beginner

I was asked to work on a new instant payments system that I had never used before. I started by reading the scheme rules and the message specifications so I understood the standard. Then I asked operations to show me the current system and walked through a real payment with them, asking questions at each step. I mapped the flow on paper: where the instruction comes from, how it is validated, how it is routed, how the response comes back and what happens when it fails. I read the existing requirements and test cases to see what the system was expected to do. I asked engineering to explain the architecture in plain terms: which components exist, how they talk to each other and where the data lives. I also spoke to the vendor or scheme support to clarify the parts I did not understand. Within two weeks I could write requirements and test scenarios for the new system. The key was not trying to learn everything before starting. I learned enough to ask good questions, then I learned the rest by doing the work and checking my understanding with the people who knew the system. I also wrote down what I learned so the next person would not have to start from zero.

Read the full chapter →
Q309.Tell me about a time you disagreed with your manager about a payment design.Advanced

My manager wanted to build a new payment feature as a custom addition to the existing system. I thought that was the wrong approach because the existing system was already hard to maintain, and adding a custom feature would make it worse. I did not just disagree in a meeting. I prepared the evidence: the current system's complexity, the cost of maintaining custom code, the risk of breaking existing payments, and an alternative approach using the payment hub's standard configuration. I presented both options side by side with the pros and cons and the cost of each. My manager listened and asked questions, and we agreed to do a small proof of concept for the standard approach to confirm it could meet the requirement. The proof of concept worked, and we went with the standard approach. The lesson is that disagreeing with a manager is fine if you do it with evidence and respect. Bring the facts, propose an alternative and let the better option win. Do not disagree for the sake of it, and do not agree when you believe the decision is wrong. A good manager wants to hear the concern before the build starts, not after it goes live and fails.

Read the full chapter →
Q310.Tell me about a time you spotted a risk nobody else saw.Advanced

During a testing cycle, I noticed that the test scenarios only covered payments where the beneficiary bank was in the same country. No one had tested a payment where the beneficiary bank was in a different time zone and the value date crossed a weekend. I raised it because I knew from experience that value dating across a weekend is a common source of errors: a payment sent on Friday for a Monday value date can be processed as Friday if the system does not handle the weekend correctly. I wrote a test scenario for it and ran it. The test failed: the system applied the wrong value date, which would have meant the beneficiary received the money a day early and the bank's liquidity forecast was wrong. I raised the defect with the evidence and worked with engineering to fix the value date logic. The fix was included before go live. The lesson is that risks hide in the cases nobody thought to test. A BA adds value by thinking about the edge cases: the weekend, the holiday, the time zone, the leap year, the unusual character. I now keep a checklist of edge cases for every payment change, and I run through it before signing off the test scenarios. Spotting a risk early is far cheaper than fixing it in production.

Q311.In a job interview for a payments business analyst role, the interviewer says: tell me about yourself. How do you structure a strong answer that is not just a list of your jobs?Beginner

Use a simple three part structure: **present, past, future**. Start with the present: what you do now, in one sentence, such as I am a senior business analyst working on payments transformation at a large bank. Then go to the past: pick two or three experiences that prove you can do this job, such as I spent three years on cross border payments, I led the ISO 20022 migration analysis, and I worked with operations to cut exception rates. Keep each one short and tie it to a result. Then finish with the future: why this role, such as I want to apply that experience to your payment hub programme because it is the next step in building modern payment platforms. The whole answer should take **60 to 90 seconds**. Do not list every job on your CV, and do not start with your childhood or your degree unless it is directly relevant. The interviewer is really asking: can you summarise yourself clearly, and does your experience match this role. Practise the answer out loud until it sounds natural, not rehearsed, and always end by connecting your experience to the job you are applying for.

Read the full chapter →
Q312.The interviewer asks: tell me about the biggest payments failure you have handled. How do you answer honestly without making yourself look bad?Beginner

Use the **STAR** structure: situation, task, action, result. Describe the situation briefly, such as a cross border payment of 125,000 pounds that vanished between banks and the customer was waiting. Explain your task: to find the payment, keep the customer informed, and prevent a repeat. Then describe the **actions** you took: you traced the payment through the gpi tracker, you found it stuck at an intermediary bank because of a missing field, you raised an MT199 to the intermediary, and you gave the customer a daily update. Finish with the **result**: the payment was found and credited, the customer stayed, and you wrote a new validation rule so the missing field could not happen again. Be honest about what went wrong and what you learned, because interviewers trust candidates who own their mistakes. Do not blame other people, and do not pretend the failure was not serious. The interviewer is not looking for a perfect record. They are looking for someone who stays calm under pressure, investigates properly, communicates with the customer, and fixes the root cause so it does not happen again.

Read the full chapter →
Q313.The interviewer asks why you are leaving your current bank. You are unhappy there, but you know you should not criticise your employer. How do you answer?Beginner

Keep the answer **forward looking**, not backward looking. Talk about what you want to move towards, not what you want to escape from. A good answer is: I have learned a great deal in my current role, I have built deep experience in payments operations and ISO 20022, and now I want to apply that experience to a larger transformation programme, which is what this role offers. That is honest, positive, and it connects your experience to the job. Never criticise your current employer, your manager, or your colleagues, even if the interviewer invites you to. Interviewers hear criticism of a past employer as a warning sign, because they assume you will criticise them next. If you are asked directly about a problem, acknowledge it briefly and move on: the team was restructured, and I decided it was the right time to look for a role where I could focus on payments transformation. Keep the tone calm and professional, and always end by saying something positive about the role you are applying for, so the interviewer remembers your enthusiasm, not your frustration.
